abrege-de-la-doctrine-de-paracelse-et-de: Abregé de la doctrine de Paracelse, 1724. The Paracelsus abridgement. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
adler-practice-theory-radin-1924:
Alfred Adler published The Practice and Theory of Individual Psychology in German in the 1920s. The English text here is P. Radin's translation of 1924. The book gathers Adler's mature system in papers on therapy, childhood, and social life. Birth order, social interest, and style of life are its key ideas.

Adler argues that each child builds a unique style of striving for significance. Health lies in social interest: caring for others as equals. Case studies show his method of early recollections and dream reading. The book shaped counseling, education, and parenting advice. Adler's influence runs wide though his name is less known than Freud's.
al-baladhuri-origins-islamic-state-murgo:
Francis Clark Murgotten finished the English Futuh al-Buldan of al-Baladhuri in 1924, taking up the work Philip Hitti had begun. This second part completes the ninth-century Arabic account of the conquests that built the caliphate. Al-Baladhuri wrote at the Abbasid court from records, reports, and named chains of witnesses.

The later campaigns run east and west: the frontiers of Persia, the marches of Armenia, Sicily, and the far Maghreb. Murgotten adds the taxes, garrisons, and land terms that made conquest into a state. Together the two parts give the fullest early picture of how the Islamic empire was won and run. Hitti's project stands whole in this volume.
apocryphal-new-testament-james-1924:
M. R. James gathered the standard English collection of apocryphal New Testament writings in 1924. James, better known for his ghost stories, was also a leading manuscript scholar. His volume translates non-canonical gospels, acts, letters, and apocalypses.

Readers meet the child Jesus working miracles in the Infancy Gospel. Paul battles sorcerers, and apostles tour heaven and hell in vivid detail. These texts show how wide and varied early Christian storytelling became. Some were treasured by churches for centuries before exclusion. James's introductions explain each work's age, sources, and survival. Anyone studying early Christianity beyond the canon starts with this collection.
arabische-alchemisten-ii-gafar-alsadiq-1: Arabische Alchemisten II, Gafar Alsadiq, 1924. The Arabic alchemists. This book preserves that study. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The paper lived through the years. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
arnim-svf-vol4-1924:
A set of fragments gathered from hundreds of old books is only as good as its index. Maximilian Adler built the index volume for Hans von Arnim's Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, and it appeared in 1924 as the fourth volume of the set. It keys the Greek and Latin material of the first three volumes.

Adler listed names, subjects, and Greek terms so a reader can track one idea, such as fate or impulse, through every passage that names it. With these lists the huge collection becomes a tool a scholar can search by hand. The volume closes von Arnim's project, the standard source book for the early Stoa.
arxiv-2512-00224:
Von Neumann algebras are the mathematical home of quantum mechanics and much of operator theory. Jananan Arulseelan begins a model-theoretic study of group actions on these algebras in 2025, expanding earlier work. The focus is dynamical systems where a group acts while preserving a weight.

The author axiomatizes continuous weight-preserving actions of locally compact Hausdorff groups on von Neumann algebras. Crossed products, which build new algebras from such actions, are part of the study. Model theory can reveal which properties of these systems follow from simple logical principles, a perspective algebraists are only starting to use. Crossed products turn symmetry actions into new algebras, a construction with many physical uses.
arxiv-2512-00524:
Hierarchical clustering groups data into a tree of nested clusters, a dendrogram. Guangjie Zeng and co-authors present a hyperbolic continuous structural entropy method for the task in 2025. Most existing methods specify dendrograms without any global objective to optimize.

Graph-based methods often neglect graph structure, optimizing on complete or fixed predefined graphs instead. Structural entropy gives a principled global objective, and hyperbolic geometry suits trees naturally. A better objective could produce hierarchies that reflect real structure in networks, from biology to social graphs, rather than artifacts of greedy merging. A global objective gives the clustering a target that greedy merging lacks. Hyperbolic space expands like a tree, which is why it hosts dendrograms comfortably. For folks who sort firms, genes, or posts into trees, the gain is a tree with a point. Each split can be scored, not just drawn by habit or haste.
arxiv-2512-00624:
Hilda asteroids circle the Sun in step with Jupiter, locked in a three-to-two resonance. Alexander Fleming and co-authors study rotational light-curve recovery for these objects in 2025, and predict what a coming survey will find. The Hildas offer a window into solar system evolution, including collisional processes.

The NSF-DOE Vera Rubin Observatory will run the ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time. Knowing how many Hilda light curves the survey can recover helps plan its asteroid science. Rotation periods reveal shapes and spin states shaped by billions of years of collisions in the outer asteroid belt. Light curves encode rotation in brightness dips as an asteroid tumbles.
arxiv-2512-01224:
Ruixiang Feng and a team from a hiring platform's lab present CoSineVerifier in a 2025 paper. Answer verification is widely used in training language models, for curating data, judging evaluations, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. A verifier checks whether a model's answer is right, so its own errors matter.

Prior work built unified verifiers for many reasoning settings. Questions that hinge on computation pose special challenges, like checking algebraic equivalence and using physical constants correctly. CoSineVerifier is a tool-augmented verifier built for those cases. Calling tools to recompute answers could make checking far more reliable in math and physics.
arxiv-2512-01324:
Samuel Young and Kazuhiro Terao work on reading data from argon detectors. These tanks give dense three-dimensional views of particle hits. They back big tests on neutrinos and rare events. Reading the hits now takes long chains of hand-built steps.

Those chains need large sets of labeled fake data and slow tuning. The team offers Panda, a method that learns from the data itself. It distills sensor-level traits that can be reused across tasks. Reusable traits could cut the need for fresh labels each time. That would speed up work for next-wave neutrino tests.
arxiv-2512-01424:
Xusen Hei and co-authors build a test for fixing errors in video reasoning. Large models that mix text and video often err on hard clips. Fixing those errors is key to growth. Past tests did not score that fixing skill in a set way.

Their test, ViRectify, asks models to spot and fix wrong steps in video thought chains. It spans many kinds of clips and errors. Scores show if a model can catch its own slips. That skill matters for safe use in class, work, and media tools where a wrong read can mislead users.
arxiv-2512-02124:
The Flame Nebula region, NGC 2024, is an active stellar nursery where the newest stars still move with the cloud that bore them. Alena Rottensteiner and eight co-authors measure in 2025 the motions of its young stellar objects using infrared proper motions, the slow drift of stars across the sky.

Because these objects formed most recently, their positions and dynamics trace the parent cloud's motion with little distortion. Comparing stellar motion with the gas reveals when the two decouple, a key timescale for how clusters form and disperse. Infrared measurements matter here because dust hides these young stars from ordinary visible-light surveys.
arxiv-2512-03124:
Finding the shape of a molecule from distances is a key task. Michael Souza, Júlio Araújo, John Kesley Costa, and Carlile Lavor study a step in that task in this 2025 work. The step is the ordered covering problem in distance geometry.

The order in which edges are pruned shapes how fast a search runs. That search, called SBBU, is used to find protein structures. The authors study how hard the ordering problem is in theory. Knowing its difficulty helps builders design better tools for protein work, where speed can decide if a method is practical. Better ordering tools could shorten the search for protein shapes from distance data.
arxiv-2512-03224:
Electric signals in brain tissue depend on its fine structure. Halvor Herlyng and co-authors model ion flow in dense reconstructions of cerebral tissue in this 2025 work. Brain tissue is so complex in shape that detailed modeling is a formidable task.

The team needs efficient numerical methods and robust code to handle real cell shapes. Their model covers electrodiffusion, the joint flow of ions and electric fields. Faithful models can explain how signals spread and where models of the brain go wrong. They also guide safer brain stimulation methods. Real tissue shapes, not idealized blocks, decide whether a model matches brain signals.
arxiv-2512-03324:
Long answers from language models need lots of memory. Ngoc Bui and co-authors present a smarter way to keep that memory small in this 2025 work. The key-value cache grows with text length, and self-attention costs rise fast.

Old fixes quantize, offload, or drop entries by rough attention scores, each with drawbacks. The authors keep tokens that last, based on lasting value rather than fleeting attention. Keeping the right tokens could let models handle long documents on limited hardware. That matters for chat and research tools. Token choice is a budget call, since each kept token costs memory through the whole reply.
arxiv-2512-03524:
Self-driving fleets run by competing firms could destabilize traffic. Grzegorz Jamróz, Rafał Kucharski, and David Watling model that risk in this 2025 work. Drivers may switch between individual routing and collective routing run by a fleet operator.

In individual routing, drivers pick routes that minimize their own travel costs. In collective routing, an operator assigns routes centrally to maximize market share. The authors study the dynamics and equilibria of this routing game. Their warning matters for cities planning rules for autonomous fleets. Chaos in routing would hurt all drivers, not just fleet customers, in dense cities.
arxiv-2601-06624:
Marco Martinelli and two co-authors find a cheap way to grade name linking in a 2026 paper. Name linking is a core step in pulling facts from health texts. Grading it at scale is hard, for two clear reasons they name.

Skilled graders cost a lot, and the text sets are huge in size. Their test case is GutBrainIE, a health fact set on gut and brain. They grade by sampling, which gives a sound grade at low cost. The grade comes with a known margin and a fixed budget of grading hours. Teams need not grade each line to trust the score for the whole set. The plan suits any large text set where skilled help is scarce. It makes honest quality scores cheap enough to use often.
arxiv-2601-06924:
Research by Hedieh Abdollahi and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with isaac newton telescope monitoring survey of local group dwarf galaxies – VIII.. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors present a comprehensive catalog, in the Sloan i i and Harris V V filters. Of long-period variable (LPV) stars in the spheroidal dwarf satellites of the Andromeda galaxy.

Based on a dedicated survey for variable stars in Local Group dwarf systems. Using photometric time-series data obtained with the Wide Field Camera (WFC) on the 2. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07024:
Dario Borrelli wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on graphs that grow by a copy-and-change rule. In such a graph, a node is copied, and some of its links are then lost or kept. The two steps are called duplication and divergence. Borrelli asks how large the biggest linked chunk of the graph can grow.

The copy rule here is paired, so the loss on one side mirrors the loss on the other. As the rate of loss shifts, the graph hits a sharp change point. Past that point, the biggest chunk acts in a new way. Borrelli finds that point by a size-scaling test. The rate at the change sits near the place where a graph count called the Euler characteristic hits zero. That count is known to mark this kind of shift in graphs of set size.
arxiv-2601-07624:
Chris Lambie-Hanson and Pedro Marun study which topological properties survive when a mathematical universe is extended by forcing. Forcing is a set theory method that builds new models with chosen features. A property preserved under forcing stays true in every such extension. Their 2026 preprint answers a question posed by Gilton and Holshouser, in a strong form.

The focus is on games played on topological spaces, including the strong countable fan tightness game. If player II has a winning strategy at a point, the authors show it persists in every set forcing extension. The same holds for the Rothberger game, but not for two related games. Such fine distinctions map the border between stable and fragile properties. Set theorists and topologists are the intended readers.
arxiv-2601-07824:
Piotr Sierant, Jofre Vallès-Muns, and Artur Garcia-Saez compute how magical a quantum state is. Magic, formally non-stabilizerness, measures how far a state departs from the easily simulated stabilizer set. It is a central resource behind quantum advantage. It also probes the complexity of quantum many-body states. Standard measures include stabilizer Rényi entropy for qubits and mana for qutrits.

Those measures are costly to evaluate numerically. Their cost grows rapidly with the number of qudits in the system. Faster computation would let scholars map magic across larger states and devices. Knowing where magic sits helps explain when quantum computers beat classical ones. The paper serves quantum information scientists who benchmark resources. It tackles a measurement problem that limits how magic can be studied at scale.
arxiv-2601-08424: Roohani Sharma and Michal Wlodarczyk revisit protrusion decompositions for graph deletion problems. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies F-deletion, where k vertices are removed so no minor from a finite family remains. Protrusions are well-structured graph parts that kernelization algorithms can shrink safely. The authors derive uniform lossy kernels for reducing treewidth. They also give linear kernels for hitting disconnected minors. Kernels matter because they shrink huge inputs to small cores before exact solving, making hard graph problems practical.
arxiv-2601-08524:
Richard Stiskalek and co-authors revisit the Great Attractor with digital twins of the nearby universe. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses the Manticore-Local simulation suite. The Great Attractor idea has been asked to answer three distinct questions at once.

First, what sources the Local Group's velocity in the cosmic microwave background frame. Second, where present-day velocity streamlines converge. Third, where the Local Group is actually moving to. Separating these questions matters because one attractor may not answer all three. The simulations trace the Local Group's streamline trajectory and dynamical fate, giving cosmologists a cleaner account of our cosmic motion.
arxiv-2601-08624: Mauro Barbieri and Abraham Loeb point out a rare alignment of the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes the object will align with the Earth-Sun axis on January 22, 2026. The angle is exceptionally small, just 0.69 degrees. Such near-opposition geometry offers unique circumstances for observation. Astronomers can measure the opposition surge, a brightness spike at tiny phase angles. They can also measure polarimetric properties of interstellar cometary dust, testing how material from another star system scatters light.
arxiv-2601-08824:
Kenta Kasai works on quantum codes that guard data spread in a sparse net. In plain codes, a known trick links the shape of the net to both good fix work and long safe span. Round loops in the net help on both counts. In quantum codes, a rule that parts must cross at right angles blocks that trick.

Kasai looks for a way past that right angle wall. The goal is a quantum code that keeps the sparse ease of plain codes, yet gains the loop gains that plain codes enjoy. Such a code would fix flaws well and guard data far. A reader in quantum codes gets a new path past a long held bound. It may shape how next codes are built.
arxiv-2601-09224:
Eung Jin Chun gives a joint birth tale for the stuff of space and for the mass we can not see. Space holds more plain mass than star counts can explain. That gap is the baryon asymmetry, why stuff beat anti stuff in the early cosmos. Dark stuff is a next gap, a hid mass that holds galaxies. Two gaps may share one cause.

His tale turns on the QCD axion, a light bit set to solve a deep force ask. Early spin of that field, sped by growth era pulls, can yield both gaps at once. The frame ties that spin to the seesaw path for neutrino mass. A reader in cosmos work gets one cause for two gaps.
arxiv-2601-09624:
Jiali Cheng, Ziheng Chen, Chirag Agarwal, and Hadi Amiri ask why some facts resist being unlearned. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies machine unlearning, the removal of chosen data from a trained language model. Success varies sharply by sample: some items erase cleanly, others persist.

The authors argue the gap is not only about the data. Internal mechanisms in the model can encode and protect memorized content. They take a mechanistic view and propose a circuit-guided difficulty metric. Knowing which items will resist erasure helps firms meet privacy and compliance duties honestly.
arxiv-2601-10524:
Frank Bobe III, Gregory Vetaw, and Chase Pavlick probe why tuned models fail on new data, with phishing hunts as the test. Fine tune steps can make a model top at one task. Yet the same model can break on a slight shift in the data. Why it breaks is oft not clear.

The team use a multi layer probe frame. They fine tune a Llama model and kin on phishing texts. They then test each net form for where skill is lost. The aim is to name the parts that make a tuned model frail. That may guide tunes that hold up more well.
arxiv-2601-10724:
Rishabh Dev Yadav, Viswa N. Sankaranarayanan, and Spandan Roy study control for platoons of self-driving vehicles. A platoon is a line of cars that drive close together under shared control. The road grip each car feels is uncertain and changes with its state. That unknown friction can shake the line's spacing and safety.

The work develops adaptive sliding mode control that copes with state-dependent friction uncertainty. It grows out of Yadav's master's thesis at IIIT Hyderabad from 2023. A shorter version ran at the ICAR 2021 robotics conference. The control design aims to keep each car at its set gap even as grip shifts beneath it.
arxiv-2601-11224:
Barbara Dietz, Dung Xuan Nguyen, and Tilen Cadez study scarred states in billiard systems. Their 2026 preprint sets relativistic cases next to plain ones. A scar is a state that piles up along a classical orbit. The team looks at neutrino billiards and at graphene ones.

A third case uses Haldane graphene billiards for compare runs. In the range near the Fermi energy, the physics is linear. There all three cases share one Dirac equation for light spin-half parts. The authors also sum up scars for the plain quantum case. Those use the shape of a full stadium and a quarter stadium. The side-by-side view shows what the speed of light changes in scars.
arxiv-2601-11524:
L. Schilcher, P. Waldert, B. Kantz, and T. Schreck build a dashboard for patient data. Their 2026 preprint is named Clusters in Focus. Exploring tables to find cohorts is key in biomarker discovery. Feature pairs split patients into groups in many such hunts.

Comparing clusters across many feature pair views is hard. A dashboard must keep detail on demand, simple and robust. The team's tool does just that for tabular patient data. Users can focus on one projection and pull detail as needed. Cohorts can then be checked across views with less strain. The work comes from Graz University of Technology. It aims at clinical data work that stays readable.
arxiv-2601-11724:
Muditha Fernando, Kajhanan Kailainathan, Krishnakanth Nagaratnam, Isuranga Senavirathne, and Ranga Rodrigo work on a hard learning task. A model must learn from few marked cases and still work on new domains it has not seen. This task is called semi-supervised domain generalization in the field.

Their method, named SemAlign in the work, is guided by language. Past work shows two chief risks in this task. One is wrong tags made for unmarked cases. The other is a model that fits its training data too well and fails on new data. The new method aims to cut both risks at once.
arxiv-2601-11824:
A. Brennan, L. Matrà, S. Mac Manamon, and the ARKS team report new views of the debris disk round the star HD 121617. Debris disks are rings of dust and rock left round young stars. About twenty such disks show carbon monoxide gas, split into gas-poor and gas-rich kinds.

HD 121617 is gas-rich, so it is a key case in the ARKS survey. That survey uses the ALMA array to map fine rings in such disks. Fine maps can show gaps and clumps made by unseen planets. The work adds one rich case to that map set.
arxiv-2601-11924:
Ming Shi studies shared bandit tasks where reward data can be spoiled. Many agents pick arms over many rounds and share what they learn. Each reward is a vector, so more than one goal is in play. A foe can spoil the shared data, but only up to a set total budget.

A check step can test some data, but checks are scarce. Shi links how much spoil is used with how checks are placed. The work aims for methods that still learn well under attack. Such guards help shared learning in open, risky nets.
arxiv-2601-12224:
Meng Wei, Kun Yuan, Shi Li, and a large team find surgical tools in video by how they move, from a text brief. Language-led work with surgical scenes could aid smart operating rooms and robot help. The task is to cut out the tool named in words.

Past tools rest on static visual cues and fixed tool names. Those fail on new tools and phrasing. Motion gives a strong extra cue, since the used tool is the one that moves with intent. The team's motion-led method aims to generalize better.
arxiv-2601-12424:
William Dorrell and James Whittington review a puzzle from neuroscience: grid cells. These neurons fire in a neat hexagonal pattern as an animal moves. For twenty years, that pretty code has raised a basic question. What computation does this pattern serve, and why does it take this curious form?

The first answer came fast: grid cells track position as an animal moves. That skill is called path integration. Dorrell and Whittington survey normative theories, which ask what an ideal system should do. Such theories try to derive the grid pattern from a goal, not just describe it. Their review weighs how well that project has worked so far.
arxiv-2601-12724:
Rishabh Iyer works on set functions that come from entropy, a core idea in the theory of data and codes. Shannon entropy is one such function, and it has a clean shape that math can use. But the set of all such entropy based functions is smaller than some had hoped. A newer frame stretches entropy style measures to a wider class of set functions.

Those wider measures have found many uses in the past few years. Teams use them to pick data, to guide learning, and to shift a model to a new domain. Iyer gives hands on forms of them for three classic tasks. The tasks are coverage, facility location, and graph cuts. Clear forms let users plug proven measures straight into real tools.
arxiv-2601-13124:
Donglei Du, Qizhi Fang, Bin Liu, Tianhang Lu, and Chenchen Wu sort the core of a broad class of games where pay offs bend. In game theory the core is the set of splits that no group can beat by breaking off. For straight line games the core is well known.

For bent games the core was far less clear. The team finds a fit loosening of the bent form. With it they give a full mark of when the core holds and what it holds. Their result grows the set of joint games that can be read in this way. It also links to games that spring from opt tasks, a rich source in trade and nets.
arxiv-2601-13224:
Michael Hanus and Steven Libby ease the work of tools that reshape code. Compilers, code probes, and proof tools all walk a code tree and change nodes as they go. To write such walks by hand is slow and prone to flaws. Each tool must loop the whole tree and act at the right nodes.

Hanus and Libby work in functional logic programming, a style that joins two code styles. They give ways to state code reshapes in a more brief and safe form. Their aim is less boiler plate for tool builders. For language tool teams, clean reshape rules mean tools that are more quick to build and more safe to change.
arxiv-2601-13424:
A. Martinez-Mendez and co-authors cut waste in the vast compute pool of the LAGO project. LAGO is a Latin American watch for high energy bits from space. It runs heavy sims on high performance clusters. Such sims eat time, power, and funds, so yield per run counts for both science and green aims.

The team counts where cluster time goes in the LAGO set up. They then tune how jobs are placed and run to lift yield. Their marks are tied to astroparticle sims, which have long runs and big data. For big sim teams, the work shows how yield checks pay off in more science per watt.
arxiv-2601-13624:
A team with Xin Zhang weighs two puzzles in the study of the early universe in 2026. One is cosmic birefringence, a slight twist in the light left from the Big Bang. The twist would link the two modes of that light in a new way. Such a link is a sign of parity violation, a break in mirror symmetry.

The team joins data from ACT, Planck, DESI, and PantheonPlus to set joint limits. They test birefringence next to early dark energy, a brief extra push in the young cosmos. New high-grade sky data make such fine effects worth a fresh look. Joint limits keep one puzzle from skewing the other.
arxiv-2601-14024:
Sergio López-Baños and co-authors boost a hybrid quantum-classical solver for hard planning problems in 2026. Mixed-integer linear programming, or MILP, is used widely in industry optimization. As problems grow larger, classical solvers struggle within practical time limits. Quantum annealers could in principle accelerate some of these tasks.

The problems map to quadratic unconstrained binary optimization instances for annealers. Limited annealer scale currently prevents practical speedups. The team enhances the hybrid Benders' algorithm, which splits a problem into parts. Better splits may bring quantum help closer to real industrial use. The split must be smart, or the gain is lost in extra work. Their tests show where the split helps most and where it does not.
arxiv-2601-14124:
Saad Mankarious and Ayah Zirikly use style transfer to build mental health text data in Arabic in 2026. Synthetic data promises a fix for data scarcity and demographic bias. Existing approaches rely largely on pretrained large language models. Those models may suffer limited output diversity in what they generate.

They may also propagate biases inherited from their training data. The team uses diffusion models for synthetic mental health text instead. Style transfer can recast real text in new voices while keeping content. Fair Arabic datasets could improve mental health tools for Arabic speakers.
arxiv-2601-14224:
Sahel Sharifymoghaddam and Jimmy Lin study where deep search agents should spend their compute in 2026. Deep research agents rely on iterative retrieval and reasoning to answer complex queries. Scaling test-time computation raises significant efficiency concerns for them. The team studies how to allocate reasoning budget in deep search pipelines.

Listwise reranking, which reorders a whole list of results at once, is their focus. They analyze reranking tradeoffs through effective token cost. Their title gives the advice: rerank before you reason. Spending tokens on better sources first may beat deeper thought on poor ones.
arxiv-2601-14724:
Haowei Zhang, Shudong Yang, Jinlan Fu, and their co-authors present a video understanding system in this 2026 paper. Streaming video understanding means answering questions about a video while it still plays. Long streams strain the KV cache, the memory a model keeps for past frames. HERMES treats that cache as a hierarchical memory.

HERMES is a training-free approach, so it needs no new model training. It reuses the KV cache and performs hierarchical management of the video tokens stored in it. Key tokens stay at fine detail, while older ones are compressed in tiers. Readers get stable, efficient inference for long videos, where naive systems run out of memory or forget the plot.
arxiv-2601-15024:
Nipun Agarwal reviews how to keep wireless links private when the listener stays silent. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with massive MIMO, a system where a base station uses a great many antennas. The tech drives 5G and later networks, with big gains in spectrum and energy use.

A passive eavesdropper never transmits, so the station cannot learn its channel. That makes secure links hard to promise. Agarwal surveys the known challenges at the physical layer. He also sets out open research directions for guarding these systems against such silent, hidden listeners.
arxiv-2601-15324:
Mark Wind bolts a memory onto a language model without touching its weights. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a common problem: adding memory to a pre-trained model usually means changing its architecture or its weights. Prometheus Mind takes a different route.

The base model, a Qwen3-4B, stays frozen. Eleven modular adapters add the memory, at seven percent overhead, and removing them undoes the change. Building the system took four fixes. One finds semantic directions from minimal pairs with no labeled data. Another trains each adapter in stages, since end-to-end training collapses.
arxiv-2601-15424:
Juan Gomez Quispe, Matheus Medina, and co-authors tune carbon sheets to make hydrogen production cheaper. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with graphynes, carbon frameworks that mix two bond types. The mix gives distinct electronic regimes and site-selective reactivity across the sheet.

The team studies the hydrogen evolution reaction, a key step in splitting water. They dope two graphyne forms with boron, nitrogen, or both. Density functional theory and reactive molecular dynamics simulations judge each doped variant in turn. The goal is to control both the reaction's activity and the material's stability.
arxiv-2601-15524:
Ni An, Bhola Nath Saha, and Bidyut Sanki work on curves on hyperbolic surfaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are filling pairs. A filling pair is two simple closed curves in minimal position. Cut the surface along both curves, and what remains is a union of topological disks. Nothing else is left over. Such pairs are basic tools in the study of surfaces.

The title names the paper's goal: length minimization for these pairs. Among all filling pairs on a surface, which ones are shortest? The abstract in the record states the definition and little more. Readers should expect a specialist geometry paper with proofs at its core. Short filling pairs give concrete ways to measure and compare surfaces.
arxiv-2601-15724:
Chenglin Li and a large team build video models that use tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-form video remains a hard problem for video language models. Most models reason over uniformly sampled frames. That static approach weakens timing: they cannot pinpoint when things happen. It also loses much information in long videos. The team's system is called VideoThinker. It is built as an agentic VideoLLM.

Agentic tools let the model explore a video adaptively. The tools include temporal retrieval, spatial zoom, and temporal zoom. Guided by a language model, the system picks where to look closer. That mirrors how a person scans a long recording. For tasks like surveillance review or lecture search, active looking beats uniform sampling.
arxiv-2601-15824:
Joan Vendrell Farreny and colleagues at NeuralTrust propose a new security layer in a 2026 arXiv paper. They call it the Generative Application Firewall, or GAF. It is an architectural layer for securing language model applications. Existing defenses are fragmented, they argue. Prompt filters, guardrails, and data masking each guard one spot. GAF unifies them into a single enforcement point.

The model is the web application firewall. A WAF coordinates defenses for web traffic in one place. GAF aims to do the same for generative apps. It also covers autonomous agents and their tool interactions. Agent actions are a new attack surface that old tools miss. For security teams, one chokepoint is easier to audit than scattered patches.
arxiv-2601-15924:
Brainard Philemon Jagati and four co-authors fix learning on skewed class data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep networks degrade badly under long-tailed distributions. A few head classes dominate the training data. Tail classes get very few examples. The model then masters the common and fumbles the rare. Their method is class-confidence aware reweighting, per the title. Training examples are reweighted by class and by model confidence.

Reweighting shifts attention toward what the model gets wrong. Class awareness counters the head classes' bulk. Confidence awareness focuses on uncertain cases. Rare classes matter in medicine and safety, where the rare event is often the important one. Methods that lift tail performance without hurting the head are in real demand.
arxiv-2601-16324:
Rebecca Lopez and coauthors screen student minds with Fitbit data from the plague years. Their 2026 preprint deals with stress in college life. High stress drives high rates of fear and low mood in students. Wear gear gives quiet sense data through the day. Such data could flag ill minds at an early stage.

Past work used few mind tests and few body sense types. The team widens both the tests and the sense types in use. Wide data should give a more true screen of mind state. Early flags could guide help to students in time. The work uses data drawn in the COVID span.
arxiv-2601-16724:
Kevin Fan and Eric Yun study bias in machines that grade essays. Schools now use such tools for tests with high stakes. Tools trained on native speech can grade harshly. Students who learn English as a new tongue may lose marks. Their style traits get read as flaws. Their 2026 preprint seeks a fairer way to grade.

The team uses a learn-by-contrast trick in training. The trick pulls the tool's eye to real skill. It pushes the eye off surface traits of new learners. Fair grades guard life paths like school seats and jobs. This work shows one path to tame such bias in code.
arxiv-2601-16824:
Rongjun Ma, Shijing He, Jose Luis Martin-Navarro, Xiao Zhan, and Jose Such study love chats with AI. Apps now sell AI partners for romance and chat. Folks share deep, private woes with these bots. The risks of that share stay little known. Their 2026 preprint draws on talks with users of such apps.

The talks span first tries, close bonds, and break-ups. Users told what they share and what they guard. They also told who they think holds power in the bond. Their tales show where privacy lines blur with bots. The work can guide safe design for such apps.
arxiv-2601-17124:
Bin Lin and a large team fix a split in how AI makes shots. Shot bots come in two camps with a wall twixt them. One camp builds shots step by step from codes. The next camp spreads noise to shots in a smooth wash. Code roots split too, in VQ and plain forms. Their 2026 preprint heals one such code form, FSQ. A one-line code change does the work.

The fix is named iFSQ. It aims to lift shot grade from code-based bots. Fair tests twixt camps need such shared ground. Small fixes with big gains are prized in code work. The team shares the change for all to use.
arxiv-2601-17424:
Hanamichi Kawamura links two deep tools in the theory of multiple zeta values. Brown's lifting method solves double shuffle equations one level up. It builds full solutions from linearized ones, modulo products. Kawamura shows this method fits in Ecalle's dimorphic transportation frame. That frame moves structures between two unlike worlds while keeping their core.

A shared frame can make hard proofs shorter. It can also move results from one field to the other. Multiple zeta values sit at a crossroads of algebra and number theory. Tools that unify their study draw wide interest. Kawamura's link gives researchers a new path through old equations. It may spark fresh attacks on open cases.
arxiv-2601-17624: Sean McGuinness studies short rainbow circuits in regular matroids. His 2026 preprint takes up a conjecture of DeVos and co-authors. The setting colors the elements of a simple regular matroid with one more color than its rank, each color used at least twice. The claim under study is that a rainbow circuit, one using each color at most once, must exist with a bounded small size.
arxiv-2601-17824:
Saber Zerhoudi, Michael Dinzinger, Michael Granitzer, and Jelena Mitrović build a search tool that lets users set the bounds of what it reads. Their 2026 preprint presents OwlerLite, a browser-based system for retrieval-augmented generation. Such systems let a language model pull facts from outside sources as it answers. Most of them search a fixed index that can be stale, and users cannot choose the sources.

OwlerLite puts source scope and freshness at the center of the design. Users can say which sources count and how new the material must be. That control cuts the risk of answers that mix trusted and weak sources. It also cuts the risk of basing replies on old facts. The tool runs in the browser itself.
arxiv-2601-18024:
P. Brearley and T. L. Howarth give a method for writing hard operators as sums of easy ones. Their 2026 preprint deals with linear combinations of unitaries. Quantum computers can run unitary operators directly, but many tasks need non-unitary ones. Writing a non-unitary operator as a weighted sum of unitaries is a standard trick. The cost of the trick hinges on how fast the sum's error shrinks.

The authors base their split on a smooth periodic extension of the identity map. A Fourier extension gives a sine series whose terms decay very fast. Fast decay means fewer terms for the same accuracy. That saving matters for quantum algorithms that use the trick at their core.
arxiv-2601-19124:
Sang T. Nguyen, Nguyen Q. Pham, and Tho Quan build translation between Vietnamese and the Bahnaric language. The Bahnar people are an ethnic minority in Vietnam with a deep ancestral heritage. Their language holds great cultural and historical weight, and the state backs efforts to keep it alive and online across generations.

The team pairs sentence level data augmentation with a transformer based design. More training pairs, grown with care, help a model learn a low resource tongue. Machine translation for small languages is a preservation tool: it keeps the language usable in the digital spaces where young speakers live.
arxiv-2601-19324:
Zhen-Yang Peng and Mehdi Abdi propose a quantum device where a vibrating graphene sheet steers supercurrent. Graphene Josephson junctions join two superconductors with a graphene bridge. Here the bridge is a membrane that can flex, and its motion couples to the circuit.

The flexing of the membrane controls how Cooper pairs tunnel through, giving a strong, tunable link between motion and current. The link stays strong even at the level of zero point motion, the faintest jitter quantum rules allow. Such devices could turn tiny motions into readable signals, or cool and control motion with circuits.
arxiv-2601-19424:
Taylor J. Hoyt and five co-authors measure the home galaxies of two thousand Type Ia supernovae in one consistent way. Type Ia blasts serve as distance markers for the cosmos, judged from their light curves over time. The traits of the galaxy each blast lived in can shift that judgment, so they must be measured with care.

The Union3.1 work applies one self consistent method across the whole set. Uniform measures let cosmologists correct the distance scale without method noise. Sharper distances feed the long debate over how fast the universe expands and what drives that growth.
arxiv-2601-19924:
Yitian Chen and four colleagues probe the limits of language models at optimization modeling. Turning a word problem into equations a solver can crack is a skilled task. Language models have progressed fast at it, spawning new methods and benchmarks. Yet the boundaries of their ability remain poorly understood, especially as problems grow complex.

Their benchmark, OPT-Engine, scales problem complexity in a controlled way. Watching where models break reveals which ingredients defeat them: size, structure, or wording. Real-world tasks are exactly where benchmarks are thinnest. A scaling view helps users judge when to trust a model's formulation. It also directs research toward the failure modes that matter most.
arxiv-2601-20224:
Yi Zhang, Weicheng Lin, and Liang-Jie Zhang study how to adapt vision-language models like CLIP to new tasks with little labeled data. CLIP learns from images and text together and extracts features that transfer well. The challenge is to reuse that knowledge downstream without full retraining.

The authors propose feature projection learning as the adaptation route. Better light-weight adaptation would let small teams use strong pretrained models on their own tasks. It also cuts the compute and data needed to reach good accuracy, which widens access to modern vision-language tools.
arxiv-2601-20324:
Jingyuan Zhou, Haoze Wu, and Kaidi Yang work on formal safety guarantees for neural network controllers in large interconnected systems. Such controllers are hard to certify, above all when many units interact. The authors use neural certificates that capture cooperative behavior between units, expressing the idea of reaching a goal while avoiding bad states.

The challenge is twofold: the certificates must model cooperation, and they must be verified at scale. Existing methods fall short on both fronts, the authors argue. Progress here would let engineers deploy learned controllers in grids, traffic, and robot fleets with proof-backed safety.
arxiv-2601-20524:
Matic Fučka, Vitjan Zavrtanik, and Danijel Skočaj present AnomalyVFM, which turns vision foundation models into zero-shot anomaly detectors. Zero-shot detection must find and locate abnormal regions in an image with no training images from that domain. Recent methods lean on vision-language models like CLIP to transfer high-level concepts.

Methods based on purely visual foundation models, such as DINOv2, have lagged behind. The authors aim to close that gap. Strong zero-shot detection matters in medicine and industry, where defects are rare and labeled examples of each new fault cannot be gathered in advance.
arxiv-2601-20924:
Yuya Kusuki, Sridip Pal, and Hiroyasu Tajima build measures for how much a quantum state breaks a symmetry. Their 2026 paper works in quantum resource theory. That frame gives strict rules for such measures. The measures describe phases, far-from-balance dynamics, and open systems. The authors start with a warning case. One known measure, the second-Rényi entanglement asymmetry, can grow under symmetric steps.

A measure that grows under free steps cannot serve alone. It should not by itself capture the Quantum Mpemba effect. That effect is the odd faster cooling of some hotter states. The paper moves past the flawed measure toward stronger ones. Its title promises measures of both weak and strong symmetry breaking. The work sharpens tools used to grade quantum order.
arxiv-2601-21124:
Artem Dementyev and five co-authors give multimodal models ears that work on any device. Their 2026 paper presents PhaseCoder, a spatial audio encoder. Current multimodal LLMs process audio as a mono stream. That ignores the rich spatial information vital for embodied AI. Existing spatial audio models fix the opposite problem poorly. They are constrained to fixed microphone geometries. A model trained for one array fails on another.

PhaseCoder is a transformer-only encoder that ignores geometry differences. It reads phase cues that reveal where sounds come from. Any microphone layout can feed it. That frees spatial hearing from bespoke hardware. Robots and glasses with unlike mic arrays could share one model. The work brings direction-aware listening to general multimodal AI.
arxiv-2601-21324:
Mengqi Chen, Thomas B. Berrett, Theodoros Damoulas, and Michele Caprio make robust decision tools safer to use with messy data. Robust methods plan for the worst case inside a set of plausible data patterns. A classic way to model contamination lets a small share of points be arbitrary.

That freedom can blow the worst case up to infinity and make the whole exercise useless. The authors build ambiguity sets that can be calibrated in bulk. Their sets stay firm without demanding strong extra assumptions. The payoff is robust choices that remain fast to compute and honest about dirty data.
arxiv-2601-21424:
Anderson de Andrade, Alon Harell, and Ivan V. Bajić apply a classic idea from information theory to modern image coding. Many vision tasks share much of the same information in an image. Standard codecs ignore that overlap and store the same content again and again.

The Gray-Wyner network splits shared content from task-specific detail. The authors make that split learnable and lossy, tuned for real compression. A coder that stores shared parts once can serve many tasks from one stream. That saves bandwidth and storage for systems like camera networks, where the same scene feeds many different analyses.
arxiv-2601-21624:
Vasileios Sevetlidis and George Pavlidis survey the hidden memory inside deep learning training. Training is often treated as if each update stood alone. In truth, updates depend on optimizer state, data order, and a trail of auxiliary records.

The survey sorts these memory mechanisms by source, lifetime, and how visible they are. Teacher averages, contrastive queues, and normalization statistics all carry traces of the past. Staged augmentation and replay policies do too. Mapping this memory matters because it shapes results, reproducibility, and even privacy, yet it is rarely measured in a unified way.
arxiv-2601-21724:

arxiv-2601-21824:
Xinwei Qiang and co-authors address a quiet cost in training large language models: determinism. arxiv-2601-21924:
Jinhang Chai, Enpei Zhang, Elynn Chen, and Yujun Yan study how a learning agent can borrow experience from related tasks. The team's 2026 preprint uses a superconducting quantum processor to probe entanglement and symmetries in random states. Angel Reyero Lobo, Bertrand Thirion, and Pierre Neuvial test whether two variables are independent given others. Conditional independence testing guards scientific discovery against spurious findings. Recent methods use machine learning models as stand-ins for the data distribution.

arxiv-2601-23224:

Adaptive termination is part of the design, so the system stops searching once the evidence is sufficient for an answer.

brazilian-constitution-1824:
Brazil received its first constitution in 1824, granted by Emperor Pedro the First two years after independence from Portugal. An elected assembly had drafted a charter the emperor disliked, so he dissolved it and issued his own through a council of state. The result made Brazil a constitutional monarchy, the New World's great exception.

The text divides power among legislature, executive, and courts, then adds a fourth, the moderating power, held by the emperor above the rest. Catholicism is the state religion, with other faiths tolerated in private. Property and civil rights receive formal guards. The charter governed Brazil for sixty-five years, longer than any later Brazilian constitution. It was the empire's founding law, order and hierarchy under the Braganza crown, and it steadied a vast new nation through a difficult century.
byron-don-juan-1824:
Lord Byron began Don Juan in 1818 and kept adding cantos until his death in 1824. He wrote it in ottava rima, an eight-line stanza that suits jokes as well as high drama. Sixteen cantos were published in his lifetime, and the poem was never finished.

Young Juan is sent abroad after a scandal and stumbles through shipwreck, slavery, love affairs, and war. Unlike the cold seducer of older tales, Byron's Juan is mostly the one being seduced. The narrator keeps interrupting with witty attacks on poets, politicians, and British manners. Many readers call it Byron's masterpiece and the greatest comic poem in English.
carnot-reflexions-puissance-motrice-1824:
Sadi Carnot asks how much work heat can do in his Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, in French from 1824. A young engineer studies the steam engine's limits with a philosopher's depth. His cycle of expansion and compression sets the most that any heat engine could ever yield in theory.

From that simple model grew the second law of thermodynamics in time. Carnot died young, and his book was nearly lost before men of science grasped it. Few works of physics match its reach from so slim a start. Written at twenty-eight, it stands as the founding text of a whole science of heat and energy.

Speculum Mentis, published in 1924, is Collingwood's map of knowledge: a mirror of the mind surveying its own forms in order. Art, religion, science, history, and philosophy are arranged as stages of a single dialectic.

Each form, Collingwood argues, claims to be the whole truth and fails in a characteristic way, driving the mind onward to the next. History stands high in his order, with philosophy as the self-knowledge of the whole. The book is ambitious, schematic, and alive with a young system-builder's energy. Collingwood later disowned parts of it, but it remains his most Hegelian and most daring work.

Legal Foundations of Capitalism, published in 1924, is the masterwork of John Commons. The Wisconsin economist had spent a career arguing that markets do not run on nature alone. In this book he gives that argument its full legal and historical form.

cooper-pilot-1824:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Pilot in 1824, answering readers who thought no American could match the sea tales of Walter Scott. Cooper had served in the navy himself and knew ships from the deck up. He modeled his mysterious pilot on John Paul Jones, the Revolution's great naval raider.

An American frigate cruises the English coast on a secret mission, guided by a stranger whose seamanship borders on magic. Raids, chases, and narrow escapes fill the action, while two young officers court English ladies ashore. Cooper's exact knowledge of sails, winds, and naval discipline made the book a revelation. The Pilot is the first sea novel in American literature and a direct ancestor of the tradition that led to Moby-Dick.

Two writers, David Davidson and Herbert Aldersmith, joined forces in 1924 on The Great Pyramid: Its Divine Message. Their first volume, Pyramid Records, runs to 568 pages. It tries to read the great stone tomb of Egypt as a storehouse of hidden measure and meaning.

Davidson and Aldersmith work through old documents and dig reports, matching them against the pyramid's own dimensions. They sought to square Flinders Petrie's careful survey with the claims of Charles Piazzi Smyth, the best known pyramid writer before them. Fans of pyramid studies still treat the volume as a key summing-up of that school.
defoe-general-history-of-the-pyrates-172:
Charles Johnson published A General History of the Pyrates in 1724, long attributed to Defoe. The history covers Blackbeard, Bartholomew Roberts, and the golden age of piracy in the Atlantic world. It is the source of nearly every pirate myth that later books and films repeat today.

Johnson gives lives of some thirty captains, from Avery and Kidd to Bonnet and Rackham in turn. Misson and his utopian colony of Libertalia mix fable with fact in its early chapters here. Battles, trials, and scaffold speeches fill the record with color no archive could fully check later. The Jolly Roger, buried gold, and the pirate code all trace to these vivid pages in print. Scholars still mine it, warily, as the best near-source on the pirates' brief reign.
defoe-roxana-1724:
Daniel Defoe published Roxana in 1724, his last and darkest novel of a fortunate mistress. The tale tracks the Fortunate Mistress and her slow moral collapse into guilt and dread. Critics call it the first novel of bourgeois guilt in English prose fiction of the age.

Roxana, left penniless with five children, becomes mistress to landlords, merchants, and a prince abroad. Her maid Amy urges the hard choices, and Roxana grows rich while her conscience rots in silence. A Dutch merchant offers honest marriage, which she dodges to keep her wealth and false rank. Her lost daughter Susan hunts her, and the close is a masterpiece of dread and evasion. Defoe lets no easy repentance wash this heroine clean at the end.
defoe-tour-of-great-britain-1724:
Daniel Defoe published A Tour thro' the Whole Island of Great Britain in parts from 1724. The pioneering work of travel writing and social observation surveys Britain before the Industrial Revolution changed it. Defoe traveled as a spy, a trader, and a journalist, and the Tour uses all three eyes.

He rides county by county through ports, fairs, mines, and new estates, counting trade at every stop. Roads, rivers, and manufactures matter more to him than ruins, though no curiosity escapes his brisk pen. London's growth, Scottish union, and the cloth towns get the fullest and most forward-looking treatment in the Tour. His Britain is busy, trading, and improving, a nation on the edge of industrial change in 1724. Later social historians mine the Tour as a census of a world about to vanish.
