The paper starts from the armistices signed by Finland, Rumania, Hungary, and Bulgaria. Those deals obliged each state to pay for war damage, much of it to the Soviet Union. The question was what happened when the goods or plants handed over belonged to American owners, a problem that ran through the whole reparations fight.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d424:
Coal famine drives a Washington cable to Pauley in Moscow dated July 3, 1945, signed by Secretary Byrnes. The Potter-Hyndley mission's report on northwest Europe, it says, concludes that without immediate and drastic steps, next winter will bring a coal famine there and in the Mediterranean area. Its severity would destroy all semblance of law and order.

The American government, the cable states, concurs in the report's major findings. It backs instant action on two points: reach maximum coal production in Germany early, and export to northwest Europe and the Mediterranean all coal above German needs. The President, it adds, proposes a directive to the American commander to that effect.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d524:
Soviet cooperation in Europe's recovery is sought in a briefing book paper on solving immediate European economic problems. Its recommendation: the Soviet Union should be urged and encouraged to participate actively with the United States, the United Kingdom, and other countries in combined endeavors on relief and reconstruction. The steps it calls particularly important begin with organizations.

The paper seeks Soviet agreement to participate fully in four bodies: the Emergency Economic Committee for Europe, the European Coal Organization, the European Central Inland Transport Organization, and the United Maritime Authority. Soviet representatives would cooperate in their day-to-day work. A second section turns to UNRRA, and the terms on which Soviet agreement should be sought there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d624:
Secretary of State Byrnes wrote to Harold Ickes, the wartime petroleum chief, on July 6, 1945. The top secret letter is document 624 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It brings Ickes up to date on the oil situation in Eastern Europe.

Byrnes says reports of Ickes's interest in eastern oil for Western Europe have reached him. He encloses three papers for Ickes's use. One is the Department's airgram to Moscow of June 29. The others cover the use of U.S. property by satellite states for reparations, and a goods deal between Rumania and the Soviet Union. The airgram, he notes, shows Ambassador Harriman fully briefed on the oil picture. It also stresses the link between reviving that industry and the world output needed for war and civil needs alike.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1024:
Philip Mosely sent this secret memorandum to Assistant Secretaries James Dunn and William Clayton on July 17, 1945. It sums up the plan to create a Rhineland-Ruhr state, then tests the case for and against. Most plans would make the area a lasting separate unit, run by France, Belgium, and the Netherlands under the Security Council.

Supporters claim separation would keep Germany's basic resources out of German hands forever. A weaker Germany would also tempt no outside power as an ally. Mosely answers that maps cannot erase a people's numbers, skills, and drive. Germans, he argues, would never sincerely accept partition. Holding it would demand permanent unity among the four great powers, which partition itself would strain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1124:
A second message from the Acting Secretary of State went to Assistant Secretary Clayton on 20 July 1945. It followed the first by two days. Clayton led the State Department's work on trade, loans, and the money terms of the peace.

Money questions sat near the top of the Potsdam agenda. What Germany would pay, how trade would restart, and who would fund relief all ran through Clayton's office. Repeat contact of this kind shows how central that track was to the summit. The message is one more link between the talks in Germany and the staff who ran the home office.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1224:
Togo cabled Sato again on 17 July 1945, a second message the same day. Tokyo's foreign minister was pressing his Moscow envoy hard at the very start of the Potsdam talks. Japan's leaders knew the summit would speak to their fate.

The traffic between Tokyo and its Moscow embassy ran through American hands in secret. Codebreakers broke Japan's codes, and the Potsdam team read the pleas as they flew. That hidden fact gives these plain cables their drama. This second note of the day shows Tokyo's urgency. Japan sought Soviet help to end the war on terms softer than surrender, and every day counted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1324:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 25 July 1945. It came the day before the Allied terms to Japan went out and the British government changed hands. The summit's drafting machine ran at full speed that week.

A proposal at this stage aimed at closing text: words the other teams could sign. The paper is one of the American moves in the drive toward the final protocol. Kept in the official record, it lets readers follow the drafting fight clause by clause. Its fate, kept or cut, can be traced in the approved texts printed near it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1424:
A text submitted to the heads of government themselves forms document 1424, dated 24 July 1945. Papers addressed to the leaders, rather than to the conference staff, were meant for the highest eyes at Potsdam. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Most summit paper moves among officials; a text laid before Truman, Churchill, and Stalin directly marks a question the staffs could not settle. Readers should note the channel as much as the words: escalation to the top was the summit's way of breaking deadlocks. This paper belongs to the crowded middle of the talks, when the leaders' days filled with points their aides had failed to close below.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-124:
A rapporteur reported on July 27, 1945, summing up a working group's progress for the Potsdam Conference's senior levels. The report dates from the final week, when subcommittees raced to close their files. It was printed among the conference papers in the second Potsdam volume. Rapporteur reports were the hinges between detailed work and top-level choice.

Inside, the group's gains and gaps stand side by side. Leaders could see at a glance what a final push might settle. The form teaches readers how the conference processed hard problems in layers. Few documents show the method as clearly as these short, factual reports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-24:
Robert Murphy, political adviser in Germany, memoranda'd an experts' session on German economics dated July 19, 1945. The memo is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The subcommittee of experts agreed to work informally and to report back only its disagreements.

Soviet delegate Maisky led off by asking what decentralization meant. Will Clayton tied it to breaking up trusts, cartels, and monopolies. Another U.S. man tied it to ending tight central control of industry and commerce. A joint definition was agreed on the spot. The German economy would be decentralized to end the excessive concentration of economic power. Maisky had no quarrel with a relief principle that followed. He did ask what relief of liberated areas meant, and he made no comment when asked if Germany meant her 1937 frontiers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d724:
Document 724 is Byrnes's reply to his acting deputy, sent July 16, 1945 as he settled at Potsdam. The Secretary of State answered Joseph Grew, who held the Department in Washington. Their exchange frames the volume's Washington channel. This letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Replies from the field show what the traveling team needed most. A secretary at a summit depends on home for facts, drafts, and calm judgment. Readers see that dependence in writing. The document pairs with Grew's letter of the same day. Together they show the two ends of one working line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d824:
Cannon wrote from Lisbon to Assistant Secretary Dunn on July 28, 1945, in document 824. The first secretary at the Lisbon embassy now reported to a higher desk. His letter dates from the conference's final days. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

A report routed to an assistant secretary gains speed. Dunn could carry a point straight to the Secretary's circle. Readers see Cannon's Lisbon view climbing the ladder at a key moment. The document shows the Department's wiring at work: a quiet post, a senior reader, and a summit drawing to its close in the same week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d924: Emile Despres, adviser on German economic affairs, wrote to William Clayton on July 24, 1945, about safeguards in a possible reparations deal. If the Russians gain a free hand in their zone plus set removals from the Ruhr, he says America should insist on two protections. Looted property that can be identified must be returned, and Allied teams must be free to locate it. Allied-owned property in Germany must not be removed without the owners' government's consent, and fair payment must be arranged.
frus-1964-68v23-d24: A 1964-1968 FRUS telegram from the Central Intelligence Agency on the Congo. The agency reported from Africa. This document preserves that cable. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
galsworthy-white-monkey-1924:
John Galsworthy opened his second Forsyte trilogy, A Modern Comedy, with The White Monkey, published in 1924. The Forsytes return, but the center shifts to the younger generation. Soames's daughter Fleur is now married and restless in postwar London.

Fleur and her husband Michael Mont drift through parties, publishing work, and marital strain. A Chinese statue of a white monkey, holding a squeezed fruit, becomes the symbol of their grasping age. Meanwhile Soames, older and less sure, watches his daughter repeat family patterns. Galsworthy mixes satire of the 1920s smart set with real sympathy for people trapped by wealth.
gao-gaoreports-b-297524: NVT Technologies doubled its February 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299424: Global Solutions Network took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Global name, local rules: the bid law applies exactly the same to everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-299624: Tennier Industries took its July 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Every protest, big or small, gets the full fair-play reading.
gao-gaoreports-b-306424: The Presidio Trust's audio equipment spending got a fiscal ruling in this March 2006 GAO call, which tests using appropriated funds. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the sound gear was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-224: HUD's rent subsidy errors got a GAO check in 2005, and the report covers progress and challenges in measuring and cutting improper payments. The review counts the wrong dollars. The tenants deserved the fair rents. The subsidies had to be proper.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-324: Secure Flight's data testing got a GAO measure in 2005, and the report covers testing the impact of commercial data use. The review checks the watch-list machinery. The flyers deserved the accurate screening. The measures were tested. The flyers deserved the accurate screening.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-424: Paperwork burden reduction needed a new approach in 2005, and GAO's report says the old ways might require rethinking. The findings take the measure. The report shows the red tape was studied. The approach had to be new. The red tape was studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-724: FAA air traffic cost controls needed addressing in 2005, and GAO's report says major operating costs required attention. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the taxpayers deserved honest costs. The controls had to be addressed. The taxpayers deserved honest costs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-24: FHA loans with down payment assistance needed risk management in 2005, and GAO's report says additional action was needed on the insured loans. The findings demand the caution. The report warns that the homebuyers' safety net needed protecting. The action had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-324: Federal buyouts were on the rise in 2006, and GAO's report says agencies were using early-outs more often to reshape workforces. The findings track the trend. The report warns that the workforce surgery needed care. The reshaping had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-624: Federal wood research got a GAO inventory in 2006, and the report catalogs research, product development, and technology transfer. The findings do the counting. The report shows the nation's forests were a laboratory. The research deserved the record. The forests were a laboratory.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-724: Mammogram access was adequate but uneven in 2006, and GAO's report says nationwide capacity was fine, though some locations had problems. The findings balance the good and the gaps. The report warns that the screening should reach every woman. The access had to be even.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-824: The bank award program's impact was murky in 2006, and GAO's report says the effect on investments in distressed communities was hard to determine. The findings admit the fog. The report warns that the do-good dollars needed proof. The impact had to be measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-224: The Army's officer pipeline was springing leaks in 2007, and GAO's report says a strategic plan was needed for accession and retention. The findings demand the blueprint. The report warns that the lieutenants of tomorrow needed a reason to stay. The ranks had to be kept full.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-24: Darfur's death toll needed better counting in 2007, and GAO's report says the estimates showed the crisis's severity, though their accuracy could improve. The findings respect the horror and question the math. The report warns that the world's worst crisis deserved the world's best numbers. The counting had to be credible.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-424: Homeland Security's tech buying needed a rulebook in 2007 — GAO's report says the department had to write and live by real IT policies. The findings demand the missing manual be finished. The report's refrain: big systems need big discipline, or big waste follows.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-424: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on mine Safety: Additional Guidance and Oversight of Mines' Emergency Response Plans Would Improve the Safety of Underground Coal Miners. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-624: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation: A More Strategic Approach Could Improve Human Capital Management. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
ghazali-mishkat-anwar-gairdner-1924:
Al-Ghazali, the great Muslim theologian of the eleventh century, wrote Mishkat al-Anwar, The Niche for Lights, as a commentary on the Quranic Light Verse. Gairdner's 1924 translation for the Royal Asiatic Society is the classic English rendering. The short work is among the most prized in Sufi thought.

Ghazali unfolds the verse's image of God as the Light of the heavens and the earth through layers of symbol. Niche, lamp, glass, and oil become stages by which the soul rises toward true sight. Readers meet here a mind that joined strict theology to deep mystical longing.
gide-strait-is-the-gate-bussy-1924:
Strait Is the Gate, published by André Gide in French in 1909, was the first of his books Englished by Dorothy Bussy, in 1924. Jerome loves his cousin Alissa, a devout girl who believes earthly love bars the road to heaven. The title quotes the hard, narrow gate of the Gospels.

Alissa renounces Jerome again and again, urging him toward a purer life without her. He waits, writes, and hopes across many years of separation. Her diary, read after her death, reveals the cost of her choice. Gide tells the story quietly, letting faith and desire wound each other. Many readers judge it his most perfectly made short novel.
goldman-further-disillusionment-russia-1:
Emma Goldman returned from Soviet Russia with her hopes broken, and My Further Disillusionment in Russia tells why. The 1924 book follows her first account of the Russian Revolution's betrayal. Goldman had gone to Russia as a supporter of the revolution. She left as a critic of the Bolshevik state.

She describes the crushing of the soviets and the Kronstadt rising of 1921. Free speech, unions, and rival socialists all faced prison or worse. Her case is the anarchist case against Bolshevism, from a witness. The book angered many on the left who still defended Moscow. It stands as a primary record of dissent.
guillaume-traditions-islam-1924:
Alfred Guillaume, an English scholar of Islam, wrote this first English guide to the hadith books in 1924. Hadith are the tales of the words and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad, passed down by a chain of names. They form the Sunna, the model life that stands by the Quran in the faith.

Guillaume tells how the tales were gleaned, sifted, and set in the great books of the Sunna. He gives samples in English so the reader can see their form and range at first hand. The book is the first door in English to a vast field of Islamic lore.
haldane-daedalus-1924:
John Burdon Sanderson Haldane was a young British biologist when he gave the lecture printed in 1924 as Daedalus. He used the Greek maker Daedalus as a sign of science pushing past old limits. The talk looks a century ahead at what biology might do.

Haldane foresaw babies grown outside the body, new foods, and vast changes in energy and daily life. Some of his guesses missed, but the method of bold, reasoned forecast struck home. The book is often named as a founding text of speculation about remaking human life. He meant the lecture to stir debate, and it did so at once.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol4-1924:
William Holdsworth's History of English Law reached its fourth volume in the 1923 third edition. Holdsworth, an Oxford professor, spent his life on this vast history, which grew to many volumes. The work traces English law from its medieval roots toward modern times, court by court and doctrine by doctrine.

Volume 4 covers the later medieval law: the growth of the central courts, the rise of the legal profession, and the law books of the period. Holdsworth writes with steady command of the records, showing how procedure and pleading shaped the substance of the law. His history became the standard account of how English law grew, and lawyers still cite it as an authority. The volume shows the medieval common law in its mature, working form.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol5-1924:
The fifth volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law, in its 1923 edition, takes the story into the sixteenth century. Holdsworth's multi-volume history was already the standard account of English law's growth. Each volume follows the courts, the profession, and the books of the law through one stretch of time.

Volume 5 covers the Tudor revolution in law. The Reformation changed the courts and the church's place in the legal order, while the common lawyers rose to new power and wealth. Holdsworth unfolds the transformation with vast learning and calm judgment. He shows how old forms bent without breaking under religious and political upheaval. For the legal history of the Tudor age, this volume remains a first port of call.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol6-1924:
Holdsworth published the sixth volume of his History of English Law in 1924. The Oxford historian was building, volume by volume, the fullest account of English law ever written by one man. By this point the history had reached the century of civil war and revolution.

Volume 6 takes up the 1600s: Coke on the bench, the king's prerogative courts, and the struggle between crown and Parliament fought through law. Holdsworth tells the legal side of England's revolution with a master's authority, showing how courtroom battles over jurisdiction became battles over the constitution itself. The courts appear as a true battleground of English liberty. Students of the period still start with Holdsworth, whose learning has never been matched in a single-author history.
houdini-magician-among-spirits-1924:
Harry Houdini, the most famous magician of his age, spent his last years hunting fake spirit mediums. His A Magician Among the Spirits, published in 1924, reports that hunt in detail. Houdini had hoped the dead might speak, and his failure to find honest proof made him fierce.

He describes seances he attended in disguise, slate tricks, spirit photos, and messages faked by hidden hands. As a stage magician he could copy every effect the mediums claimed came from ghosts. The book stands as the landmark skeptical investigation of Spiritualism by an insider of the craft of illusion.
huizinga-waning-middle-ages-hopman-1924:
Johan Huizinga's The Waning of the Middle Ages appears in F. Hopman's translation of 1924. Huizinga, a Dutch historian, portrays France and Burgundy in the 1300s and 1400s. Chivalry, court love, tournaments, and vivid religious life fill his pages. Yet beneath the color he finds weariness and a sense of ending.

He calls the age an autumn: ripe, ornate, and overripe. Forms of ritual and symbol govern thought so fully that fresh life stirs elsewhere. The book created a model for cultural history of an age's mood. Its prose, even in translation, is rich and melancholy. It remains a beloved classic on the medieval mind's last flowering.
jeffers-tamar-1924:
Robinson Jeffers published Tamar and Other Poems in 1924, the book that made his name. Jeffers wrote long narrative poems set on the wild coast near Carmel, California. The title poem, Tamar, is a tragedy of passion and doom in a farming family. Its story involves forbidden love, ghosts, and fire.

Other poems in the book also deal with violence, desire, and fate. Jeffers used loose, rolling lines and stark images of hawks, rocks, and sea. He saw human pride as small against the vast natural world. The book shocked readers and won strong praise. It marks the start of his major career.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-24:
Jogues goes back to the Mohawk in Volume 24, from 1898. Thwaites covers Quebec and the Hurons across 1643 and 1644 in this book. The priest returns in peace to the very men who tortured him.

He carries the cross this time, not a sword, by choice. Old wounds mark his hands as he greets his former captors. The act strikes many readers as the most Christlike in the set. Priests at Quebec weigh the risk and bless his hard road. Readers know how his story ends, and they read on in awe. His courage shames and lifts them at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mi-kamokah-who-:
Mi-Kamokah, Hebrew for Who is like unto Thee, names the verse from Exodus chapter fifteen sung as a response in Jewish daily services. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on its music in 1906. The verse, with the chapter's closing line, sits between the Shema and the Shemoneh Esreh prayers.

Most days the verse takes the melody pattern of the service around it, the article explains. But for the penitential evening service between New Year and the Day of Atonement, its own later, major-key setting sets the tone for everything else. The entry prints that melody and traces how such tunes became signature themes reused across the northern liturgy.
journal-of-discourses-vol-24:
Maximum pressure bears down through Volume Twenty-Four, issued in 1884. Much of the kingdom's leadership sits behind bars or in hiding. The government's full weight rests on one small, stubborn people.

Discourses of endurance preach patience when the heavens seem like brass. Hidden apostles surface to bless the flock, then vanish once more. Wives run farms, shops, and wards while their husbands dodge marshals. Faith stays unbroken under a strain few churches have ever borne. The Saints hold their ground, and these sermons are their dispatch from the siege lines. Patience itself becomes a weapon in the preachers' hands here.
kafka-ein-hungerkunstler-1924:
Ein Hungerkunstler, A Hunger Artist, was Kafka's last story, published in 1924 in the collection of the same name that he corrected on his deathbed. Its hero is a professional faster, once a star of fairs and circuses, whose art the world has stopped wanting.

Caged and forgotten, he fasts on, and at the end confesses his secret: he never found a food he liked, so fasting was no feat at all. A panther takes his cage, fed and glorious. The story is Kafka's bleak joke on art, fame, and appetite, written as he himself starved of breath.
laclos-liaisons-dangereuses-aldington-19:
Choderlos de Laclos, a French army officer, published Les Liaisons dangereuses in 1782. Richard Aldington translated the novel into English in 1924 as Dangerous Acquaintances. The whole story unfolds in letters between two cold, clever aristocrats and the people they set out to ruin.

The Marquise de Merteuil and the Vicomte de Valmont plot seductions as moves in a game. Their targets include a virtuous married woman and a convent-bred girl. Letter by letter the plots tighten, until pride and revenge turn the players on each other. Laclos builds the trap with icy control and no wasted scene. The novel remains the sharpest portrait of desire used as a weapon.
lawrence-boy-in-bush-1924:
The Boy in the Bush, published in 1924, is Lawrence's Australian novel, written with Mollie Skinner. She ran the guest house where the Lawrences stayed in Western Australia. She supplied a draft; he rewrote it into his own fierce idiom.

Its hero, Jack Grant, is an English boy sent to the colony, who grows up in the outback among settlers, stockmen, and Aboriginal people. The bush tests him toward a hard, free manhood outside English rules. The collaboration gives the book a double texture: local knowledge under Lawrence's prophetic voice. It remains the most Australian of his novels.
lowie-primitive-religion-1924:
Robert Harry Lowie, a leading Boasian anthropologist, wrote this 1924 survey to give religion among stateless peoples a clear, systematic treatment. Rather than ranking beliefs as stages, he described them as living systems that deserved study on their own terms.

Lowie covers awe and the sense of the extraordinary, prayer, sacrifice, shamans, visions, and myths across many peoples. He draws heavily on his own fieldwork with the Crow and on reports from every continent. His tone is dry and skeptical of grand theories. The book became a founding textbook of the anthropology of religion, used for decades.
machen-ornaments-in-jade-1924:
Arthur Machen wrote short prose poems late in his career, and Ornaments in Jade, published in 1924, gathers them in one slim book. Each piece is brief. Each one tries to catch a flash of awe, fear, or joy in plain, rich words.

Readers meet brief scenes rather than full tales. A street, a face, or a scrap of song can open onto a vast hidden world. The book shows Machen at his most pure and spare. Fans prize it as the heart of his strange, bright style. Late in life Machen still held that the world hides bright, dread truths. Each short piece gives that faith a sharp, clear shape.
mann-magic-mountain-1924:
Thomas Mann published The Magic Mountain in 1924, a German novel set in a sanatorium in Davos, Switzerland. Hans Castorp visits his sick cousin for three weeks and stays for seven years. The Berghof sanatorium cuts its guests off from normal time. Illness, idleness, and talk fill their days.

Two guests argue over Castorp's soul: Settembrini, a humanist, and Naphta, a radical critic of the West. Love, music, seances, and snow deepen the spell of the mountain. Castorp at last leaves as the First World War begins. Mann turns a health resort into a mirror of European thought. The novel is vast, ironic, and humane.
mead-gnostic-john-the-baptizer-1924:
A living Gnostic community, the Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran, still honors John the Baptist as its greatest prophet. G. R. S. Mead presented their scriptures to English readers in The Gnostic John the Baptizer, published in 1924. The book offers selections from the Mandaean John-Book in translation.

Mead, a tireless student of forgotten religions, treats the texts with care and sympathy. Hymns, teachings, and the Baptist's story appear in a form few Western readers had ever seen. The volume opened a window on a faith that never died out, unlike its ancient cousins. Scholars and seekers both took notice of his pioneering English treatment. The tradition he introduced still draws researchers to the marshes of southern Iraq.
melville-billy-budd-1924:
Herman Melville left Billy Budd unfinished at his death, and it first saw print in 1924. The novella was his final word on justice, innocence, and martial law. Its spare, grave tone differs sharply from his wild early sea tales of youth.

Billy Budd, a fine young sailor, is pressed into a British warship's crew. The master-at-arms Claggart hates his goodness and charges him with mutiny plots. Billy, tongue-tied, strikes and kills him, and the law demands his death. Captain Vere hangs him though he believes the lad is guiltless of intent. The tale asks hard questions no court at sea can settle.
moore-observations-1924:
Marianne Moore published Observations in 1924, a book of poems marked by precision and restraint. Moore wrote about animals, art, sports, and American scenes. Her lines often use syllable counts rather than a steady beat. Quotations from other writers appear inside the poems themselves.

Pangolins, ostriches, and baseball players share space with paintings and gardens. Moore looks closely and judges with dry wit. She avoids grand claims and favors exact detail. The book helped define American modernist poetry at its most disciplined. Later poets learned from her care with facts and form. Her work rewards slow reading and a second look.
nasa-tm-19640005950-motion-of-the-sub-sa: 24-hour orbits got sub-point-motioned, and this 1964 NASA memo covers satellite point motion. The pages detail the motion findings. The engineers get their memo. The orbits were 24-hour. The memo was engineer. The sub-satellite were point. The hour were 24.
openalex-w2037115424: Cities sprawl in patterns — metrics try to capture them. Lowry and Lowry's 2013 study compared spatial metrics that quantify urban form. The thin catalog record hides the details, but the work judged which metrics measure city shape best.
openalex-w2048299524: Qualitative research has three classic forms. Godoy's 1995 Portuguese work on fundamental types of qualitative research covers documentary research, case study, and ethnography. The book mapped the three paths for qualitative inquiry in Brazil — a lasting methods guide.
openalex-w2142467924: Alzheimer's brains burn — plaques and tangles tell why. A 2013 review covers inflammation in Alzheimer's disease. The review examined tangles and plaques surrounded by inflammation — dementia's fire, reviewed at last for researchers now — the brain on fire.
openalex-w2143704424: A century-old worm still waits for action. A 2013 paper is a plea for action on Strongyloides stercoralis. Though researchers pay more attention now, systematic action plans still lag behind — neglect's cost, counted at last.
openalex-w2144183424: The Amazon's productivity hid below ground. A 2009 study measured total productivity across ten Amazonian sites. The work quantified a least-measured piece of the global carbon cycle — the forest's budget, balanced at last for science now.
openalex-w2145585224: Muscles can tire and strengthen at once. A 2000 paper covers the coexistence of boost and fatigue. The catalog record is thin, but the paper covers muscle's dual response — a paradox, explored at last for all to see and study.
openalex-w2165312224: In the Peruvian Amazon around Iquitos, malaria cases looked puzzlingly sparse — until researchers looked closer. This 2005 Malaria Journal study finds that infections cluster in certain households and neighborhoods, and that many people carry the parasites silently, without symptoms. Combining active and passive case detection, the paper shows that hidden, asymptomatic infections help explain how malaria lingers where official counts look low.
openalex-w2337502624: What a fish eats shapes the microbes in its gut — and those microbes shape what the fish can digest. This 2016 Scientific Reports study analyzes over 985,000 DNA sequences from wild freshwater fishes, asking how trophic level (where a fish sits in the food web) influences its gut microbiota and their enzyme activity. The findings link diet, microbes, and metabolism in the wild.
openalex-w2587206624: Classical physics says light beams pass through each other untouched — quantum mechanics disagrees. This 2017 Nature Physics paper reports evidence for light-by-light scattering in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC, made possible by the enormous electromagnetic fields of speeding lead nuclei. It's a direct glimpse of the quantum vacuum at work.
openalex-w2729161724: Intra-abdominal infections are common surgical emergencies and major killers in emergency departments. This 2017 World Journal of Emergency Surgery paper delivers the World Society of Emergency Surgery's global guidelines: early recognition, adequate source control, and the right antibiotics. The consensus gives surgeons worldwide a shared playbook.
openalex-w2774787224: Since 1970, experts have catalogued the genetic defects that leave people without working immune defenses. This 2017 Journal of Clinical Immunology paper is the International Union of Immunological Societies' latest report on inborn errors of immunity — the primary immunodeficiencies. The classification guides diagnosis and treatment for these rare but severe disorders.
openalex-w2794674724: Argentina has many vegetation maps — but none detailed enough to distinguish vegetation units within Cabrera's 1976 phytogeographic provinces. This 2018 paper in Ecología Austral (in Spanish) analyzes published vegetation descriptions to build that country-level map. The synthesis gives botanists and land managers a finer-grained picture of Argentina's plant geography.
openalex-w2809430324: Eliminating malaria from Asia-Pacific by 2030 requires curing the dormant liver stage — and that means primaquine. This 2018 Malaria Journal paper reports a round-table of the APMEN Vivax Working Group on quantifying primaquine's effectiveness and improving adherence. The discussion tackles the practical barriers to delivering radical cure safely and widely.
openalex-w3014759824: Comparing climate projections across studies needs common ground — literally. This 2020 Earth System Science Data paper updates the IPCC's climate reference regions for subcontinental analysis, with definitions and aggregated datasets. The regions give researchers a shared map for regional climate synthesis.
openalex-w4321076624: This 2023 research article presents GLORIA: a globally representative hyperspectral in situ dataset for optical sensing of water quality. The Data Descriptor gives remote-sensing researchers ground truth for monitoring Earth’s waters from orbit.
openalex-w4401164724: This 2024 Lancet paper — by Livingston, Huntley, Liu and colleagues — delivers the standing commission’s 2024 report on dementia prevention, intervention, and care. The authoritative update synthesizes what works against one of aging’s greatest threats.
openalex-w7204665824: Teaching Spanish at a university built for Afro-Brazilian and Lusophone exchange brings unique chances and hurdles. This experience report from UNILAB's language center describes teaching Spanish there: what worked, what was hard, and what it taught the instructors. The authors write from direct classroom experience. A lively account of language teaching at the crossroads of cultures.
openalex-w7204669824: Parents shape what their children eat, but many never learned to cook well themselves. This scoping review maps programs that teach parents cooking skills and nutrition knowledge, aiming to bring home cooking back. The authors survey what has been tried and what the studies show. A public-health look at the kitchen as the front line of childhood nutrition.
physiologus-carlill-1924:
The Physiologus is an early Christian book about animals, first written in Greek in the second century. J. B. Carlill translated it into English in 1924. From this short work grew the whole medieval bestiary tradition, the animal books found in every great library.

Each beast carries a moral. The pelican stands for sacrifice, the phoenix for rising again, and the unicorn for purity. The writer mixes real habits of animals with legend and reads both as lessons in faith. Monasteries copied and expanded the text for a thousand years. Every later bestiary, with its painted lions and dragons, flows from this spring.
pigafetta-first-voyage-round-the-world-1:
Antonio Pigafetta sails round the world in The First Voyage Round the World, his tale of Magellan's trek, writ near 1524. Pigafetta was a young gent who went for the fame of the feat. He kept a log of all: straits, storms, trade, fights, and the death of his chief in the far isles. His tale is the chief source on the first such voyage in man's past.

Midst the log stand the giants of Patagonia, men so tall, he says, that his mates stood waist high to them. That tale launched years of giant lore. The book is a prime trek text.
plaw-118-121-2024: Enacted in 2024, this federal law designates the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 517 Seagaze Drive in Oceanside, California, as the “Charlesetta Ree. The operative clause states exactly what Congress authorized. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plaw-118-201-2024: Enacted in 2024, this federal law designates the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 1106 Main Street in Bastrop, Texas, as the “Sergeant Major Billy D. The operative clause states exactly what Congress authorized. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plaw-118-46-2024: In 2024, Congress named the facility at 985 Michigan Avenue in Detroit, Michigan the "Rosa Parks Federal Building". Naming laws like this one permanently honor people and places at federal sites. It stands as Public Law 118-46 of the 118th Congress. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
plos-pbio-0020024:
Sidarta Ribeiro, Damien Gervasoni, Ernesto S. Soares, and their team recorded brain activity during sleep for PLOS Biology in 2004. Rats that had explored new objects showed replays of brain patterns in several forebrain areas during slow-wave sleep. The replays lasted far longer than many expected.

Sleep replay is thought to help move new memories into long term store. Finding it spread across many areas, and lasting for hours, hints at a broad, slow process of memory fixing. The study gives weight to the idea that sleep is active work for the brain, not rest alone. It also offers a model for testing how poor sleep might weaken learning and recall.
plos-pone-0000024:
Taisheng Li, Jing Xie, Yuxian He, and co-authors checked the immune memory of people who had recovered from SARS, in work published in 2006. SARS, the severe lung disease that spread in 2003, left a key question behind: how long does protection last after infection? The team drew blood from recovered patients well after their illness.

They found robust responses still in place: antibodies against the virus and cytotoxic T cells, the killer cells that destroy infected cells, had both persisted long-term. Lasting immunity of this kind shapes vaccine hopes and tells doctors whether survivors can be reinfected. For a virus that vanished, the study also left a template for judging immunity to its later cousins.
plos-pone-0000124:
Ilaria Roato, Giacomina Brunetti, Eva Gorassini, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It looks at patients with solid tumors and examines a signaling protein called IL-7. The team reports that IL-7 raises the activity of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone, through a pathway tied to TNF-alpha.

Bone loss is a serious problem when cancer spreads or when the immune system runs hot. The authors connect an immune signal to the cells that erode bone. That link matters for understanding why some tumor patients lose bone strength, and it may point to ways of slowing that damage.
plos-pone-0000224:
Servane Blanvillain, Damien Meyer, Alice Boulanger, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacteria that live on plants or in water need to scavenge carbohydrates for food. The authors show these bacteria share a route for that scavenging: TonB-dependent receptors, gates in the cell surface that pull in nutrients.

The receptors were best known from other bacteria, so finding them as a shared feature broadens the picture. Both plant pathogens and aquatic bacteria use this system to harvest plant sugars. The work identifies a possible weak point in bacteria that damage crops, since blocking food intake can stop growth.
plos-pone-0000324:
Gareth A. Wilson, Edward J. Feil, Andrew K. Lilley, and colleagues published this comparative genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Taxonomically restricted genes are genes found in only one group of organisms, with no known relatives elsewhere. The authors carry out a large-scale ranking of such genes across bacterial and archaeal genomes.

Orphan genes like these are often ignored because nothing is known about them. Ranking them by properties such as length and conservation highlights which ones look genuinely functional. The paper gives microbiologists a shortlist of mysterious genes most worth the cost of experiments.
plos-pone-0000424:
Cristiana Cavina-Pratesi, Melvyn A. Goodale, and Jody C. Culham used brain scanning to separate grasping from seeing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. People can judge an object's size and also reach out and size their grip to it, and the two abilities may use different brain systems. The fMRI study used real three-dimensional objects rather than pictures.

The authors report a dissociation: brain activity for grasping an object split apart from activity for perceiving its size. Using real objects matters because flat images can mislead studies of the hand. The finding supports the idea that the brain runs a dedicated system for guiding actions, distinct from the system that builds what we consciously see.
plos-pone-0000524:
R. David Shankar and colleagues described a teaching experiment from a medical school in Nepal, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Students practiced personal drug selection, the skill of choosing the right medicine for a condition from evidence rather than habit, through problem-based learning in pharmacology. The authors reported their experience running the course.

Choosing drugs well is a core clinical skill, and prescribing habits formed at school persist for careers. Problem-based learning makes students defend choices on real cases instead of memorizing lists. A report from Nepal carries weight. Settings with few resources must teach economical prescribing. Each rupee spent on the wrong drug is care someone else does not get.
plos-pone-0000624:
Martin R. Miller, Andrew White and Kenneth Wilson modeled what happens when parasites hit males harder than females. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study starts from growing evidence that male hosts tend to carry higher levels of parasitism. What that bias does to the host population as a whole was not yet understood.

The team built on an established two-sex model and ran it under different mating systems. Mating patterns change how a male-skewed parasite burden feeds through births, deaths, and population growth. Modelers and disease ecologists get a framework for asking when male-biased infection stays a detail and when it reshapes the whole host population.
plos-pone-0000724:
Mark S. Bretscher and Margaret Clotworthy improved a genetic trick in a social amoeba, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dictyostelium discoideum amoebae are haploid, carrying one gene copy, and share many features with animal cells. That makes them ideal for studying basic processes such as cell locomotion. But isolating mutants had largely been limited to non-essential genes.

Their method uses single loxP sites to enhance homologous recombination, the swapping of DNA at matched sequences. Temperature-sensitive mutants in the Sec1 gene are the demonstration case. Mutants in essential genes, which kill cells when fully removed, need gentler tools. A better recombination method widens what this model organism can teach.
plos-pone-0000824:
Alexander Moffett, Nancy Shackelford and Sahotra Sarkar mapped malaria risk across Africa from the mosquitoes' point of view, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A central goal of epidemiology is building spatial models of disease prevalence and risk, including maps for the potential spread of infectious disease. Malaria risk depends on which vector species live where, and each species has its own ecological niche.

The team provides three continent-wide maps of relative malaria risk in Africa, based on ecological niche models of the vector species. Risk maps built on mosquito habitat can anticipate transmission where case data are sparse. They also show where risk could shift as environments change.
plos-pone-0000924:
Michael Lodes, Dominic Suciu, Jodi Wilmoth and colleagues built an electronic test to name the germs behind throat and lung infections, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Upper respiratory infections from bacteria and viruses look much alike at the bedside. Symptoms alone cannot name the culprit, yet the right treatment depends on knowing it, since antibiotics do little against viruses.

Their method uses an oligonucleotide microarray, a chip of short DNA probes, with electrochemical detection to flag matches. Naming the pathogen fast and correctly could cut wasted antibiotic use. It could also speed care for patients whose infection turns serious. The paper presents the test as a working system, not just a concept.
plos-pone-0001024:
Martina Bielaszewska, Robin Kock, Alexander Friedrich and colleagues challenged how a severe gut illness is diagnosed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hemolytic uremic syndrome is a dangerous condition caused by certain E. coli that make Shiga toxin. Diagnosis looked for the toxin genes and a second marker called eae.

The team report cases where stool samples held E. coli lacking the toxin genes yet positive for eae. If toxin genes can be lost during infection, tests that demand them will miss real cases. The authors ask whether the diagnostic paradigm needs to change. For a syndrome that can damage kidneys fast, a missed call is costly.
plos-pone-0001124:
Museums and herbaria hold centuries of records on where species live, and a global effort is digitizing them. Chris Yesson and colleagues audited that effort in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their subject is the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, the largest single gateway to this occurrence data.

The authors ask how global the facility's coverage really is. Gaps matter: records cluster in some regions and taxa while others stay sparse, which can skew studies of how life is spread across the planet. Their check gives data users and collectors a clearer picture of what the archive holds and what it still lacks.
plos-pone-0001224:
Detecting a specific molecule quickly and cheaply is a basic need in medicine and research. William Chiuman and Yingfu Li engineered fluorescent sensors from catalytic DNA in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Most sensors built from nucleic acid enzymes pair an RNA-cutting catalytic motif with an aptamer, a receptor piece that grabs the target.

Their design, called MgZ, rests on a non-classic allosteric scheme, where target binding switches the catalyst's activity through a shape change. When the sensor fires, it produces a fluorescent signal. DNA-based sensors are cheap to make and stable, so better designs widen their use.
plos-pone-0001324:
Dog genetics is powerful because breeds are closed populations, but that structure can also fool association studies. Pascale Quignon and colleagues assessed population structure within breeds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Studies usually sample cases and controls from a single breed, often from one country, to control structure.

The authors examine intra-breed stratification, hidden subgroups within a breed, and its impact on SNP-based association studies. If cases and controls come disproportionately from different subgroups, false associations follow. Their assessment tells dog geneticists how finely they must match their samples.
plos-pone-0001424:
Morgane Rolland and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on immune responses and HIV control. Certain gene variants help some people hold the virus at low levels. The team asked whether the breadth of the killer T cell response explains that control. Past work had given mixed answers on breadth alone.

They found that broad responses, with a bias to one virus protein, went with lower virus levels. The protein bias mattered as much as sheer breadth. That nuance helps shot design, since it names which targets to favor. Shots that train the right breadth on the right protein may copy what natural control does best.
plos-pone-0001524:
Laura Wesolowski and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on fast HIV tests that clash. Fast tests on blood or mouth fluid that react must be checked with a lab test. When the lab check says no, the results clash. The team drew on watch data after the tests reached wide use.

They set out how often such clashes occur and what repeat checks show. Clear rules for repeat testing spare people long waits in doubt. The data help clinics write those rules on proof, not habit. They also show the worth of tracking test performance once tests leave the lab.
plos-pone-0001624:
Sandra Macedo-Ribeiro, Carla Almeida, Bárbara M. Calisto, and their co-authors isolated a new protein from the cattle tick in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein, named boophilin, blocks protein-cutting enzymes. It comes from Boophilus microplus, a tick that feeds on cattle blood and is one of the most widespread parasites of farm animals.

Animals that feed on blood often make blockers of blood-clotting factors, and these blockers come in many shapes and work in many ways. Boophilin is a Kunitz-type blocker with more than one job, and the team cloned its gene and worked out its structure. The full text gives the isolation steps, the gene sequence, and the structural details. Proteins like this can hint at ways to control ticks or to design new drugs that act on clotting.
plos-pone-0001724:
Fang Ji, Zhanjie Liu, Jianping Cao, and their co-authors studied immune lumps caused by a parasitic worm in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Schistosoma japonicum eggs lodged in the liver trigger granulomas, balls of immune cells that wall off the eggs but also scar the organ. What B cells do in building these granulomas was not fully understood.

The team reports that B cell function is required for granuloma formation in early infection. The full text gives the infection model, the B cell tests, and the granuloma measurements with and without working B cells. B cells are usually cast as antibody makers. A structural role in granulomas widens their part in parasitic disease and in the liver damage it causes.
plos-pone-0001824:
Sean M. Rollins, Amanda Peppercorn, John S. Young, and their co-authors applied a screening technique to the anthrax bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In vivo induced antigen technology, or IVIAT, identifies bacterial antigens expressed during infection but not during standard lab culturing. It works by probing the bacterium with antibodies from infected hosts.

Applying IVIAT to Bacillus anthracis, the team identified PagA, a known protective antigen, plus seven members of a sugar-uptake family among the infection-specific antigens. The full text gives the screen and the antigen list. Antigens the germ only shows inside a host are prime vaccine and diagnostic targets, since lab-grown bacteria hide them.
plos-pone-0001924:
RuiRong Yuan and co-authors tested a blood hormone as an immune calmant in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The hormone, erythropoietin or EPO, is best known for boosting red blood cell counts. Short courses of EPO had helped in animal models of acute nerve harm, among them EAE, the animal model of multiple sclerosis.

In EAE, the immune system attacks the nerves, much as in the human illness. The authors report that EPO treatment strongly shifted immune and inflammatory signals in the body at large. If a known drug can retune that attack, it could offer a new line of care for multiple sclerosis. More work would still be needed.
plos-pone-0002024:
Gaik Theng Toh and co-authors tested young Malaysian women with breast cancer for inherited gene faults, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In Malaysia, about half of breast cancer cases strike women under fifty, an early pattern for the illness. Some of those cases likely have a genetic part, yet its size there was unknown.

The team checked the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes in women with early-onset disease who had no family history of it. Hidden faults in such women would be easy to miss if testing is offered only to those with sick kin. Local data guide who should be offered genetic tests in Asia.
plos-pone-0002124:
Nina Movsesyan, Anahit Ghochikyan, Mikayel Mkrtichyan, and co-authors tested a vaccine idea for Alzheimer's disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They used the 3xTg-AD mouse, a strain bred to develop brain changes much like those seen in the human disease. A safe vaccine for this illness must raise antibodies against the amyloid-beta protein without stirring up harmful T cell attacks on the brain.

The team built a DNA vaccine that presents only small pieces, called epitopes, of the target protein. Their goal was to cut the Alzheimer's-like damage in the mice while avoiding the risky immune response that had blocked earlier vaccine tries. The paper adds one careful route toward immune therapy for the disease.
plos-pone-0002224:
Mohit Sahni, Neeraj Verma, D. Narula, and co-authors examined a century of birth records at one Indian hospital, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. India is estimated to be missing 44 million women, lost through neglect of girls, infanticide, and sex-selective abortion. The sex ratio at birth offers a way to measure how strongly prenatal sex selection shapes those numbers.

The team reviewed records of 321,991 deliveries over 110 years at a single hospital. A long run of data from one place shows how the ratio changed as ultrasound and other tools spread. Their analysis gives rare historical depth to a debate often run on recent numbers alone.
plos-pone-0002324:
Emilie Lefèvre, Balbine Roussel, Christian Amblard, and co-authors surveyed the smallest eukaryotes living in a French lake, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Freshwater microbes with nuclei, too small to see without a microscope, have been undersampled in biodiversity studies. What lives in lake water at that scale was largely unknown.

The team read 18S ribosomal DNA from Lake Pavin samples taken in spring and summer 2005, extending an autumn 2004 survey. They found a high occurrence of putative parasitoids, organisms that live off and kill other microbes. A hidden layer of parasites inside plankton changes how lake food webs must be drawn.
plos-pone-0002424:
Penkov and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Dmitry Penkov, Martina Palazzolo, Anna Mondino, and others. Its subject is cytosolic Sequestration of Prep1 Influences Early Stages of T Cell Development. Prep1 and Pbx2 are the main homeodomain DNA-binding proteins of the TALE (three amino acid loop extension) family expressed in the thymus.

We before reported reduced Pbx2 expression and defective thymocyte maturation in Prep1 hypomorphic mice. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002524:
Led by Stein, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Amelie Stein, Patrick Aloy, and others. Its subject is contextual Specificity in Peptide-Mediated Protein Interactions. Most biological processes are regulated through networks of brief protein interactions.

In these interactions, a domain in one protein recognizes a short peptide from another, forming a small contact surface. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002624:
Work by Tom G. Connell and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a Three-Way comparison of tuberculin skin testing, QuantiFERON-TB gold and T-SPOT. TB in children. Authorship is credited in the record to Tom G. Connell and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. There are limited data comparing the performance of the two commercially available interferon gamma (IFN-γ) release assays (IGRAs) for the diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB). Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002724:
Work by Sarika Mehra and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a bistable gene switch for antibiotic biosynthesis: the butyrolactone regulon in streptomyces coelicolor. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Sarika Mehra, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Many microorganisms, including bacteria of the class Streptomycetes, produce various secondary metabolites including antibiotics to gain a competitive advantage in their natural habitat. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002824:
Work by Jeffrey B. Locke and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was streptococcus iniae M-Like protein contributes to virulence in fish and is a target for live attenuated vaccine development. The catalog record names Jeffrey B. Locke first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Streptococcus iniae is a significant pathogen in finfish aquaculture, though knowledge of virulence determinants is lacking. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002924:
Jonathan Butchar, Thomas Cremer, Corey Clay and co-authors profiled human monocytes infected with Francisella tularensis in 2008. That bacterium causes tularemia and can sicken people even at low doses. A key trait of the germ is its power to dampen or subvert the host immune response.

Using microarrays, which read thousands of genes at once, the team mapped how infected monocytes change their gene activity. The aim was to find new targets where the germ bends the host response. Published in PLOS ONE, the list helps immunologists see the levers this dangerous pathogen pulls.
plos-pone-0003024: Mun-Gwan Hong, Amanda Myers, Patrik Magnusson and colleagues carried out a transcriptome-wide assessment of senescence in human brain and lymphocytes, published in PLOS ONE in 2008. Senescence here means the ageing of cells and tissues, and a transcriptome-wide study reads activity across all genes at once. The catalog record supplies title, authors, and year but no abstract detail beyond the title itself. The article therefore stands as a gene activity survey comparing ageing signals in brain tissue and in blood lymphocytes.
plos-pone-0003124: Laura E. Middleton and colleagues published a population based study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on exercise in late life. The title states its scope: how changes in cognition and in mortality relate to exercise among older adults. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record adds no claims about methods or findings.
plos-pone-0003224:
Rong-Xia Li and co-authors count blood proteins in type 2 diabetes in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. New proteomics tools had let labs hunt for serum proteins that could track how diabetes advances and show how the disease works. The team studied blood serum from people with diabetes and from people without it.

Their method gives local, statistical counts of the serum proteome tied to type 2 diabetes. Readers get both a counting method and a disease use in one study. Sound blood markers could flag diabetes shifts sooner than clinic measures alone do now.
plos-pone-0003324:
Souvenir D. Tachado and co-authors study how Legionella germs enter macrophages in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Legionella pneumophila lives inside host cells and causes Legionnaires' disease, a pneumonia that can kill. To cause disease it must first get into cells and grow there. The team measured that entry with cell invasion assays.

The title reports entry without antibody coating, called non-opsonic phagocytosis, runs through a host enzyme, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase. Readers learn the germ uses the cell's own uptake path. Blocking that path might add to antibiotics in severe cases. That is a concrete lead.
plos-pone-0003424:
Nilgun Isik, Dale Hereld, and Tian Jin watched pairs of cell receptors in this 2008 imaging study. Two surface receptors, CXCR4 and CCR5, are best known as HIV entry aids. Signals called chemokines bind these receptors to guide immune cells. The team asked whether binding changes how the receptors pair up.

They used a light method that glows only when two molecules sit very close. The images showed chemokine binding reshaping the paired receptors, called heterodimers. Pairs formed or shifted as signals arrived. The work shows outside messages can rebuild the cell surface from within.
plos-pone-0003524:
Laura Ratier and co-authors compared enzyme variants of a parasite in this 2008 paper. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease in the Americas. It coats itself with stolen sialic acid for protection. An enzyme called trans-sialidase does that stealing, and its gene family is large.

The team used single-domain antibodies from camelids to probe family diversity. Each antibody tested a different member of the enzyme clan. Why the parasite keeps so many versions is the core question. Diversity in a surface tool may help it dodge host defenses. Chagas affects millions, yet drug options for it stay few and old.
plos-pone-0003624:
Miguel A. Aon, Marc R. Roussel, Sonia Cortassa, and colleagues published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks how cells keep their many processes timed and in step. The team studied energy rhythms in yeast cells and in heart muscle cells taken from animals.

They tracked the cells' energy output over time and measured how the signals rose and fell. The patterns had no single fixed tempo, with swings at many time scales at once. The authors call this scale-free behavior. It suggests cell timing works more like a flexible web than a simple clock.
plos-pone-0003724:
Hyuna Yang, Christina A. Harrington, Kristina Vartanian, and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Microarrays measure the activity of thousands of genes at once. Their data quality had improved since the late 1990s, yet results still varied between laboratory sites. The team hunted the cause.

They found that randomizing the order of steps in the lab procedure is key to reproducible results. Without shuffling, hidden batch effects creep into the data. The simple fix targets a quiet source of error that plagued early gene-expression studies across many labs.
plos-pone-0003824:
Manuela Silva, H. Sofia Pereira, Miguel Bento, and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. When two species hybridize, one parent's ribosomal RNA genes often fall silent, a phenomenon called nucleolar dominance. The genes sit in clusters called nucleolar organizer regions, or NORs.

Working in a wheat-rye hybrid system, the team studied how the dominant NORs win. They found the winning set is up-regulated through changes in chromatin, the DNA's packaging. The work shows how cells pick a side when two parental genomes must share one nucleus.
plos-pone-0003924:
Katja Klemm, Christian Eipel, Daniel Cantré, and co-authors tested a hormone's effect on liver regrowth in 2008. Surgeons who remove liver tissue need the rest to regrow fast. Erythropoietin, known for boosting red blood cell output, was one candidate to help. Few good strategies exist to speed liver regeneration.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the opposite of the hoped-for effect. Repeated doses of erythropoietin hindered regrowth in their tests. The harm tied to higher TNF-alpha, a shifted Bax to Bcl-xL ratio, and more cell death. The warning matters for patients given the hormone around liver surgery.
plos-pone-0004024:
Toshiko Sakihama, Takato Sato, Hiroko Iwanari, and co-authors presented a method for weak protein contacts in 2008. Membrane proteins govern how cells recognize each other. Immune and nerve systems depend on those contacts heavily. Making membrane proteins in active form has blocked their study.

Their PLOS ONE article uses baculoviral display to catch low-affinity interactions. Weak contacts are often the most important in cell recognition. Displaying proteins on virus surfaces keeps them in natural shape. The method opens weak immune interactions to direct measurement. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004124:
Teresa Mairal and colleagues published this drug design study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns transthyretin, a protein that carries thyroid hormone and retinol in the blood. When transthyretin clumps into fibres, it causes one of the known amyloid diseases, where harmful protein deposits build up in tissue.

The protein forms a four-part unit with a central channel and two matching binding sites. The authors test whether adding iodine atoms to drug-like molecules makes them grip those sites more strongly and block fibre growth. The work points to a design feature for stronger drugs against this kind of protein clumping.
plos-pone-0004224:
Jennifer Jackson, Laura Higgins, and Xiaorong Lin published this fungal study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The greater wax moth, Galleria mellonella, is widely used as a stand-in host for studying fungal pathogens such as Candida and Cryptococcus. Results in the moth have matched results in animal models for those yeasts.

The team turned to Aspergillus fumigatus, a mould that threatens people with weak immune systems. They also used mutants that changed the colour of its spore formation. They report that these conidiation colour mutants are highly pathogenic in the moth host. The work tests the moth as a fast model for a dangerous mould.
plos-pone-0004324:
Cornelius Schüle and colleagues published this psychiatry study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The combined dexamethasone and CRH test probes the stress hormone system, which is often abnormal in major depression. The team investigated whether the test predicts how patients respond to acute antidepressant treatment.

In 114 depressed inpatients with unipolar or bipolar depression, the test was performed at admission and again shortly after. A hormone test that forecasts who will respond could spare patients weeks of trial and error. The study checks whether the stress system's state at the door predicts recovery.
plos-pone-0004424:
Lysosomes are the cell's waste and recycling units, and Carla Cardoso, Line Groth-Pedersen, Maria Hoyer-Hansen, and co-authors studied what moves them around inside cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Busy lysosome traffic is linked to cancer that spreads. The team compared the proteins on lysosomes from mild breast cancer cells and from a much more invasive line.

Their focus fell on a motor protein called kinesin 5B, which hauls cargo along cell tracks. When the team depleted it, lysosomes lost their normal spread and stability. Sac-like structures called autophagosomes then piled up near the cell nucleus. The work names a motor that cancer cells may lean on as they invade, and a possible target for slowing them.
plos-pone-0004524:
Do protein domains, the reusable parts of proteins, move between species as units? Cheong Xin Chan, Aaron Darling, and Robert Beiko ask in PLOS ONE in 2009. In bacteria and some other organisms, genes can pass sideways between unrelated lineages. The new genes give the receiver fresh abilities, reshaping what it can eat, resist, or build.

Transfer is usually described gene by gene. The authors ask whether domains, the modular chunks inside proteins, are themselves modules of lateral transfer. If domains travel, evolution can remix old parts into new proteins more freely. The answer affects how scientists read family trees of proteins. It also affects how they trace the spread of traits like drug resistance through microbial communities.
plos-pone-0004624:
More boys are being born in Viet Nam than nature would predict, document Christophe Guilmoto, Xuyen Hoang, and Toan Ngo Van in PLOS ONE in 2009. Since the 1980s, the sex ratio at birth has increased in many Asian countries as a result of selective abortions. Until now, there had been no such evidence for Viet Nam.

The authors set out to ascertain the situation with respect to sex ratio at birth in the country. Their title records the finding: a recent increase. A skewed birth ratio is a demographic signal with long echoes, affecting marriage and family patterns a generation later. Establishing the trend early gives policymakers a chance to act before the imbalance deepens, as it has elsewhere in Asia.
plos-pone-0004724:
Diane Bennett and colleagues updated the shared list of HIV mutations used to track spread of drug resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Programs that watch resistance levels guide treatment rules across regions. They also show if HIV care and prevention plans are working as hoped.

To compare rates fairly, all sites must use the same mutation list. The team revised that list for 2009 based on new proof. A shared, current list keeps counts honest across countries and years. It helps health leaders spot rising resistance early and adjust first line drugs. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004824:
André Brunoni and colleagues performed a systematic review and meta review of placebo response in major depression trials, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Meta analyses show placebo responses are large in major depressive disorder trials. The placebo response of devices such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation had not been step by step assessed. Prompting comparison across pharmacological and non pharmacological interventions in this quantitative synthesis.

Placebo magnitude affects how true treatment effects are judged. Device trials may carry distinct expectation effects. Knowing baseline response improves trial design. Patients and regulators benefit from honest effect sizes. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004924:
Botulism is a paralyzing and often fatal disease. It is caused by botulinum neurotoxins, among the most potent toxins known. The toxins come from the bacterium Clostridium botulinum and exist in several serotypes. Miles Scotcher and colleagues studied one defense against them in PLOS ONE in 2009. They characterized F1-40, a lab-made antibody. F1-40 binds tightly to the type A toxin from the Hall strain.

The team mapped the exact spot where F1-40 attaches. They also read the sequence of its variable regions, the parts that grip. A precise blueprint like this can speed the design of antibody treatments. Such treatments are badly needed against a feared toxin.
plos-pone-0005024:
Ant trails are usually two-way roads. Outgoing and returning workers meet and touch along the way. Pedro Leite Ribeiro and colleagues trained ants on a different system. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The trails were made one-way. Outbound and homebound lanes were separated.

The ants learned to forage on the one-way trails. They reached food and returned by the assigned routes. Ant traffic rules proved flexible, not hardwired. The finding reshapes how we think about ant organization. Their road systems can adapt to new layouts. That flexibility may help colonies exploit changing environments. It also offers a tidy model for studying how simple rules produce orderly traffic.
plos-pone-0005124:
Rats are workhorses of medical research. Gene targeting, routine in mice, was not established in rats. Katarina Kotnik and colleagues built an alternative in PLOS ONE in 2009. They made transgenic rats with shRNA technology. The shRNA knocks genes down rather than out. A switch makes the knockdown inducible. Pronuclear microinjection created the animals.

The model was built for diabetes mellitus. Researchers can dial a gene down on demand. Timing control matters for studying disease onset. The rats fill a long-standing tool gap. They bring rat physiology within reach of modern genetics. Diabetes research gains a flexible new model. Other diseases can use the same strategy.
plos-pone-0005224:
People with fibromyalgia feel strong pain from pressure that others barely notice. Brain responses to pain can also last longer than the stimulus itself. Pujol and colleagues mapped those responses with brain scans in PLOS ONE in 2009, using a timing-based analysis.

Standard scan analysis can miss drawn-out responses, so the team tracked how activity unfolded over time. Their maps characterize how the fibromyalgia brain handles painful pressure. A clearer neural picture of this pain may help test treatments and give an objective handle on a condition often doubted.
plos-pone-0005324:
Copy number changes in DNA have opened new routes to find genes behind complex disorders like autism. The hard part is pinpointing which changed genes truly matter. Van der Zwaag and colleagues used gene-network analysis in PLOS ONE in 2009 to narrow the field.

Their analysis identified susceptibility genes related to glycobiology, the biology of sugar chains on proteins. Sugar chains guide brain wiring, so the link is biologically interesting. Network methods help turn long lists of candidate genes into a short list that labs can test. Sugar chains coat most cell parts and change how they meet. So a gene set from that world is a fresh place to seek the roots of how the young brain wires itself.
plos-pone-0005424:
Ge Li and co-authors wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE study on a brain protein and memory in older adults. The protein, called BDNF, helps nerve cells connect and change with use, most of all in the brain area tied to memory. The team asked whether low levels in spinal fluid track with weaker thinking skills.

They tested people who did not have dementia and compared fluid levels with scores on thinking tests. The work checks whether a simple fluid measure could warn of age-linked decline. Such a marker could help doctors spot risk early and follow how the aging brain changes.
plos-pone-0005524:
Sheng Sun and Jianping Xu studied chromosome changes in a fungus that infects people, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Cryptococcus neoformans can cause severe brain infection in people with weak immune systems. It comes in two main varieties, plus hybrids that mix the two.

The team compared the order of genes along chromosomes in the two varieties. They found places where blocks of genes had been swapped or flipped between them. Such shuffling may help explain how hybrids form and why some strains spread or resist drugs better than others. Such shuffling can also break up useful gene combinations, which may limit how freely the varieties can cross.
plos-pone-0005624:
Michael Chisamore and co-authors characterised a new blocker of a nuclear receptor in breast cancer cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The receptor ERR alpha is related to the estrogen receptor but has no known natural trigger. Compounds that block it could slow cancers that rely on it.

The team described a small molecule that blocks ERR alpha without hitting its close relatives. They tested it in a common breast cancer cell line. A selective blocker is both a lab tool and a possible first step toward a new drug class.
plos-pone-0005724:
Misagh Alipour and colleagues tested in 2009 whether wrapping antibiotics in fat bubbles helps them work in the thick sputum of cystic fibrosis patients. The lung germ Pseudomonas thrives in that sputum and resists many drugs. Sticky strands like DNA and actin in sputum can trap or weaken free drugs.

The team compared wrapped and plain forms of two antibiotics, tobramycin and polymyxin B. They checked how sputum parts block each form. Wrapped drugs that survive sputum could reach the germ at full strength. The results guide how inhaled antibiotics for CF might be built better.
plos-pone-0005824:
Mohamed Bouzaffour and co-authors watched two signal paths cooperate during zebrafish fin regrowth in 2009. A zebrafish can regrow a clipped fin fully, a feat mammals lack. The FGF path was already known to drive that regrowth.

The team found the SDF-1 path, which guides cell movement, interacts with FGF during regeneration. Signals must both build tissue and steer cells to the right places. Their crosstalk may be a general recipe for repair. Learning how fish coordinate it could inform efforts to improve healing in people, even if full regrowth stays out of reach.
plos-pone-0005924:
For many people with spinal cord injury, losing hand use hurts most of all. Eric Pohlmeyer, Emily Oby, Eric Perreault and colleagues reported a step toward fixing that loss in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their work links brain signals to electric pulses that make forearm muscles contract, a method called functional electrical stimulation.

The team tested the setup in a paralyzed monkey, aiming to restore a working hand grasp. Brain control could give users a more natural grip than preset patterns allow. The study shows the path from thought to muscle can be rebuilt, and it points toward aids that let injured people use their own arms again.
plos-pone-0006024:
