In wasps and bees, an unlucky mating can produce males with two gene copies, and such males are usually sterile or die young. Jan Elias, Dominique Mazzi and Silvia Dorn studied a parasitoid wasp that breaks that rule in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers a species whose sex is set by a single gene locus, a system called complementary sex determination.

Against expectation, its diploid males can reproduce, so the authors argue there is no need for the wasps to tell mates apart by risk. Fertile diploid males soften the genetic load that the sex system was thought to impose. The finding changes how biologists judge the cost of inbreeding in these useful insects, which farmers deploy against pests.
plos-pone-0006124:
Leukemia cells learn to shrug off the drug that once controlled them. Clara Aceves-Luquero, Anupriya Agarwal, Juan Callejas-Valera and colleagues found a driver of that resistance in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies imatinib mesylate resistance in chronic myelogenous leukaemia, beyond the well-known route of mutations in the drug's target, BCR/ABL.

ERK2, but not its close sibling ERK1, mediates both acquired and de novo resistance, the title reports. Splitting two near-identical kinases matters, because a drug can then block one and spare the other. The result gives CML therapy a concrete second target for cases where imatinib alone stops working.
plos-pone-0006224:
BAD is a protein best known for promoting cell death as part of the Bcl-2 family. Adrienne Smith and colleagues report a surprising twist in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper: making BAD in prostate cancer cells promotes tumor growth. Signals from growth pathways can switch BAD off by adding a phosphate tag.

The result flips the usual story of a death protein acting only as a brake. Context inside the cancer cell decides whether BAD helps or hinders growth. That nuance matters for drugs aimed at the Bcl-2 family. It warns that targeting one family member can yield effects opposite to expectations.
plos-pone-0006324:
Corals bleach when heat drives out the algae that feed them, and warming seas make it worse. Jessica Carilli and colleagues asked whether local stressors also weaken corals before heat strikes, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The question is fundamental to reef ecology: does chronic local harm reduce resilience to bleaching?

Local stressors do reduce coral resilience, the title reports. Reefs under pollution or other local pressure fare worse in hot periods. That gives local action real value even under global warming. Cutting local stress is one lever managers fully control.
plos-pone-0006424:
Bente Köten and colleagues published a 2009 PLOS ONE study of how human skin defends itself against germs. Skin can react fast to invading microbes by releasing proteins that kill them. One such protein is RNase 7. Because RNase 7 acts strongly against the gut germ Enterococcus faecium, the team explored its role more closely.

The study treats RNase 7 as part of the skin's first line of defense. It looks at how the protein helps the skin hold off this germ. Such work matters because skin germs can cause hard-to-treat infections. Knowing the skin's own weapons may guide new ways to support them.
plos-pone-0006524:
Antonio Ramos and co-authors designed a high-density genotyping assay for pigs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dissecting complex traits of economic importance to the pig industry requires many genetic markers. Single nucleotide polymorphisms, single-letter DNA differences, are the markers of choice. Next generation sequencing had newly identified and characterized many pig SNPs.

The team designed an assay to genotype those markers at high density. A good assay lets breeders link DNA to traits like growth and disease resistance across whole herds. That supports marker-based breeding decisions. The resource serves both farm economics and basic pig genetics.
plos-pone-0006624:
Mai Elobeid, Miguel Padilla, Theresa McVie, and colleagues reviewed missing data in weight-loss trials in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dropouts and missing data are nearly ubiquitous in obesity randomized controlled trials. They threaten validity and generalizability of conclusions. The team meta-analyzed the scope of the problem and the state of the field.

They also assessed performance of methods used to handle missing data. How dropouts are handled can change a trial's verdict. Diet trials lose many participants, making this a first-order issue. Their review gives trialists guidance on planning and reporting. It also helps readers judge published weight-loss claims skeptically.
plos-pone-0006724:
Chunliang Li and colleagues made mouse stem cell lines on human support cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Induced pluripotent stem cells draw huge interest for medicine and research. They can be screened for drugs and studied for basic biology. Most lines were grown on mouse embryonic fibroblast feeders. Those cultures usually needed an added factor called LIF to stay pluripotent.

The new lines were generated on human fibroblasts instead. They needed no added leukemia inhibitory factor from outside. The lines stayed germline-competent, the strictest test of quality. Germline competence means the cells can contribute to offspring. Human feeders reduce animal contamination worries for future clinical work.
plos-pone-0006824:
Fabio Verginelli and his team tied bowel cancer gene faults to place and food in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bowel cancer is blamed in large part on diet. Which foods count is still not clear, since so much is in play. Where a man lives shapes what he eats. The gene TP53 is faulty in a great many of these cancers.

The team read one kind of fault at CpG sites in TP53. The faults clumped by land and by place. They set those clumps next to food supply maps. Fault maps by land may keep a record of what men ate. Reading them could show which food risks are real.
plos-pone-0006924:
Kristian Remes, Francisco Ortega, Ignacio Fierro, and colleagues announced a new dinosaur in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their fossil came from Middle Jurassic rocks in Niger. It belonged to an early, basal sauropod, the group of giant long-necked plant eaters. Early sauropod evolution was poorly known because the fossil record is so incomplete.

The authors describe the new animal and place it among its relatives. They use it to rethink patterns in early sauropod history. Each new Jurassic find fills a real gap in the record. Finds like this one help show how sauropods grew into the largest land animals ever.
plos-pone-0007024:
Windy Boyd, Marjolein Smith, Grace Kissling, and colleagues modelled pesticide effects on worms in PLOS ONE in 2009. The nematode C. elegans is being tested as an alternative model for toxic chemical screening. Government agencies want faster, cheaper safety tests. Their assays record worm size with flow sorting machines.

The team built a math model for chlorpyrifos, a common insecticide. The model describes how the chemical changes worm development over time. A good model turns raw sorter output into clear dose measures. That helps regulators compare chemicals without testing each one in large animals.
plos-pone-0007124:
Aruna Balgi, Bruno Fonseca, Elizabeth Donohue, and colleagues screened compounds that tune cell recycling in PLOS ONE in 2009. A complex called mTORC1 senses nutrient supply inside cells. It controls many cell functions, including autophagy, the self-eating that starts when food runs low. Modulating that system has clear therapeutic promise.

Their screen found chemical modulators of autophagy. Among them were new inhibitors of mTORC1 signaling with possible medical use. Compounds that dial this hub up or down are valuable tools. They may serve in cancer and in diseases where cell cleanup fails.
plos-pone-0007224:
Jake Ormond and Melanie A. Woodin studied memory-related brain changes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The hippocampus plays a central role in forming memories in the mammalian brain. Its encoding power is thought to depend on plasticity, the ability of synapses between neurons to change strength.

Pyramidal neurons carry the main hippocampal output to the cortex. The authors examine a form of long-term potentiation in area CA1. They report that disinhibition, a lifting of normal restraints on neuron firing, mediates this strengthening. Their result adds a mechanism to models of learning in the brain.
plos-pone-0007324:
Michael D. Sumner, Simon J. Wotherspoon, and Mark A. Hindell presented a statistical framework for animal tracking in 2009. Reliable estimates of animal location, with honest error bars, are fundamental to animal ecology. Archival and satellite tags give noisy positions, and older handling methods were often ad hoc or used in isolation.

The authors build a Bayesian framework for estimating movement from tag data. Bayesian methods combine prior knowledge with observations to estimate locations and uncertainty together. Their PLOS ONE paper unifies location error handling. Ecologists can apply it to seals, birds, and other tagged animals.
plos-pone-0007424:
Heh-In Im and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the brain turns new learning into lasting memory. Locking in a memory requires the brain to build fresh proteins. That building work is controlled by several molecular switches, and how they act right after learning was poorly understood. The team focused on one switch, a protein-making factor called eEF-2.

Right after training, eEF-2 loses a chemical tag that normally slows it down. With the tag removed, protein building speeds up during the exact window when memories settle into long-term storage. The study shows that this release is not incidental. It actively supports the consolidation process. The result adds a concrete step to the chain between experience and stored memory.
plos-pone-0007524:
Rebecca Davis and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on nicotine and lung cancer. Nicotine is the addictive core of tobacco smoke. It is generally not thought to start cancer on its own. Yet it can make cells multiply and can encourage new blood vessel growth. The team asked whether those properties help existing lung tumors grow and spread in mice.

In mouse models of lung cancer, nicotine did exactly that. Tumors grew faster, and metastasis to new sites increased. The result warns that nicotine actively assists established tumors. That matters beyond cigarettes, since nicotine products are marketed as safer alternatives. A chemical that keeps smokers hooked may also feed their cancers. The study gives that concern direct experimental support.
plos-pone-0007624:
Ralf Linker and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 hunting for protein markers of multiple sclerosis stages. New biomarkers could predict the disease's course and reveal how it damages tissue. Most marker work focuses on early phases. This team profiled proteins during the later, chronic phase in mouse models of the disease. They compared the protein inventory against earlier stages.

The profiling yielded markers specific to the chronic stage. It also named culprits suspected in the ongoing tissue damage. Stage-specific markers could one day tell doctors where a patient stands. That knowledge guides how aggressive treatment should be. The mouse work cannot be copied straight to patients, but it supplies candidates. Each candidate is a hypothesis the clinic can test.
plos-pone-0007724:
Vedakumar Tatavarty and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It watches tiny structures in rat brain cells at very fine detail. Dendritic spines are small knobs on neurons where synapses form. Changes in their shape are thought to underlie learning and memory.

Inside each spine, a scaffold of actin fibers drives those shape changes. The team used super-resolution imaging to follow actin motion within single spines. Seeing movement at that scale was not possible with standard microscopes. The work gives memory research a sharper view of its basic machinery.
plos-pone-0007824:
Carol Kilkenny and co-authors published a survey in PLOS ONE in 2009. It grades how well animal experiments are designed, analyzed and reported. Good design matters for science, ethics and cost alike. A sound study wastes fewer animals and yields results others can trust.

The authors checked published animal research against basic standards. They looked at experimental design, statistical analysis and transparency of reporting. Much of the work fell short of what good practice requires. Their survey backs calls for minimum reporting rules. Better reporting would maximize the knowledge gained from every experiment.
plos-pone-0007924:
Nicolas Vermeulen and colleagues published a study of emotion and attention in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their work asks how the face a person sees shapes what the mind notices next. Fear and disgust are the focus, two feelings that push the body in very different ways.

People in the tests had to spot targets shown in quick bursts. A scared face before the burst made people miss less, while a disgusted face made them miss more. The authors read this as the senses opening wider under fear and closing down under disgust, each response fit for the threat it evolved to meet.
plos-pone-0008024:
Ralph Oude Ophuis and colleagues studied a tail-carrying form of a muscle disease protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein comes from the gene behind myotonic dystrophy, a disease that wastes muscle and traps it in spasm. Most past work chased the gene's repeated DNA stretch.

This form carries a small tail that anchors it in place. Cells bearing it dragged their power plants into clumps near the nucleus, began eating their own parts, and died more often. The result gives the disease a second suspect beyond the famous repeat.
plos-pone-0008124:
Steven Suhr and colleagues checked whether rewound human cells truly grow young again in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adult cells can be reprogrammed into stem cells with huge promise for patient-matched tissue. A fair test of youth is the telomere, the chromosome end cap that shortens as cells age.

The team tracked telomeres as the rewinding proceeded. Caps lengthened in the rewound cells, though not all lines reached the length of true embryo stem cells. The telomere reading gives makers a yardstick: a batch whose caps stay short may not be as fresh as it looks.
plos-pone-0008224:
Yi-Hsuan Lin and colleagues studied aging yeast cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Telomeres cap chromosome ends and keep them stable. Normally an enzyme called telomerase rebuilds those caps. Without it, yeast and tumor cells can use recombination to maintain telomeres instead. The team worked with senescent budding yeast, cells near the end of their dividing life.

They found that Rad51 and Rad52 proteins gather at short telomeres. That gathering triggers a Mec1-mediated sensitivity to DNA breaks. The result links telomere state to how old cells handle damage. It informs basic research on aging and genome stability.
plos-pone-0008324:
Thomas S. A. Wallis, Mark A. Williams, and Derek H. Arnold studied visual persistence in PLOS ONE in 2009. A shape defined only by motion can seem to linger after motion stops. It then gradually fades into the background. The team investigated whether that lingering impression is a real signal. They asked if it could improve objective sensitivity to static form.

Pre-exposure to moving form did enhance sensitivity to the static shape. Subjective persistence thus reflects a usable visual signal. The result shows motion processing leaves a trace that helps later seeing. It informs models of how the brain combines motion and form.
plos-pone-0008424:
Carlos Solis and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a way to turn genes off in a gut germ. The germ, Entamoeba histolytica, is a one-cell beast that lives in the gut and can make man quite ill. To learn what each of its genes does, labs must be able to shut a gene down and watch what fails. The tools at hand for that job, made of small RNA bits, still had flaws and were hard to use in bulk.

The team used RNA made by a far more plain germ, a bacterium, to shut genes down. Bacterial RNA is cheap to make in large lots. A cheap source makes gene tests in this gut germ much less hard. That speed can help find weak spots for new drugs.
plos-pone-0008524:
Melanie Cushion and co-authors test a drug class in rodent models in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Pneumocystis fungi cause pneumonia in hosts with weakened immune systems. They also worsen chronic diseases such as COPD. Treatment choices are limited, and the fungal life cycle is poorly understood. The team treat infected rodents with echinocandins. Those drugs attack the fungal cell wall.

Treatment depletes the cyst forms of the fungus. But trophic forms, the other life stage, remain in the lungs. Those remaining forms cannot transmit the infection to new hosts. The result splits the life cycle in a useful way for therapy.
plos-pone-0008624:
Pei-Wen Chen and co-authors study trafficking regulators in an amoeba in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Arfs and ArfGAPs regulate membrane trafficking and actin dynamics in mammalian cells. Their study organism is Dictyostelium, a social amoeba and model eukaryote. They identify a primordial Arf, called ArfA, and two ArfGAPs named ACAP-A and ACAP-B. Those proteins contain several classic domains for membrane binding and regulation. The team disrupt the ACAP genes and observe the amoebae.

ACAP-A and B prove involved in sporulation but not in chemotaxis. Sporulation is how Dictyostelium forms resistant spores to survive hardship. Chemotaxis, movement toward chemicals, proceeds normally without them. The split assigns a specific developmental role to these ancient regulators.
plos-pone-0008724:
Deborah Yoder-Himes, Konstantinos Konstantinidis, and James Tiedje hunted weak points in a stubborn germ. Their study ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. Burkholderia cenocepacia lives in soil yet infects people with cystic fibrosis. Lung infections with it are hard to cure. The species varies so much that single-strain studies miss shared weaknesses.

The team compared gene activity across strains of the germ. Shared patterns point to core habits the germ cannot drop. Those habits make better drug targets than strain-specific traits. Their list narrows the search for treatments that work across the whole species.
plos-pone-0008824:
Kazumasa Nakamura, Junpei Sasajima, Yusuke Mizukami, and colleagues linked a growth pathway to new vessels in pancreatic cancer. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pancreatic tumors are among the deadliest cancers. The hedgehog pathway helps drive their growth, largely through surrounding support cells. Tumors also need fresh blood vessels to expand. Bone marrow sends pro-vessel cells to help build them.

Hedgehog signaling raised two vessel-promoting factors in those marrow cells. They are Ang-1 and IGF-1. Blocking hedgehog might therefore starve tumors of new vessels. The link adds a stromal angle to pancreatic cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0008924:
Lina Guerra, Ami Albihn, Susanna Tronnersjö, and colleagues showed a famous cancer protein is needed to raise the DNA damage alarm. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. MYC drives growth, division, and cell death decisions in many cells. Cells with too much MYC die when their DNA is damaged. The ATM pathway runs the checkpoints that respond to such damage. Which MYC-controlled helpers act before the death pathway was unknown.

Without MYC, cells failed to activate the ATM-dependent checkpoints properly. Damage signals thus stalled upstream of the response. MYC emerges as a gatekeeper of genome surveillance, not just growth. The dual role deepens the puzzle of why cancers love MYC.
plos-pone-0009024:
Alessio Nencioni and co-authors watched breast cancer cells adapt to a targeted drug, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drugs like trastuzumab and lapatinib block HER2, a growth signal in some breast cancers. Many tumours resist them from the start or learn to resist over time. Surviving cells must switch on backup plans.

Under long HER2 blockade, the cells raised levels of the protein Grb7. Blocking HER2 freed a gene switch, FOXO3A, that Akt normally keeps off. That release lifted the brake on Grb7 production. Grb7 thus marks one escape route drug makers may need to close.
plos-pone-0009124:
Maria-Teresa Illnait-Zaragozi and co-authors fingerprinted a disease yeast collected across Cuba, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that causes grave infections, mostly in weak immune systems. Bird droppings are a likely source of the yeast in the environment. Typing methods for tracking this fungus were slow or hard to share between labs.

The team used a fast DNA typing method on samples from patients and the environment. Clinical and outdoor isolates could then be compared side by side. Cuba's isolates fell into several distinct family lines. Many lines suggest repeated arrivals, or a long local history for the yeast.
plos-pone-0009224:
Yang Zhou and co-authors published this lung study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It focuses on adenosine, a signal the body makes when cells are stressed or damaged. Adenosine levels rise in the lungs of people with chronic lung disease. Through its receptors, the signal can amplify long-term lung damage.

The team studied patients with two diseases: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. They measured how adenosine is made, broken down, and sensed in these patients. Both diseases showed changes in that system. Mapping those changes supports the idea of drugs that block adenosine signals to slow chronic lung disorders.
plos-pone-0009324:
Tristan Guttridge and co-authors published this shark behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many fish live in groups, but watching wild individuals interact is hard. Who meets whom, and how that changes over time and place, stayed mostly hidden. The problem is worst for wide-ranging animals like sharks.

The team describes new acoustic technology that logs encounters between tagged sharks. Each tag records when its wearer comes near another tagged shark. The logs build a social record without anyone watching. That record can reveal whether free-ranging sharks keep company by choice, a question basic to understanding their lives.
plos-pone-0009424:
Ronan Jambou and co-authors published this malaria genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Artemisinin drugs were about to become the world's main malaria treatment in combination therapies. Those drugs target a calcium pump in the malaria parasite called PfSERCA. Heavy drug use could select for pump variants that resist.

The team collected baseline sequences of the pump gene from parasites around the world. They mapped how its diversity is structured by geography. A baseline taken before drug pressure peaks lets future surveys spot real change. It is the reference point against which resistance would first appear.
plos-pone-0009524:
Jesse Meik, Michelle Lawing, and Andre Pires-daSilva studied island rattlesnakes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Speckled rattlesnakes live on fourteen islands off Baja California in Mexico. Island animals often evolve sizes unlike their mainland kin. Two island forms of this snake had been named as subspecies, mostly for their size. The team measured body size across populations.

They asked how size changed after the snakes reached each island. Their analysis traces the pace and pattern of that change. Island snakes form a clean test of claims about size evolution in isolation. The results feed the wider debate on why islands reshape the animals that live on them.
plos-pone-0009624:
Sina Saari and co-authors located a newly found enzyme in mouse kidney in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carbonic anhydrases are enzymes that help control acidity in the body. The kidney uses several of them to acidify urine. The newest family member is called CA XV. Earlier work had found its gene message in the kidney. This team found where the protein itself sits.

The protein occurs in the thick ascending limb of Henle and in the collecting ducts. Those are segments that fine tune urine acidity and salt. Placing the enzyme there assigns it a concrete job in kidney function. The map helps physiologists fit the newest enzyme into a well studied system.
plos-pone-0009724:
Bacillus subtilis is a common soil bacterium used widely in research. Reindert Nijland and colleagues worked with wild strains gathered from the environment, not lab stocks. Their method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wild strains often refuse the DNA tricks that work in the lab.

To study a bacterium's genes, scientists first need to get new DNA inside it. The team briefly switched on genetic competence, the state where cells take up outside DNA. That trick made wild isolates accept DNA changes like lab strains do. It opens genetic study of bacteria taken straight from soil.
plos-pone-0009824:
Some palm species grow male and female flowers on separate plants. Verónica Cepeda-Cornejo and Rodolfo Dirzo compared how the sexes divide their resources in three such palms. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Dioecious means male and female functions live on different individual plants. The team measured reproductive allocation, growth, defense, and damage from plant-eating animals. Males and females often invest differently, since seeds and pollen carry different costs. Three species let the authors test whether patterns repeat. The palms grow in the neotropics, the tropical zone of the Americas.
plos-pone-0009924:
Cancer cells survive by refusing to die when damaged. Nelly Buron and colleagues used mitochondria from human cancer cell lines to probe drugs that break that refusal. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The membrane in question is the mitochondrion's outer skin.

Mitochondria decide many cell deaths by opening their membranes. BH3 peptides and the drug ABT-737 push that membrane toward permeabilization, letting death signals escape. The team explored the mechanisms in isolated mitochondria. Understanding the trigger helps design drugs that kill cancer cells cleanly. Mitochondria sit inside nearly every human cell.
plos-pone-0010024:
Taranjit Gujral and Gavin MacBeath mapped a key cell signal system in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The Wnt pathway helps cells grow and divide, and faults in it are tied to many cancers. Most parts of the network were known, yet how they act together over time was not.

Using broad, measured, time-based methods, the pair tracked Wnt signaling across the whole system. They found new phases in how genes get switched on or off after the signal starts. That timing view matters, because a drug may work in one phase and fail in another.
plos-pone-0010224:
The authors were Sarah Green, David Studholme, Bridget Laue, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared genomes to trace a tree disease. A bleeding canker is spreading on European horse chestnut trees in northwest Europe. Its cause is a bacterium, Pseudomonas syringae pathovar aesculi, about whose origin and biology very little was known when it emerged.

By comparing seven gene sequences and whole genomes, the team traced its evolution and adaptation. They asked how this strain became a horse chestnut specialist. Knowing a new pathogen's past can hint at where it came from and how it may spread.
plos-pone-0010324:
H. Branch Coslett, Martin Wiener and Anjan Chatterjee studied how people judge time, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2010. Timing feels simple, yet the brain systems behind it were still unclear. Many clues, from animal work to brain scans, pointed to a deep brain area called the basal ganglia. Lesion studies, where damage already exists, offered another way to test that claim.

The authors worked with people who had harm in that region. Their results support the idea that separate brain systems handle separate parts of timing. Damage in one place does not break every kind of time judgment. That split helps explain mixed findings from earlier work. It also gives future studies a sharper map of which brain parts do what.
plos-pone-0010424:
Martin Gulliford and colleagues asked whether good diabetes care in local practices lowers eye disease risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diabetes can damage the retina and blind if unchecked. Practices in England are scored on hitting care targets, such as blood sugar control. The team linked those scores to cases of retinal disease found by screening. Patients came from the practices' own registered lists.

If better-scoring practices have less eye disease, the target system is doing real good. If not, the scores may reward paperwork over outcomes. Linking process scores to patient outcomes is how health systems learn. Eye screening gives a hard outcome that matters to patients. This study checks whether the numbers on a chart match sight saved.
plos-pone-0010524:
Syamantak Majumder, M. Ilayaraja and Himabindu Seerapu built a chick embryo model for studying blocked blood flow outside the body in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ischemia, starved blood supply, damages heart and other tissues. Existing study models worked mostly in living animals. No lab-dish version existed for clean, close study. The team created partial ischemia in chick embryos as an ex vivo system.

A dish-based model lets researchers watch damage unfold under controlled conditions. It also reduces the need for surgery on adult animals. Chick embryos are cheap, accessible, and ethically simpler than mammals. If the model mimics real ischemia well, drug screens become much easier. The study offers the field a new bench tool.
plos-pone-0010624:
Anna Lee and colleagues used worms to hunt for genes that interact with a signaling regulator, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The regulator, called gdi-1, helps control Rab proteins, which direct traffic inside cells. Disease often begins when signaling networks drift out of balance.

The team altered many other genes and watched which changes worsened or eased the effects of faulty gdi-1. Several partners emerged from the screen. Each partner is a possible lever for restoring balance. Work of this kind maps the web around one gene, so drug hunters can aim at the web, not just one strand.
plos-pone-0010724:
Nicole Noren Hooten and colleagues profiled tiny RNAs in blood cells from younger and older people, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs tune gene activity throughout life. Animal studies tied some of them to lifespan, but human aging patterns were largely uncharted when the work began.

Over eight hundred microRNAs were measured in white blood cells. A clear set rose or fell with age. Their target genes clustered in pathways for growth, stress, and cell survival. Blood-based markers of aging could one day help test whether a treatment truly slows aging, rather than just treating one disease of old age.
plos-pone-0010824:
Hagai Shemesh and co-authors published this plant study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Working with pea plants, they asked whether roots respond only to how rich a soil patch is right now, or also to whether its food supply is rising or falling over time. Different roots of the same plant were placed in patches where nutrient levels stayed steady or changed.

Plants grew more root in richer patches, as expected, but they also favored patches where nutrient levels were climbing. They did this even when another root sat in a patch that was richer at that moment. Shemesh and colleagues argue that plants can sense change itself, not just current conditions. That skill could help a plant invest where food is likely to be soon, a point of interest for farming and plant ecology.
plos-pone-0010924:
Jack Rowe, Samir Shah, Stephen Motlhagodi and co-authors published this review of diarrheal disease in Gaborone, Botswana, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Botswana carries a heavy HIV burden, yet the germs behind its diarrheal illness were poorly documented. The authors mined five years of national laboratory records to map them.

Thousands of stool samples were checked for bacterial and parasitic culprits, along with drug resistance patterns. About one sample in seven yielded a pathogen, with bacteria somewhat more common than parasites and a small share carrying both. The team also tested whether white or red blood cells in stool could predict which germ was present. Rowe and colleagues give clinicians a local playbook: which organisms actually circulate, and which antibiotics are likely to fail against them.
plos-pone-0011024:
Michael Jensen, Marilyn Fukushima and Ronald Davis published this synthetic biology methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Building genes from scratch is routine except when the DNA is rich in G and C letters, which fold into stubborn structures and misprime reactions. Software can rewrite such sequences, but that sacrifices natural sequences researchers may need to keep, so the authors tested two simple additives.

They compared polymerase-based and ligase-based assembly of two GC-rich fragments from cancer-linked genes, with and without DMSO and betaine. The additives did not help the assembly steps themselves, but during the amplification step both greatly improved the yield and specificity of the correct product. Jensen and colleagues give gene builders a cheap, sequence-preserving fix for a familiar failure, useful wherever GC-rich genes are studied.
plos-pone-0011124:
Lu, Chen, Huang and colleagues studied lupus and the brain in PLOS ONE in 2010. In lupus, the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. The team focused on an antibody that targets a nerve cell protein and asked how it harms thinking.

They found the antibody blocked the growth of axons, the long fibers that carry nerve signals. It also pushed nerve cells toward death. Together those effects explain part of the mental harm seen in brain involved lupus. Naming the pathway suggests treatments that shield nerve cells while the immune attack is controlled.
plos-pone-0011224:
Nishikawa and Shibata measured noise in a bacterial sensor in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacteria steer toward food by sensing chemicals, a system known for smart adaptation. Yet the sensor also fluctuates at random, and the authors asked how much of its behavior is mere nonadaptive wobble.

Measuring that noise sets limits on how precisely bacteria can sense their world. Even a well tuned system carries variation that serves no purpose. Knowing the noise floor helps modelers build faithful accounts of cell behavior. It is a reminder that biology works with, and sometimes despite, randomness at small scales.
plos-pone-0011324:
Wiens, Lee, Shimada and colleagues studied vessel growth in zebrafish for PLOS ONE in 2010. As a fish embryo grows, blood vessels must sprout between body segments in an orderly pattern. The team tested a receptor for a growth factor, called PDGF receptor beta, for its role in forming those intersegmental vessels.

The receptor proved critical: without it, those vessels failed to form properly. That names a required regulator in the vessel growth program. Zebrafish are a standard model for development, so the result maps a step shared by vertebrates. It also informs tissue engineering, where growing vessels into new tissue is a key hurdle.
plos-pone-0011424:
Malavika Subramanyam, Leland Ackerson, and S Subramanian compared two ways of knowing a baby's birth weight in India in 2010. Birth weight guides newborn care and national health tracking, but many Indian births happen without a scale. Programs then rely on the mother's memory, sometimes years later, or on a health card filled in at delivery.

The team compared weights from memory against card records to find where the two disagree and for whom. Memory tended to bend the numbers in patterned ways, rounding and drifting for certain groups of mothers and babies. Knowing the pattern of error lets health programs correct the data they already hold. It also tells survey designers when a card check is worth the cost, so infant health statistics rest on firmer ground.
plos-pone-0011524:
Marc Bajénoff and co-authors watched in 2010 as memory immune cells in the mouse spleen woke up against bacteria. Memory CD8 T cells persist after an infection and answer far faster the second time. The team visualized the earliest moments of that reactivation in the spleen as the cells confronted intracellular bacteria, germs that live inside host cells.

Seeing the defenders wake in real time revealed the choreography of the rapid second response: where the cells gather, how fast they activate, and which partners they meet first. That choreography is the physical basis of immune memory, the principle behind every vaccine. Knowing it in detail helps vaccine designers judge whether a candidate produces the right early dance, not just the right final antibody count. The study turns a textbook promise, faster the second time, into observed motion.
plos-pone-0011624:
Lee Hamilton and co-authors tested a growth signal long linked to building muscle, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lifting weights grows muscle, and a pathway involving the fatty signal PIP3 was thought to help drive that growth. The team set out to check whether hard exercise truly depends on tight control of that signal.

They measured the pathway's activity after resistance exercise and assessed its effect on muscle mass. Regulation of PIP3 turned out to play only a limited part in the response. The modest verdict redirects attention toward other signals that explain how training builds bulk, refining how exercise scientists model muscle growth.
plos-pone-0011724:
Carlos Blondel and co-authors tested a bacterial injection system in chicken infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One Salmonella type infects only poultry, while its relative Enteritidis colonises chickens quietly yet causes much human food poisoning. Both carry secretion systems, tiny syringes that inject proteins into host cells.

The team examined the system encoded in a region called SPI-19 and its contribution to colonising chickens. Their experiments show what this particular syringe adds for each serotype. Knowing the invasion tools involved points to steps that poultry vaccines or controls might blunt.
plos-pone-0011824:
Siew-Kee Low and co-authors ran a genome-wide hunt for pancreatic cancer genes in Japan, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pancreatic cancer gives a very poor outlook and ranks as the fifth top cause of cancer death in Japan. Past work hinted at some gene factors in its growth, but reports on common variants in Japanese people were few.

Scanning the genome in many subjects, the team searched for variants tied to the disease. Their Japan-centred hunt fills a long gap in cancer gene maps, which were built mostly from European samples. The finds may point to risk marks that matter for East Asian groups.
plos-pone-0011924:
Tatsuya Ogura and colleagues described in 2010 a gatekeeping system for the mouse vomeronasal organ, the nose structure that detects pheromones. Those chemical signals steer social and sexual behavior, but the organ must control what reaches its sensors to avoid overload or damage. Scattered solitary chemosensory cells sit at the organ's entrance.

The team shows these lone cells helping to regulate chemical access to the organ, responding to what arrives and adjusting entry. A sensor guarding a sensor is an elegant arrangement. It means the pheromone system can tune its own exposure, which may explain how mice stay sensitive to faint social signals without being swamped by strong ones.
plos-pone-0012024:
Li Liu and Ralph Mason demonstrated in 2010 a glowing way to watch a reporter enzyme at work inside living animals. The lacZ gene's enzyme, beta-galactosidase, is the most common reporter in biology, marking where genes are active. Historical detection methods required killing the animal or fixing tissue.

Using a chemiluminescent substrate, a chemical that emits light when the enzyme acts on it, the team imaged enzyme activity in human tumor grafts and in transgenic mice. Light from living tissue lets the same animal be followed over time. That is a practical gain for studies of development, tumor growth, and gene therapy, where timing is half the story.
plos-pone-0012124:
Resham Gurung, Shi Ni Lim, Aik Kia Khaw, and co-authors tested a plant compound against brain tumor cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer drugs often harm healthy cells along with tumor cells, so the hunt for compounds that strike tumors more selectively never stops. Their compound, thymoquinone, comes from black seed, a plant long used in traditional remedies.

In human glioblastoma cells, the compound shortened the protective caps on chromosomes, damaged DNA, and pushed the cells into programmed death. Glioblastoma is one of the hardest cancers to treat, so any selective killer draws interest. The work gives later studies a clear chain of effects to test in animals and, possibly, in the clinic.
plos-pone-0012224:
Tomonobu Watanabe, Atsuko Iwane, Hiroto Tanaka, and co-authors measured a molecular motor with one head instead of two, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosin-V normally hauls cargo along actin tracks in long strides, using two heads that step hand over hand like a climber. The hand-over-hand picture was popular but not fully proven, and a one-headed version offered a clean test of how stepping works.

Holding single molecules with optical tweezers, laser traps fine enough to feel one motor's tug, they measured the one-headed motor's steps and forces directly. What a single head can and cannot do limits every model of the pair. Such measurements ground the physics of the cell's delivery fleet.
plos-pone-0012324:
Umesh Wankhade, Kristen Vella, Dana Fox, and co-authors removed a gene in mice and watched their fat and cold responses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The missing gene, Nhlh2, makes a transcription factor, and mice without it grow obese as adults, move less, and handle cold abnormally. Torpor, the deep energy-saving state mice enter when food is short and cold bites, is one of the responses these animals perform badly.

Their fat tissue also showed reduced levels of the receptors that respond to adrenaline, the signal that orders fat burning. A defective torpor response ties a single gene to the whole energy budget: appetite, activity, and emergency savings. Such genes help explain why body weight is so stubbornly defended.
plos-pone-0012424:
Francesca Milano, Mirta Guarriera, Agnieszka Rygiel and colleagues studied the cancer drug trastuzumab in esophageal tumors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. This cancer is aggressive and often carries extra copies of the HER-2 gene, the drug's target. Trastuzumab is an antibody best known from breast cancer care, and it can also rally T cells against tumor cells.

The team found that the T cell attack only worked when the tumor's antigen processing machinery was intact. Tumors that break that machinery can dodge the immune part of the drug. Testing the machinery in patients could help predict who benefits from trastuzumab beyond simple HER-2 counts.
plos-pone-0012524:
Marta Pérez-Garay, Beatriz Arteta, Lluís Pagès and colleagues raised a sugar-coating enzyme in pancreatic cancer cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Cancer cells often wear altered sugar coats, and the enzyme ST3Gal III adds a particular sialic acid tag. Such tags can change how cells stick and crawl, the very skills a cancer needs to spread.

Raising the enzyme changed the cells' motility and adhesion in culture and boosted their metastatic potential in animals. Pancreatic cancer spreads early and kills fast, so any lever on its spread is valuable. The enzyme joins a growing list of sugar machinery that cancer drug research can target.
plos-pone-0012624:
Li, Cheng, Xia and co-authors tested a genetic route to prevent cataracts in mice. A cataract is any clouding of the eye lens, and it remains the top cause of vision loss worldwide. Surgery is the usual fix, so a way to prevent clouding would change care for millions.

Their 2010 study raised the level of a channel protein, connexin alpha 3, which links lens cells so they can share small molecules. Stronger links between lens cells helped keep the lens clear in their tests. The result suggests lens cell communication is a target for prevention research.
plos-pone-0012724:
Sorbye, Fismen, Gutteberg and co-authors assessed a test-and-treat plan for women with minor cervical changes. Cervical screening flags many mild cell changes, most of which clear on their own. Their 2010 data concern testing for the active message of HPV, the virus behind nearly all cervical cancer.

Using the HPV E6/E7 mRNA test at this triage step could let clinics treat the women at real risk and spare the rest needless follow-up. Smarter triage cuts anxiety, cost and clinic load. Their data feed the design of national screening rules.
plos-pone-0012824:
Wang, Lacroix, Haines and co-authors found a myelin-related RNA worker sitting in stress granules of glial cells. A mouse mutant called quaking viable trembles because its myelin, the insulation on nerves, forms badly. Its QKI gene makes RNA-binding proteins, and QKI-6 is one main form.

Their 2010 study shows QKI-6 gathers with the messages for MBP, the main myelin protein, inside stress granules when cells are stressed. That placement hints at how myelin messages are stored and guarded. The finding links stress handling to nerve insulation faults.  Cell stress was applied in a controlled, repeatable way.
plos-pone-0337024:
Simeng Zhang, Tao Zhang, and Xi Wang graded the design quality of fifty four central level artificial intelligence policies issued in China from 2016 to 2025. Text mining found frequent terms and linked themes, then a consistency index with nine main and forty three sub measures scored each policys structure. Five emblematic policies were scored in full visual detail.

Overall structure rated well built. Weak spots clustered in long term planning, coordination between government levels, and incentive design. Long horizon policies were scarce and support tools uneven. A repeatable scoring frame lets any country audit whether its AI rulebook hangs together, beyond praising or blaming single rules.
plos-pone-0337524:
Anna Brandmeier and a wide team of colleagues describe a planned study of teaching outside the classroom in Germany, where the approach is still new. Lessons held outdoors promise more movement, contact with nature, and relief from social isolation, but most past studies tracked only pupils. This project, spanning thirty-three schools, also measures teachers, classroom behavior, and the living richness of the outdoor sites themselves.

Outcomes on the list include teacher stress and well-being, pupils' thinking performance, school-related well-being, and how strongly both groups connect with nature. The design is exploratory and compares schools without random assignment, so it will show patterns rather than proof. As a protocol, it reports no results. Its interest lies in the breadth: few studies weigh an outdoor lesson's effects on everyone in the schoolyard at once.
plos-pone-0338524:
Gao and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test how well large language models fit the culture of Japanese work life. They look at five models, including one built in Japan, and ask native Japanese raters to judge replies to common work scenes. Their scoring draws on a well known frame of six cultural traits.

Native raters gave the top foreign models scores as high as, or higher than, the Japanese model. A closer look split skill into three layers: polite word forms, social values, and fitting action in context. On that split, the Japanese model leaned hard on surface politeness yet lagged on values and action. The authors argue that judging culture needs more than one score, since a single mark can hide weak spots in how a model acts.
plos-pone-0340624:
Teddy Lazebnik and Avner Friedman modelled a stubborn medical problem: skin wounds that heal slowly because blood flow is poor. Such wounds, often linked to diabetes, sometimes stay open far beyond the usual month. Their 2026 paper builds two very different mathematical models of the same wound, one based on equations for spreading cell populations and one simulating individual cells as agents.

Reassuringly, both models shrank the wound at nearly the same rate. They then tested oxygen treatments in the virtual wound. Standard pressurised oxygen closed wounds only when blood flow loss was mild, while oxygen applied directly to the skin worked at somewhat worse levels. The pair offers a way to screen therapies before clinical trials.
plos-pone-0341524:
Tonmoy Chowdhury and colleagues measure nomophobia, the dread of being without a mobile phone, among medical and university students in Bangladesh. Heavy phone reliance has been tied to distress and weaker study results, but local numbers were missing. Several hundred undergraduates from eight districts answered an online questionnaire built around a validated fear scale, pilot-tested for reliability, plus questions on habits, apps, and background.

The study reports how widespread phone fear is in this group and which traits track with it, from study field to daily usage patterns. Chowdhury and colleagues frame phone fear as a campus health issue in a country where student life runs through the handset. Their baseline numbers give Bangladeshi universities a starting point for guidance and support programs.
plos-pone-0342024:
Xiaowei An and three colleagues use game theory to study data sharing on big water projects. Their 2026 model covers dams and irrigation schemes with three players: contractor, designer, and owner. Such projects run long and scatter data across all parties. Working together on data could create value for everyone. The model compares decisions made jointly against each party deciding alone, and tests what government subsidies change.

Joint, centralised decision-making won clearly. It produced both a higher data value level and higher total returns. Subsidies raised every party's effort and payoff, encouraging participation. Costs dragged the other way. When contributing data is expensive for a party, its willingness drops sharply. Perceived usefulness pulled willingness up just as strongly. For project owners and governments, the lesson is practical. Pay down the cost of sharing and prove its usefulness, and partners will build data value together.
plos-pone-0342424:
Ghazal Khalili and Manaf Zargoush led a vast study of aging veterans. It asked how loss of daily function plays out over time. Most past work crushes that story into one score. This team kept the order and timing of change. They mined more than a million checks on daily tasks. The checks came from US veterans' nursing homes. More than two hundred sixty-five thousand residents were in the data.

Thirteen clear path types stood out. Short, harsh paths carried the worst death risk. The worst group lost near half its members in year one. Long, mild paths were far more stable. Mild loss might touch just walking or bathing. The team says path type can guide care plans.
plos-pone-0342524:
Zifeng Li led a team of seven authors setting out a review protocol on nurse burnout, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nurses who absorb the suffering of others can develop compassion fatigue, a deep exhaustion that harms both nurse and patient care. Many models claim to predict who is at risk, with mixed quality.

Li's protocol plans a systematic review that will appraise those prediction models critically. Sorting models that work from those that do not helps hospitals act early, before a nurse is in crisis. Publishing the plan in advance keeps the review honest. With nurse shortages worldwide, tools that truly predict fatigue, and trigger support in time, have clear practical value.
plos-pone-0342624:
Sarah Yeoh and Mai Stafford use routine health records to measure how poor English affects health in England, in this 2026 study. More than a million people in the UK speak English poorly or not at all, yet their health burden is rarely quantified. The authors drew on a linked database of GP, hospital, and social care records for the London borough of Brent, comparing residents by language proficiency.

People who were not proficient in English had higher rates of heart and metabolic conditions after accounting for age and sex. They also used both primary and hospital care more heavily than proficient speakers. The authors present the work as the first large, representative quantification of this gap in a UK setting. They call for language support to start at GP registration, and for records to capture language properly.
plos-pone-0343224:
Shahriar Afandizadeh, Saeid Abdolahi, and Hamid Mirzahossein set out to forecast traffic on Kandovan Road, a mountainous recreational route in Iran where holiday crowds, weather, and terrain make flows hard to predict. Their 2026 study trained eight different machine learning and deep learning models on traffic, weather, and calendar data spanning 2017 to 2023.

A random forest model won the comparison, tracking actual traffic most closely, ahead of several fashionable neural networks. Blending weather and event data with traffic counts clearly sharpened every model's forecasts. The team also built working software that shows live predictions, giving road authorities a planning tool for congestion, safety, and holiday surges on difficult mountain roads.
plos-pone-0343624:
Gustavo Vieira Veloso and co-workers compare ways to draw soil maps for farming in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais. Good maps of nutrients and texture guide planting and fertilizer choices. Their 2026 study pits two classic gap-filling methods against several machine learning models, using map position and grid layouts as inputs, and weighs accuracy against computing time.

Learning models clearly beat the classic methods at predicting soil traits such as clay and phosphorus. One forest-style model led on most traits, while another led on sand. Classic methods were faster to run, and learning models slowed as grids grew finer. For farms and agencies, the trade is clear: better maps cost more computing.
plos-pone-0345524:
Zeinab Ebrahimian and co-workers build a small bench-top model that lets liver and fat tissue talk to each other without pumps. How these tissues exchange signals drives obesity and diabetes, but animal tests are slow and costly. Their 2026 device rocks four linked chambers so fluid flows between liver-like and fat-like cells grown side by side.

Cells stayed alive through four days of drug testing. A drug known to cause weight gain raised fat storage and sugar and fat levels in the shared fluid. Two other compounds, one natural and one a standard diabetes drug, blunted those effects. The simple setup could screen drug side effects earlier and cut animal use.
plos-pone-0345724:
Nobuhito Muramoto and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns metastatic renal cell carcinoma, kidney cancer that has spread. The authors assess prognosis, the likely course of the disease, using two blood-based scores combined: one built on the systemic immune-inflammation index, the other on a ratio of C-reactive protein to albumin.

Both scores are built from routine blood tests, one reflecting inflammation and nutrition, the other immune cell balance. Judging whether the pair beats either alone helps doctors sort patients by risk cheaply. Oncologists treating advanced kidney cancer are the readers who could fold such combined scores into treatment planning.
plos-pone-0346324:
Yifei Huang, Zhiyuan He, and Cheng Ding teach a neural network to forecast trade balances. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It covers two hundred twenty-nine countries. Trade links form a web, so the team used a graph network. Such models learn from webs of linked points. Rival methods included deep networks, attention models, and tree ensembles.

The graph model won by a clear margin. It explained most of the spread in trade balances. Its errors stayed low across test runs. The team also ranked which inputs mattered most. That gives the forecast some explanation, not just a number. Sharper trade forecasts help exporters, importers, and policy makers plan.
plos-pone-0346424:
Jiajun Zhu and colleagues built a featherweight vision system that lets drones spot rooftop solar panels. Counting panels from the air helps cities track solar growth, but panels vary hugely in size and drones carry weak computers. Their 2026 paper adapts a popular detection network with a finer-grained detection layer and an attention block that adjusts to cluttered rooftops.

On their test set of drone images the system reached precision and recall above ninety-five percent while weighing only a few megabytes and running at over one hundred frames per second. That balance of accuracy and speed makes it realistic to run directly on the drone. The authors offer it as a practical tool for solar inspection work.
plos-pone-0346624:
Alexander Karner and co-authors tested a computer-based way to measure fear of spiders without bringing a real spider into the room. In their test, people slowly sharpen three blurred spider pictures, stopping at the point where looking still feels comfortable. The team compared scores from this task with trusted questionnaires and with a real-life approach test in which volunteers move toward an actual spider.

The computer scores lined up moderately well with both the questionnaires and the live test at first, though the link with the live test faded at a later follow-up. Karner and colleagues judge the test quick and easy but limited, since avoidance on a screen may not capture the full force of fear. They propose a refined version that keeps the simple task while mimicking real encounters better.
plos-pone-0346824:
Sheng Jin and six colleagues improve how unmanned tracked vehicles follow a path. Their 2026 study attacks two headaches at once. Such control is accurate but heavy to compute. Hydraulic drive systems, meanwhile, resist tidy physical modelling. Their framework splits control into two layers. The upper layer plans motion with a lean planning method using Laguerre functions. That slashes the work. The lower layer learns each hydraulic motor's behaviour from data instead of equations.

Simulations showed the planning layer's speed gain plainly. A single optimisation took about a quarter of the time conventional control needed. Real-time performance improved without surrendering control quality. A standard feedback controller in the lower layer added resistance to disturbances. Field tests on a real tracked vehicle followed. Speed and trajectory tracking both confirmed the design works outdoors, not only in simulation. Cheaper computation means smaller onboard computers can steer heavy machines precisely.
plos-pone-0346924:
Welelaw Necho Mulatu and a large team interviewed twenty-three supply chain workers and experts across Ethiopia about why contraceptives, maternal, newborn, and child health goods run out at small clinics. National reforms improved the upper levels of the system, but the last mile, health centres and tiny health posts, still fails patients. Interviews were coded into themes by setting, farming regions and pastoral regions alike.

Six bottlenecks recurred: erratic deliveries, poor data that nobody uses, sloppy stock keeping, weak forecasting of need, too few staff, and broken infrastructure. Pastoral areas added bad roads and thin cold storage, while health posts often fetched goods themselves. Extra hand-offs through district offices added delay everywhere. The authors map these frictions so reform money can be aimed at the exact points where supplies stall.
plos-pone-0347324:
R. Srivats and his team fused four known image nets to find landslides in shots from space and drones. One net can miss a faint slide or blur its edge. Bad maps can slow aid when hills fall. The fused net adds a fifth part, a rival pair that sharpens the edge of each slide it finds.

On three test sets, the scores ran from near ninety-four to near ninety-seven per cent. The sets span fine drone shots, mid space shots, and quake slides. The fused net beat each lone net by a clear gap. It also draws map-ready charts fast, fit for use right after a slide.
plos-pone-0348124:
Nigar Sultanova, Rasim Bayramov, and Narmin Maharammova measured face soft tissue thickness on three hundred CT scans of adults in Azerbaijan. Thickness at twenty landmarks, midline and paired, was split by three age bands, sex, and body weight class. Such tables guide face reconstruction from skulls in forensics and surgery.

Averages, spreads, and ranges were tabled for every landmark, with differences by age, sex, and weight reported. The set forms the first such database for Transcaucasia populations. Using tables from distant populations can distort a reconstructed face; local data give investigators and surgeons a truer starting point for Azerbaijani adults.
plos-pone-0348624:
Felipe do Carmo Jorge, Gabriel Politzer Couto, and Berndt J van Rensburg spent nights listening to an Australian open forest. Or rather, they let recorders listen. Then they asked whether simple sound measures can stand in for biodiversity after dark. Night ecology is understudied because sampling in the dark is hard. The team compared several acoustic indices, numbers that summarise a recording, against hand-counted insect sound types.

No single index did the job, but a blend of four, covering activity, evenness, and how full the soundscape is, tracked the richness of insect sounds well. Index patterns also matched how sites differed from each other. The authors caution that the recipe will not transfer unchanged to other habitats, yet they offer their procedure as a cheap way to watch nighttime ecosystems over long stretches.
plos-pone-0348724:
EDITORIAL NOTE: This notice updates an earlier Expression of Concern about a published study of virus communities found in fluid around the heart of patients with unexplained heart inflammation. The PLOS One Editors explain that the journal investigated whether the original study, which used samples from patients including minors, had proper ethics approval.

A university ethics representative in Marseille reported that an internal investigation found the study met ethical standards, since it only reanalysed samples taken during routine care. The journal, however, found that one of the study's authors sat on the very ethics board that approved the work. Because of that conflict, the editors say they cannot confirm the study received independent ethics review.
plos-pone-0349024:
Wenyan Xiao, Lin Zhang, and Yangshuyi Xu built a network that reads feelings from video by letting the words lead. Judging emotion from face, voice, and speech together trips many systems, because the channels disagree in quality and timing. Their design uses the transcript as an anchor: a gated attention step aligns sound and image against the text while damping noise. A second gating stage balances each channel's contribution before merging.

A contrastive learning scheme, also anchored on text similarity, keeps the merged representation honest to both shared and unique signals. On the two standard benchmark collections for this task, the system set new best scores for accuracy and robustness. The authors argue that giving text the anchor role, rather than treating all channels as equals, is the design lesson.
plos-pone-0349124:
Matthew M Harper and Nickolas A Boehme tested whether repeated short spells of low oxygen could shield mouse eye nerve cells from blast injury. Blast waves can harm the retina cells that carry vision signals to the brain, leading to slow nerve loss. Mice received six low oxygen sessions over two weeks, then a blast or sham blast, with eye function, structure, and cell counts checked a month later.

Blast mice lost signal strength and nerve layer thickness versus sham mice. Mice pretreated with low oxygen spells looked like sham mice on both measures, and surviving cell counts held up. Training the body with mild oxygen stress beforehand, the authors conclude, can at least partly protect vision nerves from blast harm.
plos-pone-0349224:
Tao Luo, Qingpeng Huang, and Jingyan Mai studied young people who have newly taken up farming in Guangdong Province, China, asking how their job skills are developing. Drawing on interviews and questionnaires across twenty-one cities, they traced three stages of a farming career: entering the field, putting down roots, and growing a business. Skill needs differ at each stage.

Young farmers' abilities fell into three layers: hands-on professional skills, general abilities useful anywhere, and core qualities such as judgment and commitment. Each layer grows best with its own kind of training. As more young people enter farming, matching training to career stage could help them stay and help villages renew their workforce.
plos-pone-0349624:
Ryo Murata and Kenji Tanaka propose a way to fill the gaps in pedestrian flow data by blending real measurements with simulation. Cities track crowds to plan streets and marketing, but sensors miss people, while simulations are complete yet ignore real human quirks. Their method borrows data assimilation, the fusion trick used in weather forecasting, and applies a particle filter to an agent-based crowd model.

Virtual pedestrians are continually nudged toward whatever the real sensors did capture, so the finished picture is both complete and realistic. The team tested the approach against three kinds of missing data. Better crowd pictures matter for evacuation planning and station design, where decisions are only as good as the flow data beneath them.
plos-pone-0350024:
Wenxin Jiang and Peng Liu compared two chemotherapy regimens for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, a fast-growing blood cancer, in patients whose tumors showed a high growth marker. One regimen adjusts doses upward over cycles, and the other is the long-standing standard. Earlier records from three hundred seventy-six patients set the marker level that counts as high.

Twenty-nine patients received the dose-adjusted regimen in a forward-looking study, matched against similar patients who got the standard one. Survival without the disease returning, and overall survival, did not differ meaningfully between the groups. Enrollment stopped early because benefit looked unlikely and recruitment was slow. For doctors, the result argues against choosing the harsher regimen on growth marker alone.
plos-pone-0350124:
Qiuyu Li led a study of two skills in Chinese undergraduates. One skill is computational thinking: breaking hard tasks into clear steps. The other is AI literacy: grasping what AI can and cannot do. Past work linked the two at one point in time. This team tracked two hundred sixteen students over time. They asked if the first skill builds the second.

Both skills grew across the study span. The modeling showed a clear push from the first skill to the second. The link held steady as both rose. The team says courses that teach step-wise problem solving lay real ground for AI smarts. They offer the design as a guide for course planners.
plos-pone-0350224:
Mohammad Abdul Karim Khan and four colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on blood flow and aneurysms. It is a computational investigation of nanoparticle effects on hemodynamics, the forces of moving blood, inside patient-specific aortic aneurysms, ballooned sections of the body's main artery shaped from individual patients' scans.

Alongside simulation, the authors use machine learning to predict those effects more quickly. Nanoparticles are studied as possible drug carriers, so knowing how they alter flow inside a weakened aorta matters for safety. Biomedical engineers and vascular specialists share the audience for a model built on real patient anatomy.
plos-pone-0350624:
José Alejandro Valdevila Figueira and co-authors tested what Ecuadorian health students know about Alzheimer's disease in 2026. With populations ageing, tomorrow's doctors, nurses, and psychologists will all meet dementia, and training gaps are easiest to fix early.

More than a thousand students, mostly nursing, took a standard knowledge scale. Average correct answers sat near fifty-five percent, a limited level. Medical students scored highest, with nursing and psychology behind. The authors call the gap urgent and propose stronger dementia teaching across all three programs. Knowing the baseline by discipline lets universities aim the remedy where it is weakest.
plos-pone-0350824:
Brown and colleagues compared gut microbes of Eastern indigo snakes, wild and captive, in a 2026 study. The snake is a threatened species native to the American Southeast. Samples from the rear opening stood in for gut samples across three groups: captive snakes with a gut parasite, captive snakes without it, and wild snakes.

Gene sequencing measured microbe variety and mix in each group. Captivity and infection each can reshape a reptile's gut community, and separating their effects matters for breeding programs. Knowing the normal microbe profile helps keepers spot illness early and may guide release choices for captive-bred snakes.
plos-pone-0350924:
Hai Huang and co-authors built a way to score how much cultural value a heritage building holds, working in Longxing Ancient Town in Chongqing, China. Conservation teams often argue about value without a shared yardstick. The team reviewed two decades of writing on cultural value, then interviewed shop owners and visitors in the town and convened heritage experts to shape the criteria.

The finished scale sorts value into five kinds: local, historic, sustainable, scientific, and aesthetic, with twenty-four finer measures beneath them, weighted by a structured ranking method. Because owners, visitors, and experts all fed into it, the scale reflects how a town actually experiences its old buildings, not only how specialists do. Other historic towns could adapt the same scaffold when deciding which buildings to protect first and why.
plos-pone-0351124:
Rudy Brogi and colleagues asked whether the ways scientists catch wild chamois quietly filter which animals get studied. If bold animals walk into nets more easily, behavior research built on caught animals would lean bold. The team compared two methods, drug darts and drop nets, in an Alpine herd, then watched twenty-five tagged adults alongside untagged herd mates.

Key behaviors like eating, standing, and resting proved consistent within each animal, so they could fairly test for bias. Neither capture method ended up over-sampling the risk-takers: shy and bold chamois alike turned up in the caught group. That all-clear matters because personality studies across wildlife rest on the assumption that traps do not pick personalities. At least for this large herbivore and these two methods, the assumption held.
plos-pone-0351224:
Cecilia Camacho-Hubner and seven colleagues survey doctors across Latin America about a stealthy heart disease. Their 2026 study concerns transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, where misfolded protein stiffens the heart. The disease is progressive, fatal, and badly under-recognised. Four hundred seventy physicians in eight countries answered questionnaires during 2023. They described their knowledge, attitudes, and the barriers they hit in diagnosis and treatment.

Knowledge was thin. Only about half the doctors understood the disease's basic mechanism. Patients reportedly consulted four or five physicians before anyone confirmed the diagnosis. Cardiologists carried most day-to-day management. Genetic testing for the transthyretin gene was available to barely a quarter of respondents. The key drug's cost and access blocked treatment often. Most local practice simply borrowed international guidelines. The authors map a fixable problem: train front-line doctors to suspect the disease sooner, and widen access to testing and therapy.
plos-pone-0351324:
Linking power grids flexibly lets regions share electricity and cuts waste, but planners must first forecast demand well. Xiaoyan Zhao and colleagues paired a hybrid forecasting network with a chaos-driven search method to design such links, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The forecaster reads past load at several time scales, mixing pattern-spotting and memory layers. A new measure scores how well regions' demands complement each other hour by hour. The search algorithm then tunes the system's layout against balance, reliability, cost, and that complementarity score. Tests showed very small forecast errors, and the authors claim the combined approach designs cheaper, steadier interconnections.
plos-pone-0351424:
James Dickson Fiagborlo, Mexoese Nyatuame, and Stella Ahone Ntoko surveyed just over one thousand farm households across five areas of Ghanas Volta Region. Land wear harms soil and deepens rural poverty, yet uptake of better land care stays uneven. The survey asked how training and farm size shape what farmers would pay for such care, split by gender.

Training raised willingness to pay, and the effect ran stronger for men. Larger farms also paid more, since owners had more means to invest. Women started lower but gained fast when land access and training improved. Gaps thus look driven more by blocked access than by lack of interest. Fair training and land rights, the authors argue, are central to wider uptake.
plos-pone-0351624:
Justin Ofosu-Dankwa, Cristina Sisu, and Rhona Anderson examine the genomes of British nuclear test veterans in this 2026 study. These men served at Cold War nuclear test sites decades ago. Many worry the radiation left marks on their DNA. The team compared thirty veterans with thirty age-matched control veterans. Whole-genome data were processed with standard best-practice pipelines.

Somatic mutations, the small DNA changes gathered over a lifetime, were counted and classified. No variant type appeared more often in the test veterans. Tight mutation clusters, a suspected radiation fingerprint, were also no commoner. The dominant mutation signatures in both groups were the usual ones left by ageing itself. The null result cannot rule out every possible harm. Still, it offers these veterans evidence that their genomes carry no obvious excess burden.
plos-pone-0351724:
Rules against sexual harassment are clear on paper at a large Swedish university, yet Jack Palmieri, Frida Pilgaard, and Anette Agardh found daily norms tell another story. Their 2026 PLOS One study ran ten staff discussion groups, split by whether members managed others.

One theme covered everything: harassment is viewed through silence, power, and shifting boundaries. Staff described limits being negotiated on the spot, with women often checking with peers while men called the same behavior harmless. Prestigious senior researchers were seen as untouchable, and managers felt unsure how to act. Silence, many said, protected careers more than honesty would.
plos-pone-0351924:
Wonil Chung and Keonwoo Koo studied how GPT language models handle focus, the spotlight inside a sentence. Focus tells a listener which piece of news is at issue. The team used cut-off sentences with two possible completions. A question before the sentence set one spotlight. The small word only set another, placed before different items. Word-by-word surprise scores showed which ending each model expected.

The question's spotlight ruled in the first tests. It beat even a competing only. When only stood before the second object, the word-level spotlight grew stronger. It began to bend the expected endings its way. The models weigh the two cues in a graded tug-of-war, not by fixed rules. That matters wherever emphasis changes meaning in a text.
plos-pone-0352024:
Magreth Theophil, Ally Lyimo, and Joel Ambikile surveyed four hundred twenty-six adults on HIV treatment in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, asking whether their kidneys were being screened as guidelines advise. HIV and its medicines both strain kidneys, and catching damage early changes care. Records and questionnaires fed a search for what separates the screened from the missed.

Screening uptake was surprisingly high, about ninety-four percent. Patients with stronger immune counts were more likely screened, while those attending clinic only every six months were far less likely, an obvious contact effect. Oddly, patients who recalled a provider recommending screening had lower odds, a puzzle the authors flag rather than explain. In a system straining to follow its own guidelines, attendance rhythm, not distance or wealth, marked who slipped through.
plos-pone-0352124:
Zelan Wu and seven colleagues hunt for gene patterns linking inflammation, platelets, and heart failure. Their 2026 study merges bulk and single-cell gene data from human heart tissue. A protein pair called NEK7 and the NLRP3 inflammasome sits at the centre of their suspicion. Platelets, famous for clotting, also stoke inflammation. The team used network analysis and machine learning to find genes moving with both processes. A diagnostic scoring chart was drafted from the results.

Four genes formed the signature. All were turned up in failing human hearts. A mouse model of heart failure, driven by a hormone infusion, echoed the pattern for most of them. The signature also tracked with scarring genes, fitting the fibrosis story. The authors are explicit that this generates hypotheses, not proof. Still, a blood-or-tissue signature tying platelet activity to heart failure could eventually guide both diagnosis and anti-inflammatory treatment choices.
plos-pone-0352324:
Hong Nguyen-Thi and four colleagues tackle secure, energy-saving wireless design in a 2026 engineering study. Their setting is a future 6G network. Smart reflecting surfaces bounce signals to where they are needed. Several users share the same channel under a scheme called NOMA. A friendly jammer interferes with a hidden eavesdropper.

The goal is twofold: keep messages secret while wasting little energy, and treat the worst-off user fairly. The team trained a Double Deep Q-Network, a reinforcement learning method, to set power levels and surface angles. Its performance was compared with a standard learning method and with random settings. Simulations covered both shared-channel and separate-channel designs. The results highlight the shared design's edge in balancing secrecy against energy use.
plos-pone-0352424:
Shahab MohammadEbrahimi and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One spatial analysis of heart and circulation hospital admissions in Mashhad, Iran's second-largest city. More than fifty thousand admissions from 2016 to 2020 were mapped and tracked over time to find when and where the burden concentrates.

Admissions followed a repeating yearly rhythm and rose steadily until late 2019, when they dropped sharply. Men accounted for slightly more than half of cases, and the typical patient was in the mid-sixties. Mapping showed clear clustering: the city center formed a high-risk zone where admission risk ran many times higher than elsewhere. The authors say prevention and hospital resources should target that core, and offer the analysis as a template for other cities.
plos-pone-0353524:
Oronel and colleagues, in a 2026 animal study, trace how blocking a hormone system in newborn rats disturbs the growing kidney. Some adult diseases, including high blood pressure and kidney trouble, are now thought to start with early-life stress on development. The hormone endothelin helps kidneys form, and the team blocked its receptors during the first days of life.
