Treated male pups showed more oxidative damage in the kidney and a worse balance between a protective gas, nitric oxide, and harmful oxygen radicals. Activity tied to nitric oxide fell in the very structures that become the kidney's filters. Female pups were partly protected, with differences in several protective enzymes and hormone signals. Cell growth and cell death also fell out of balance. The authors argue these early chemical shifts may be the first steps toward the adult kidney problems seen in earlier work.
plos-pone-0354124:
Dongmiao Zhang and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for mapping which surface types of a dangerous newborn bacterium dominate around the world. The bacterium is a strain of E. coli that escapes the gut. It is a severe threat to newborns. Its O antigen, a variable coat component, is the leading candidate target for a protective vaccine. Yet nobody has charted its global variety in this age group.

The planned study will fuse two evidence streams. One is published serotype reports from four databases. The other is serotypes predicted from genome sequences in three public archives. Each strain's disease, site, year, and origin will be extracted. The verdict it seeks is strategic: one multivalent vaccine for the world, or regional recipes.
plos-pone-0354524:
Liu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, examine natural killer cells inside triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks the usual drug targets. These immune killer cells should attack tumors, but in this cancer they often arrive immature and weak. Using public single-cell data, the team sorted the killer cells found in tumor tissue into three subtypes.

One subtype, the strongest killer, was scarcer and weaker in triple-negative tumors than in other breast cancers. Its cells carried more of a brake receptor that switches them off. Signals from neighboring immune cells appeared to set that brake. A second subtype, marked by an alarm gene, was more active in these tumors, and high levels of that gene tracked with worse patient outcomes. The strong subtype's signature, by contrast, tracked with better outcomes. The authors say releasing the brake on killer cells is a concrete target for new treatments.
plos-pone-0354724:
Kelsey Thompson led a team of six authors on this 2026 focus group study of clinicians who treat children with pediatric feeding disorder. In this condition, eating breaks down for medical, nutritional, skill, or emotional reasons. Twenty-five providers in seven groups described their training and daily work across all four areas of the condition.

Training varied wildly between professions, clinics lacked easy access to specialist backup, and everyone wanted fuller yet workable care that honors family views. Thompson calls for earlier teaching, mentorship, and ready evidence-based resources to lift patient care.
plos-pone-0354824:
Gökşen Polat and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study in Türkiye of people whose chronic diseases leave them disabled. Twelve adults holding official disability reports described their daily limits and what they expect from disability services. Recruitment ran through clinics and personal referrals during 2024.

Disability spilled into social, cultural, school, and work life. Although services are a legal entitlement, many participants barely knew what existed or could not reach it. Polat argues the gap is informational and structural, and that fixing awareness and access matters as much as passing laws.
plos-pone-0354924:
Kaiyue Du and colleagues built lifestyle-based risk models for keratoconus, a disease that thins and bulges the cornea. They used records from 711 patients at a Chinese eye center, 275 of them with the disease. Their 2026 study combined standard regression with seven machine learning models. The models were fed demographic and habit data. The team then asked the models to explain which factors mattered most.

Seven risk factors stood out. They included male sex, higher body mass, and less schooling. A more distant childhood home and allergic conjunctivitis counted too. Above all stood rubbing the eyes, harder and more often. The best model sorted patients with fair accuracy. Because eye rubbing is changeable, the authors see a practical opening. Flag high-risk patients early, and coach the habit away before corneas deform.
plos-pone-0355124:
Rogers Kamulegeya and seven colleagues systematically review artificial intelligence models that predict whether tuberculosis treatment will fail, in this 2026 meta-analysis. Failure fuels transmission and drug resistance, so early warning matters. Searching two major databases for a quarter-century of work, they gathered thirty-four studies, most published since 2019, and pooled the accuracy of nineteen of them covering over one hundred thousand patients.

The pooled discrimination looked promising, but the ground beneath it was shaky. Results varied enormously between studies, models performed notably worse in groups including people with HIV, and only a quarter of studies had validated their model on outside data. Just one study earned a low overall risk-of-bias rating, and the analysis detected signs of publication bias. The authors conclude these tools are not ready for routine care and prioritize rigorous external validation in high-burden settings.
plos-pone-0355224:
Rafael Borges and three colleagues examine whether who you have worked alongside predicts reaching ministerial office in Portugal, in this 2026 network study. They scraped the membership of Portuguese governments and parliament over a decade, plus officials' interest registers, and built a network linking people who shared institutional venues. Then they asked whether network position, computed before the fact, screened out future ministers better than chance or a simple career-ladder rule.

It did. Their centrality-based screen caught over half of the in-network ministerial appointments, far above the baselines. Ministers also showed systematically higher institutional reach than colleagues who never made cabinet, with the sharpest gap inside party structures, where ministers scored about double on one key centrality measure. The authors are careful to call the work exploratory, but it suggests appointments flow through relational position, not just résumés.
plos-pone-0355724:
Mirjana Grdinić-Rakonjac and Vladimir Pajković survey more than thirteen hundred licensed drivers in a developing country, in this 2026 case study. They asked about four risky behaviors: speeding, drunk driving, seatbelt use, and phone use. Because crash deaths fall hardest on poorer countries, and because habits differ by road type, they compared men and women separately on high-speed, regional, and urban roads, adjusting for age and experience.

Men were generally more prone to speeding and drinking and driving. Yet women reported significantly more extreme speeding, far over the limit, on high-speed roads, a reversal of the usual pattern, while also buckling up more reliably on regional and urban roads. Both sexes texted and used social media behind the wheel at similar rates, and overall risk awareness was higher than the authors expected. They recommend campaigns aimed at men in cities and at speed among women on fast roads.
plos-pone-0356524:
Pooja Panth and three colleagues studied cancer patients at Bhaktapur Cancer Hospital in Nepal, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. How patients view their illness shapes how they cope, seek care, and keep going through treatment. Panth's cross-sectional study linked those views to resilience, the capacity to bounce back under strain.

The team surveyed patients and compared illness views with measures of resilience. Some beliefs track with stronger coping, while others track with despair. Knowing which views help lets counselors support the beliefs that sustain patients, and gently challenge those that drag them down. In a setting with few support services, that guidance helps staff focus scarce time where it lifts patients most.
plos-pone-0356624:
Alexandra N Sheldon and colleagues reviewed 173 infected artificial joints treated at one center over nearly a decade. All were treated with a joint-saving operation. Surgeons cleaned the implant and kept it rather than replacing it. The team asked which germs doom that approach. Their 2026 retrospective study graded success as lasting eradication without further surgery. It tested fungal, resistant, mixed, and culture-negative infections against the odds.

Two thirds of cases were cured. Fungal infections almost always failed, carrying heavier illness burdens besides. Infections where no germ could be grown were nearly four times likelier to clear. That is a hopeful sign for a frustrating category. Resistant and common skin bacteria also dragged success down. The authors suggest microbe identity should steer the choice between saving and replacing a joint.
plos-pone-0357124:
John Adeleke used Nigeria's 2024 national health survey to ask whether household wealth protects children equally against two kinds of undernutrition. One is stunting, the slow height loss of chronic deprivation. The other is wasting, the rapid weight loss of acute shortage. His 2026 analysis covered more than nine thousand children. It adjusted step by step for other social and geographic factors.

Wealth showed a clear graded link with stunting. Each step up the wealth ladder came with less of it. For wasting, wealth showed no link at all. Adeleke reads the split through one idea. Money buys protection against slow, cumulative harms more readily than against sudden illness or food shocks. Programs fighting wasting, he argues, need tools beyond poverty relief.
plos-pone-0357824: Agrawal and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on sleep apnea using electronic health records. Obstructive sleep apnea makes breathing stop and start during sleep, and it is tied to stroke risk. The team measured how common it is, split by age and sex, along with related conditions. The data set was large and cross-sectional. Clear rates help clinics plan screening for a disorder often missed.
plos-pone-0358224:
Quan Pham Hong leads a team of five designing a neural network that listens for damage in structures, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Bridges and towers betray cracks through subtle changes in how they shake. The warning signs are brief blips in narrow frequency bands. Models that read only the time signal miss the frequency story; models that transform the whole signal lose track of when each frequency occurred. Their network, SpectralTCN, is built to keep both.

Inside each layer of a temporal convolutional network sits a wavelet gating module. It splits the signal into sub bands that correspond to vibration modes. The network then decides how much of each band to keep. Then it rebuilds the signal before moving on. Because wavelets preserve timing and frequency together, a short damage signature keeps its moment and its pitch. The design targets inspection of structures that cannot afford missed hints.
plos-pone-0358424:
Mohamad Kazem Dehghani, Reza Ghasemi-Fasaei, Sajjad Abbasi, and Amin Mojiri wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plants and pollution. Working with spinach grown in water rather than soil, they study nanoplastics sprayed on leaves. The question is how these tiny plastic particles change the plant's handling of cadmium, a toxic metal.

The responses depend on both time and concentration, so the authors track uptake and the metal's movement from root to shoot under different doses. Cadmium in leafy vegetables is a food safety concern, and plastic particles are now common on farms. Plant scientists and food regulators share an interest in how these two pollutants interact.
plos-pone-0359224:
Sivarama Prasad Tera and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an explainable AI framework for detecting cancer from skin lesion images. Explainable means the system shows its reasoning, not just a verdict, which doctors rightly demand before trusting software with diagnosis.

Skin cancer caught early is usually curable, so faster and more reliable screening saves lives. An imaging framework that explains itself can also teach, showing trainees which features drove a decision. Dermatologists and medical imaging researchers are the readers weighing whether this framework is ready to support real clinics.
plos-pone-0359424:
Darío López-Delgado and eight colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a review that will gather studies systematically and pool them in a meta-analysis, on infections passed through sex, among women who are pregnant and who are migrants or refugees. Pregnancy plus displacement is a double vulnerability, and infections in pregnancy endanger both mother and child.

The review will gather prevalence figures, how common these infections are in this group, from studies worldwide. Migrant and refugee women often fall outside routine screening systems, so pooled prevalence can expose a hidden burden. Maternal health services designing outreach for displaced women are the audience waiting for this synthesis.
plos-pone-0359524: The PLOS One Staff published a 2026 correction notice in PLOS ONE. It amends an earlier scoping review about coach learning in youth participation sport. A correction keeps the public record straight when a detail in a published paper was wrong. Readers who cited the review can now check what changed. Notices like this are a small but real part of how science fixes its own record.
plos-pone-0359624:
Naim Gheymoumi and four colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies experimental allergic rhinitis, the laboratory version of hay fever's nasal inflammation. The treatment candidate is kynurenic acid, a natural compound made from the amino acid tryptophan, tested for whether it attenuates, or eases, the allergic response.

The authors tie the effect to the AhR receptor, a pathway that keeps immune activity in the nose in balance. A natural compound that calms nasal allergy through this pathway interests drug developers seeking gentler options than steroids. Allergy researchers are the core readers.
pmc-11168924:
Abramson, Adler, Dunger, and co-authors introduce AlphaFold 3, a model that predicts how biological molecules fit together. AlphaFold 2 had already changed the field by predicting protein shapes with high accuracy. Many teams then used it to model proteins and design new ones.

AlphaFold 3 extends that power from single proteins to interactions between molecules. It uses a substantially updated design built around a diffusion approach, the same broad family used in image tools. Predicting how drugs and other molecules bind their targets could speed drug discovery and deepen basic biology at once.

robertson-works-vol-2-1824:
The Works of William Robertson continue into volume two of the nine-volume edition of 1824. Robertson, who issued his histories from 1759 onward, wrote the past of nations as a single, connected advance. His History of Scotland, his Charles V, his America, and his Disquisition on India make up the gathered set.

In each field Robertson joined archives to argument, telling not only what happened but how society itself had changed. His calm, elevated style won readers far beyond Britain. The Works were the standard shelf form of his achievement for a century. Volume two holds its share of that achievement, from northern kingdoms to southern empires, in one historian's steady hand.
robertson-works-vol-3-1824:
Volume three of Robertson's Works, in the collected edition of 1824, carries on the nine-volume set. William Robertson published his first history in 1759 and soon stood in the front rank of European letters. The Works bind his Scotland, his Charles V, his America, and his study of ancient India into one uniform whole.

Robertson's histories trace how manners, laws, and commerce grow together across the centuries. He was the Scottish Enlightenment's great popularizer of that broad view of the past. Students of America and India still cite his volumes as starting points in their fields. Volume three keeps the set's wide world in view, told with its usual poise.
robertson-works-vol-4-1824:
Robertson's Works reach volume four in the nine-volume edition of 1824. William Robertson, whose writing career in history began in 1759, became the model of the philosophical historian in Britain. The set gathers the fruits of that career: Scotland, the Emperor Charles V, America, and the Historical Disquisition on India.

His pages move from Highland clans to Mexican temples with the same inquiring calm. Robertson asks in each place how peoples lived, traded, believed, and were governed. That method, history as the study of society, shaped generations of writers after him. Volume four stands mid-set, holding its portion of one of the Enlightenment's widest historical minds.
robertson-works-vol-5-1824:
Volume five stands at the center of the 1824 Works of William Robertson, nine volumes in all. Robertson issued his histories from 1759 and won a European name beside Hume and Voltaire. The Works collect the History of Scotland, the History of Charles V, the History of America, and the Historical Disquisition on India in one edition.

Across those fields Robertson practiced a single art: clear narrative steered by reflection on manners and causes. His America taught Britain about the Spanish conquests; his India opened ancient eastern trade to his readers. The middle volume of the set holds that range in balance. Robertson's calm authority fills every part of it.
robertson-works-vol-6-1824:
William Robertson, the Scottish historian, stands with Hume and Gibbon among the masters of Enlightenment history. Volume six here forms part of the nine-volume Works of 1824. The Works gather his History of Scotland and his History of Charles V. His History of America and his Historical Disquisition on India stand with them. Robertson wrote with a broad, philosophical sweep across nations and ages.

His histories joined deep research to a clear, elevated style that readers across Europe admired. The Charles V made his name; the America and the India carried his reach worldwide. A single volume of the Works holds a cross-section of that range. Volume six keeps the set's portrait of its author whole: Scotland's great practitioner of philosophical history.
robertson-works-vol-7-1824:
The Works of William Robertson reach volume seven in the nine-volume edition of 1824. Robertson, principal of Edinburgh University and royal historiographer, published his famous histories from 1759 onward. His books on Scotland, on the Emperor Charles V, on America, and on India form the core of this collected set.

Robertson's gift was scope joined to calm judgment: he wrote the history of continents as one connected story. His account of Charles V opened a new era in English history writing. The Disquisition on India showed his range reaching to Asia's ancient trade. Volume seven carries its share of that wide, ordered vision. The set preserves Enlightenment historiography in full dress.
robertson-works-vol-8-1824:
Volume eight of the 1824 Works of William Robertson stands one volume from the end of the nine-volume set. Robertson's histories, issued from 1759, made him a leader of the Scottish Enlightenment's historical school. Scotland, the reign of Charles V, America, and India all came under his pen, and the Works bind them together.

His method joined narrative grace to a philosopher's search for causes in society and manners. Readers in his day placed him beside Hume, and the comparison still instructs. This volume holds part of that achievement in the standard collected form. To read through the Works is to watch history become a science of human progress, in one master's hands.
robertson-works-vol-9-1824:
Volume nine completes the Works of William Robertson in the edition of 1824. Robertson, publishing from 1759, had gathered his histories of Scotland, Charles V, America, and India into a single fame. The nine uniform volumes of 1824 gave that fame its lasting shelf form for the century that followed.

The closing volume ends the set as Robertson's work deserves, in the company of all his great subjects. His school of history, calm, connected, and alive to society's growth, ruled British taste for decades. Readers finishing the Works hold the Enlightenment's historical project nearly entire. Robertson taught his age to see the past whole, and volume nine sets the last stone.
russell-icarus-1924:
Icarus, published in 1924 in the To-day and To-morrow pamphlet series, is Russell's dark little prophecy about the future of science. Written against J. B. S. Haldane's sunny Daedalus, it warns that knowledge multiplies power faster than wisdom.

Russell foresees science used to sharpen war, tighten propaganda, and extend the reach of governments and great firms. He doubts that ordinary human nature will improve to match its new tools. The pamphlet is brief, bleak, and often quoted, a founding text of the debate about technology's dangers. Its title is the whole argument: wings, wax, and the sun.
scott-hermetica-vol-1-1924:
Walter Scott spent years building his monumental edition of the Hermetica, published from 1924. The Hermetica are Greek and Latin writings ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage. Volume one gives the texts with facing English translation.

Readers find the Corpus Hermeticum, the Latin Asclepius, and excerpts preserved by Stobaeus. A long introduction untangles the writings' tangled history and authorship. These dialogues treat God, the soul, and the cosmos in mystical terms. They shaped Renaissance magic and later spiritual movements deeply. Scott's first volume became the standard English Hermetica of its age.
spr-proceedings-vol34-1924:
Volume thirty four binds parts eighty nine through ninety two, dated 1924. The SPR Proceedings are in their fifth decade, and the format holds. Experiments in thought reading appear with their chance scores computed. Long trance reports, checked line by line, fill the center.

Spontaneous experiences, from hauntings to death bed visions, arrive in steady flow. The society's committees sift them by rules set in the census years. Physical phenomena stay rare and closely watched in these parts. Volume thirty four is a late brick in the central archive. It documents a debate that shaped how Britain argued about survival. The record stays, as ever, open.
suess-face-of-earth-vol5-sollas-1924:
Volume 5 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1924, completing the English set. Eduard Suess had died in 1914, and his great synthesis closed with this volume. Sollas's translation project had run for twenty years by its end.

The final volume draws the threads together into a completed global geology: continents, oceans, and mountain systems in one account. Suess's Earth, cooling and contracting, ordered the facts his age possessed. Within decades, continental drift and then plate tectonics replaced that frame, yet his terms and maps endured. The volume completes the most ambitious work of geology written by a single author in the nineteenth century.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-vol-1-of-2-1924:
The Buddenbrook family of Luebeck rises through trade in the first half of Thomas Mann's great saga. The text is Helen Lowe-Porter's 1924 English translation, Volume One of two. Wealthy merchants across the early 1800s fill its drawing rooms: consuls, senators, and their carefully married children. Mann was twenty-five when the novel made him famous.

Mann traces the firm's prosperity and the family's vitality together, with ironic tenderness for both. Christenings, weddings, and business deals mark the generations as the century turns. Seeds of decline already hide inside the success, for readers who watch closely. The novel that eventually won Mann the Nobel Prize begins with this confident ascent. Few family sagas open at such full stretch.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-vol-2-of-2-1924:
Decline governs the second half of Buddenbrooks, in Lowe-Porter's 1924 English translation, Volume Two of two. As the nineteenth century wears on, the Buddenbrook energy drains away into art, illness, and introspection. The firm's grip loosens as each generation finds commerce less natural than the last.

Thomas Buddenbrook holds the house together by will until the effort consumes him. His son Hanno, frail and musical, closes the line with his early death. Mann renders a bourgeois dynasty's fall with love rather than scorn, which gives the book its ache. The portrait stands among the most moving in European literature. Readers finish the two volumes feeling they have lived a whole family's century.
taylor-mystical-hymns-orpheus-1824:
Thomas Taylor published his translation of the Orphic Hymns in a second edition in 1824. The hymns are ritual songs of the Orphic mysteries of ancient Greece. Taylor first issued his rendering in 1792 and later revised it.

Each short hymn calls upon a god with offerings and storied titles. Night, the Stars, Sleep, and Death all receive their invocations. Worshippers chanted these hymns at secret rites two thousand years ago. Taylor's verse keeps a strange, solemn music in English. He believed in the hymns' spiritual power, not merely their antiquity. His version became the classic English Orpheus for later occult and literary readers.
temple-word-of-lalla-1924:
Richard Carnac Temple gave English readers his own rendering of the sayings of Lalla in The Word of Lalla the Prophetess, printed at Cambridge in 1924. Lalla, or Lal Ded, was the fourteenth-century mystic of Kashmir whose vakhs passed by mouth for five centuries. Temple's edition stands independent of the Grierson and Barnett version of 1920.

Short, fierce verses tell of her leaving home, her guru, her dance of joy in the self, and her scorn for rite without love. Temple adds an introduction, notes, and an index to guide the reader. He reads her as a prophetess of the inner life for all faiths. The two English Lallas of the 1920s still frame her for the West.
theodori-kerckringii-doctoris-medici-anm: Theodori Kerckringii Anmerckungen, 1724. The Kerckring notes. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
tob-0144-54824:
Blavatsky called The Secret Doctrine, published in 1888, her masterwork, and volume one bears the subtitle Cosmogenesis. She claimed its core came from the secret Stanzas of Dzyan, an ancient text few others have seen. The volume explains how the universe unfolds in great cycles.

Worlds appear, evolve through rounds, and dissolve, again and again, over spans too vast to picture. Matter and spirit are two faces of one reality. The style is dense and demands patience, with long quotes from science and scripture. For Theosophists, Cosmogenesis stands as the movement's deepest account of where everything came from.
tob-10024:
Thomas à Kempis, a fifteenth-century monk, wrote the devotional guide known in English as The Imitation of Christ, here in an alternative translation as The Following of Christ. Only the Bible has been read more widely among Christian devotional books. Its chapters are short and direct, meant for daily use.

Kempis urges humility, warns against vanity and idle learning, and teaches readers to imitate Christ in ordinary life. Much of it reads like quiet counsel from a wise friend rather than formal theology. Saints and skeptics alike have carried the book for six hundred years, returning to its plain call to turn inward.
tob-10824:
William Q. Judge's American Theosophical magazine The Path, in its first volume for 1886-87, shows the movement's work in the United States. Contributions by various Theosophists mix practical spiritual advice with defenses of Blavatsky and reports from the lodges. Compared with Blavatsky's Lucifer, the tone is less flamboyant and more workmanlike.

Theosophy appears here as a lived discipline: study, meditation, ethics, and organized local work. News from branches shows a young occult movement building itself month by month. Readers interested in how ideas travel will value the volume as a record of American Theosophy finding its own voice beside the louder London center.
tob-13324:
A different edition of Brother Lawrence's classic presents the lay brother's method of turning kitchen work into prayer. Letters from Lawrence and the recollections of those who knew him carry the teaching. He was a Carmelite lay brother in seventeenth-century Paris, assigned to the kitchen and later to sandal repair.

Lawrence's method needs no retreat: return the mind to God, again and again, in the middle of ordinary tasks. Short enough to finish in one sitting, the account is deep enough to practice for a lifetime, as generations of readers testify. Comparing editions shows how stable the core of his conversations and letters has remained.
tob-4024:
René Descartes put out his Discourse on the Method in 1637. In it he sets rules for the search for sure truth. Doubt all that can be doubted. Split hard tasks into small parts. Move from the plain to the hard. Take as true only what is clear and plain.

In the course of the tale comes the most famed line in all thought: I think, therefore I am. From that one firm point Descartes builds back out to God, the world, and the sciences. The short book stands as the birth deed of modern rational thought. A reader can finish it in an afternoon and argue with it for life.
tob-4224:
Francis Barrett published The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer, in London in 1801, and English occultism revived around it. Barrett compiled natural magic, magnetism, Kabbalah, alchemy, and the evocation of spirits into one grand summa, much of it drawn from Agrippa and older masters. His school of magic taught from the book.

Plates of talismans, circles, and spirit forms give the volume its famous look. Bulwer-Lytton studied it for his novels; the founders of the Golden Dawn studied it for their rites. Verified from the 1919 edition, Barrett's Magus remains the great English grimoire-compilation of the Romantic age.
un-ga-res-24:
When the League of Nations died, its work had to go somewhere. Resolution 24, passed by the General Assembly on 12 February 1946, maps the handoff. Under a web of treaties and deals, the League and its arms had long held tasks that some states wished the new UN to keep alive. League members told the Assembly they would move, at the League's last meeting, to bless the steps set out here.

The Assembly keeps a free hand. It may refuse any one task after fair study. For each task it takes, it will name the UN arm or linked agency fit to hold it. Out of this dry text grew the UN's quiet grip on old League work, from drug pacts to refugee files.
un-ga-res-a-69-24:
Jerusalem's status stands at the core of Resolution A/69/24, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the 1947 partition vote and its terms for the city. It recalls a long chain of later votes as well. In them, the Assembly held that all steps by Israel, the occupying power, to change the face or status of the Holy City are void and must be undone.

One target is named: Israel's so-called Basic Law on Jerusalem, and its claim of the city as its capital. The Security Council in 1980 chose not to accept that law. The world court in 2004 ruled on the wall built in the held land. Through all these cites, the stance holds firm: the city's fate must be settled by talks, not by one side's acts.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 24, adopted on 12 February 1946, arranged the handover of League of Nations work to the United Nations as the League was wound up. The Assembly stated that the United Nations was willing, in broad terms, to take over certain duties and powers the League had held under treaties and other agreements.

The plan split the work three ways. The Secretariat would keep custody of treaty texts and handle filings and notices. Technical and non-political duties would pass after review by the Economic and Social Council. Political duties would be judged case by case. The League's library, archives, health and opium work, and its assets were also to move over.

Resolution 69/24 of the General Assembly (2014) is devoted entirely to Jerusalem. It recalls the 1947 partition plan's provisions for the city. It recalls the Assembly's earlier rulings. Under them, Israeli measures changing Jerusalem's character and status are null and void. Those measures include the 'Basic Law' proclaiming it Israel's capital.

The Assembly repeats that any Israeli action imposing its laws, jurisdiction, and administration on the city is illegal and without validity. It calls for an immediate stop to such measures. It voices grave concern at settlement activity, home demolitions, evictions, and excavations around religious sites. It stresses that a final solution must protect both sides' legitimate concerns. It must guarantee freedom of religion and free access to the holy places for people of all faiths.
un-sc-res-1024:
The Golan Heights force won its usual renewal in November 1995. On 28 November 1995 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 May 1996. The Secretary-General had reported on the force earlier that month. The decision follows the mission's standard wording. UNDOF has watched the Israel-Syria separation line since 1974.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. A report from the Secretary-General was due at the end of the term. It would cover events in the area. It would also list steps taken to apply 338. The Council treated the renewal as routine business. The calm it guarded was anything but guaranteed.
un-sc-res-1224: Catalogued with a 1999 date, Resolution 1224 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-124: Ghana became the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence in March 1957. Days later, on 7 March 1957, the Security Council considered its membership application. The Council recommended to the General Assembly that Ghana be admitted to the United Nations. The vote was unanimous. The whole text is one sentence. Ghana's entry opened the door to the great wave of African admissions that followed.
un-sc-res-1324:
The wait for a referendum in Western Sahara stretched on in the autumn of 2000. On 30 October 2000 the Council extended MINURSO until 28 February 2001. The Secretary-General's envoy was still trying to bridge the parties. Deep differences over the Settlement Plan remained open. The plan promised the people of the territory a free vote on their future.

The Council voiced full support for the envoy's work. It expected the parties to keep trying to solve the plan's problems. It also held out the hope of an agreed political solution to the dispute. The Secretary-General had to assess the situation before the new term ended. The deadlock in fact outlasted many such renewals.
un-sc-res-1424:
Prevlaka's observers won a further term in the summer of 2002. On 12 July 2002 the Security Council authorized UNMOP to keep monitoring the peninsula. The demilitarized zone sat between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Secretary-General's June report guided the vote. Ties between the two governments kept improving. A joint border commission was at work.

Both sides had to stop breaking the demilitarized regime. They had to work with the observers and ensure their safety and free movement. The Council urged faster progress toward a negotiated settlement of the dispute. It also encouraged steps to build confidence. The mission's quiet watch was nearing its end. The two states settled the issue later that year.
un-sc-res-1524: Security Council Resolution 1524 is held in this collection as a transcription of the United Nations official record. The Wikisource source line is part of its identity: this is the record text, not a retelling. Inside, opening clauses frame the problem and numbered paragraphs deliver the Council's answer, in the order the members agreed.
un-sc-res-1624:
Resolution 1624, adopted in 2005 at a summit of world leaders, targets the preaching that leads people to terrorism. Rather than weapons or money, it focuses on words: calls to carry out attacks and praise for those who do. The Council asked states to outlaw such incitement.

Inside, members are urged to keep suspected terrorists from crossing borders and to share information with each other. The text also warns states to respect free speech and refugee law while acting. It stands out among terror resolutions because its subject is propaganda, and how far governments may go to silence it.
un-sc-res-1724: Resolution 1724 is one of the Security Council's numbered formal acts, preserved in official wording through Wikisource. The text speaks with the combined voice of fifteen states, five of them permanent members. What that voice said on this occasion is kept entire in the entry, from the first recalling clause to the last decided paragraph.
un-sc-res-1824: The Council adopted Resolution 1824 on the Rwanda war crimes tribunal on 18 July 2008. Judges' terms were set to end that December, yet trials would run into 2009. Fresh arrests of senior accused in late 2007 and early 2008 had pushed the timetable back. The Council extends the terms of nine permanent judges and seventeen temporary judges to 31 December 2009. Two appeals judges serve to the end of 2010. The step keeps the completion plan on track.
un-sc-res-1924: Resolution 1924, adopted in 2010, is preserved here as a Security Council decision in official-record form. The transcription comes from English Wikisource. Inside the text, the members recall their earlier steps in the matter before taking the next one, and the entry keeps that continuity visible, which is how the Council's practice actually accumulates.
un-sc-res-24: Security Council Resolution 24, adopted in April 1947, concerned applications by states seeking to join the young United Nations. In the council's second year, membership bids from states on both sides of the late war raised hard questions. The text deals with how such bids were to be handled and passed on. Hungary was among the states whose hopes were tangled in this early bargaining; it in fact waited until 1955 for its seat. The record shows admission becoming an early Cold War contest.
un-sc-res-324:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force won a further six months in December 1972. On 12 December 1972 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 June 1973. The Secretary-General had reported that the force was still needed for peace. Cyprus's government agreed it should stay past 15 December. Conditions on the island, as his report described them, left little choice.

The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions back to 1964. It urged all sides to act with restraint. It also pressed them to speed up work toward the Council's goals. The text voices hope that progress would soon allow a cut in the force. That hope framed many renewals of a mission now decades old.
un-sc-res-424:
Rhodesia's armed invasion of Zambia on 6 March 1978 was condemned on 17 March 1978. Zambia's letter and its foreign minister set out a long list of hostile acts. Innocent people had been killed and hurt, and property destroyed. Three days earlier the Council had condemned the regime's aggression against its neighbors.

The Council strongly condemned the recent armed invasion by the illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia. It praised Zambia and the other front-line states for backing the Zimbabwean people's struggle for freedom. The liberation of Zimbabwe and Namibia and the end of apartheid were restated as the price of justice and lasting peace in the region. Britain, as the administering power, was called to take prompt and effective steps to end the regime. The Council decided that any further violation of Zambia's sovereignty would bring it back to weigh measures under the Charter, sanctions among them.
un-sc-res-724: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 724, which the catalog dates to 1991. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Another routine but vital Golan Heights renewal came on 28 November 1995. Resolution 1024 passed unanimously that day. The UN Disengagement Observer Force had stood between Israel and Syria since 1974. Its mandate was about to expire. The Secretary-General's report of 17 November 1995 informed the decision.

Members renewed the force for six additional months, through 31 May 1996. They paired the extension with a call on both sides. Both were urged to act on Resolution 338 of 1973. The Secretary-General was asked to report when the period closed. His report would cover events and progress toward that older resolution.

Security Council resolution 1224 (1999) briefly extends the mandate of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 11 February 1999. It asks the Secretary-General to keep the Council informed of all significant developments. The developments are in putting the Settlement Plan and the agreements between the parties into effect. Where appropriate, he is to report on whether MINURSO's mandate remains viable.

Ghana led black Africa into the UN with this vote of 1957. On 7 March, the Council adopted Resolution 124 without dissent. Ghana had won freedom from Britain the day before. It was the first sub-Saharan colony to do so after the Second World War. The new state applied to the United Nations at once.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Ghana. Ghana took its seat the next day. Its leaders pledged that Ghana's freedom meant little without Africa's full liberation. The pledge set the tone for the years ahead. Within three years, seventeen more African states passed through the same door.

Four more months for the Sahara vote mission came in October 2000. On the thirtieth, the Council adopted Resolution 1324 without dissent. The Secretary-General had just sent his October report. His Personal Envoy won warm praise in the text. The mission, MINURSO, had sought since 1991 to run a vote on the territory's future.

The text extends the mandate to 28 February 2001. It voices the hope that the parties keep trying under the envoy. Their deep gaps over the vote plan still had to close. A deal both sides could accept was the stated goal. The Secretary-General must assess the state of play before the term ends.

The Prevlaka cape watch gained a short new lease in 2002. UN men had kept eyes on the demilitarized cape since 1992. Croatia and Yugoslavia both claimed the small point of land. Peace there had held firm and calm. The chief's report of 28 June 2002 told a bright tale. Resolution 1424 passed with no dissent on 12 July 2002.

The watch ran to 15 October 2002. Both sides had to end breaches of the no-arms zone. The UN men needed safe, free range to do their work. Warm words marked the thaw in ties. A joint border team had been set up. The Council told both sides to speed a deal on the cape. If word of a pact came, the watch's length would get a fresh look.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 30 January 2004, and the Abkhazia peace process is pushed into a more structured form. High-level meetings of the Group of Friends in Geneva had given the talks new momentum. Georgia also had new leadership after presidential elections that month.

The lack of progress on a settlement is again called unacceptable, and those who shot down a UNOMIG helicopter in 2001 remain unidentified, the Council notes. Both sides are urged to work steadily in the Geneva task forces on economic cooperation, refugee return, and political and security questions. Those talks rest on a paper setting out how powers might be divided between Tbilisi and Sukhumi.

Incitement to terrorism is the target on 14 September 2005, during the World Summit in New York. World leaders were gathered at the United Nations for the summit. The text builds on the binding counter-terrorism duties of resolution 1373 and on later measures against listed terrorist groups.

All states are called on to pass laws banning incitement to commit terrorist acts, to prevent such conduct, and to deny safe haven to anyone credibly linked to it. States are also asked to strengthen border security and document checks, and to deepen dialogue among civilizations to undercut extremist propaganda. Steps taken are to be reported to the Counter-Terrorism Committee, and all counter-terrorism action must respect human rights and refugee law.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is set up again on 29 November 2006, for a further period. The transitional federal institutions still struggled to build effective national government, and fighting between them and the Union of Islamic Courts sharpened the need for oversight. The embargo itself dated from 1992 and kept being breached.

The Secretary-General, working with the sanctions committee, is asked to set the group up again with its standing task of tracking arms flows and reporting violations. The African Union, the regional development authority, and the Arab League are praised for backing reconciliation in Somalia. Somali leaders are urged to take real steps in political dialogue, and the transitional institutions to keep building national governance.

The Rwanda tribunal's judges are kept on to finish their trials in Resolution 1824, adopted on 18 July 2008. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was working to its Completion Strategy. Remaining trials were now projected to run to December 2009. Its president had written to the Council on 6 June 2008 about judicial terms.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the two Appeals Chamber permanent judges until 31 December 2010, or until the appeals finish if sooner. The Trial Chamber permanent judges and the ad litem judges, serving and not yet appointed alike, are extended until 31 December 2009 on the same condition. It also amends Article 11 of the Statute. The amendment caps the Chambers at sixteen permanent and nine ad litem judges. It lets Trial Chambers sit in sections of three judges with full powers.

Côte d'Ivoire was still divided after years of crisis when the Council adopted Resolution 1924 on 27 May 2010. The United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, known as UNOCI, was waiting for a review of its mandate. A new report had just set out recommendations for how the mission's work should change.

Acting under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, the Council extended UNOCI's mandate until 30 June 2010. The mission kept the tasks set out in an earlier resolution. For the same short period, French forces kept their permission to support UNOCI, within the limits of their deployment and abilities. The brief renewal held everything in place. The Council could then decide on a fuller redesign of the mission.

Botswana stepped out of British protection in September 1966. The arid southern African territory had been called Bechuanaland. Its leaders applied quickly for a UN seat. Resolution 224 was adopted unanimously on 14 October 1966. The vote came two weeks after independence day.

Members recommended Botswana's admission to the General Assembly. Admission followed within days. Botswana was poor, landlocked, and ringed by white-minority regimes. Its founding president, Seretse Khama, chose steady democracy. The country later became a model of stable governance in the region. Diamonds, found soon after independence, transformed its economy. This single-line resolution records the quiet legal moment when Botswana joined the community of states.

Hungary applied to join the United Nations on 22 April 1947. The country was emerging from the Second World War on the losing side. Its application reached the Council eight days later. Resolution 24 was adopted on 30 April 1947 by ten votes to one. Australia cast the only no vote.

The text does not admit Hungary or reject it. Instead, it sends the application to a specialist body. The Committee on the Admission of New Members would study it. That committee would then report back at the proper time. The resolution captures one early step in the UN's slow, political process for judging would-be members after the war.

The last calm Cyprus renewal before the storm came in December 1972. On the twelfth, the Council adopted Resolution 324. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China held back. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-December.

The text restates the whole Cyprus series through June 1972. It urges the parties to speed up joint work in the hopeful climate. The posting then runs to 15 June 1973. The standing hope closes the text once more. Progress by then might let the force shrink or go home. Eighteen months later, a coup and an invasion split the island for good.

Rhodesia's armed raid into Zambia is condemned in Resolution 424. It passed by a full vote on 17 March 1978. Zambia's foreign chief told of raid after raid by the white-led rebel regime. The raids broke Zambia's skies and soil, killed and hurt the blameless, and wrecked homes and goods. They peaked on 6 March 1978 with troops crossing the border in force.

The Council's wrath had a long past, which it spelled out. Texts from 1973 and 1977 had condemned the same regime for the same acts, in Zambia and in two more states. It restated the right of Zimbabwe's people to rule their own land. Freeing Zimbabwe and Namibia, and ending South Africa's race laws, were named as the roots of true peace in the region.

Arms still reached Yugoslavia despite the embargo of 1991, and the Council moved to make the ban work better in December that year. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 11 December, had found that conditions for sending peacekeepers did not yet exist. Resolution 724 followed that report. Its adoption date is given as 14 December 1991 in the chain of later resolutions.

The Council approved the report and agreed that the time for a peacekeeping force had not come. All states were told to report within twenty days. Their reports had to set out the steps taken to enforce the embargo. A committee made up of the whole Council was created. It would collect those reports and follow up claims that the embargo was being broken. It would also recommend ways to make the ban bite harder.
velleius-paterculus-compendium-shipley-1:
Velleius Paterculus served as a soldier under Tiberius in Germany and wrote his Compendium of Roman History around 30 CE. Frederick W. Shipley's Loeb translation of 1924 carries the text. In two short books Velleius runs from the fall of Troy to the reign of Tiberius, his own master.

He writes as an insider of the Augustan age, the only connected account of it by a man who served in it. Praise of Tiberius flows freely, and scholars read him with that in mind. His quick portraits of great men are sharp and warm. The little book shows how the new empire wished its past to look.
waite-brotherhood-of-the-rosy-cross-1924:
Waite dug the Rosy Cross out of legend and set it in documents in 1924. The Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross tells the history of Rosicrucianism from its first prints onward. The tale begins with the manifestos that burst on Germany in the early 1600s.

Waite prints and weighs the Fama, the Confessio, and the claims of a hidden brotherhood of wise men. He asks what was real, what was jest, and what was hope in the famous story. Later study of the Rosy Cross stands on the ground he cleared. The book splits the history from the myth with a firm hand.
walter-map-de-nugis-curialium-tupper-192:
Walter Map, a witty clerk at the court of Henry II, wrote De nugis curialium, the Trifles of Courtiers, in the twelfth century. Tupper and Ogle Englished it in 1924. Map mixes court satire with ghost stories, fairy tales, and sharp gossip about the great men he served.

King Herla rides forever with his wild hunt through these pages. Walter also tells of vampires, fairy brides, and men raised from the dead. Between marvels he mocks the greed and folly of courtiers, his own class. The mix makes it the twelfth century's most entertaining book. The 1924 translation keeps Map's voice lively for modern readers.
wharton-false-dawn-1924:
Edith Wharton wrote False Dawn as the first of her Old New York novellas, a set of four tales about the city across four decades. It appeared in 1924 and covers the 1840s, the 'Forties of its subtitle. Wharton, in her sixties, was looking back at the New York of her grandparents.

A rich father sends his son Lewis Raycie to Europe to buy safe, famous paintings for the family gallery. Instead Lewis buys daring modern Italian art that his father calls daubs. The collection gathers dust, scorned by everyone, until later generations grasp its value. Wharton uses the story to mock a city that feared new ideas. The novella opens the Old New York sequence with quiet irony.
wharton-new-years-day-1924:
Edith Wharton closed her Old New York sequence with New Year's Day, the novella of the 'Seventies. The four tales appeared together in 1924. This last one looks at New York society in the 1870s through a scandal everyone remembers and nobody discusses.

Lizzie Hazeldean, a beautiful widow, was once seen fleeing a hotel fire in the company of a married man. Society quietly branded her for decades. Only after her death does the narrator learn the truth: she sacrificed her reputation to save her sick husband. Wharton revisits old gossip and reverses its verdict. The novella is the most moving of the four, a study of honor hiding inside disgrace.
wharton-old-maid-1924:
Edith Wharton set The Old Maid in the New York of the 1850s, as the second of her Old New York novellas. Published in 1924, it became the best known of the four tales. Wharton drew on the strict, watchful society of her own family's generation.

Delia Ralston gives up her wild lover and marries safely. Her cousin Charlotte, the old maid of the title, secretly bears that same man's child. Delia adopts the little girl, and the two women raise her together under one roof. Years of silent rivalry follow over who is truly the girl's mother. The final scenes, on the eve of the daughter's wedding, are among the most painful Wharton ever wrote.
wharton-the-spark-1924:
Edith Wharton placed The Spark in the 1860s, the third decade of her Old New York novellas. The four tales were published together in 1924. A narrator who knew the central couple in later life tells this story as a puzzle he solves only slowly.

Hayley Delane is a rich, easygoing man whom his clever wife treats with open contempt. During the Civil War he served in the hospitals, where the poet Walt Whitman tended wounded soldiers beside him. Late in life his wife discovers the quiet heroism her husband never mentioned. That wartime spark, Wharton suggests, explains the man's patience and hidden depth. The novella is a gentle study of unnoticed goodness.
woodroffe-serpent-power-1924:
Sir John Woodroffe, a British judge in India who wrote as Arthur Avalon, brought kundalini yoga to the West in The Serpent Power. The book renders the Sanskrit Sat-cakra-nirupana, a text on the six centers of the body, with rich commentary. Its English form here is that of 1924.

The serpent power sleeps at the base of the spine, the text says, and yoga wakes her to rise through each center. Woodroffe explains the rite, the signs, and the physiology of the subtle body. His work gave Tantric practice a learned Western voice. The book opened a path that yoga study still walks.
woolf-mr-bennett-mrs-brown-1924:
Woolf's famous lecture-essay began as a talk to the Heretics society at Cambridge in 1924 and was printed the same year. It is modernism's declaration of independence from the Edwardian novelists who came before.

Woolf imagines Mrs. Brown, an old lady in a train carriage, as the human character every novelist must catch. Writers like Arnold Bennett, she argues, pile up houses and incomes and miss the woman herself. Her most quoted line claims that on or about December 1910 human character changed. The essay is witty, unfair, and decisive: after it, the old realism had to answer for itself.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol24:
Liverpool printed Volume XXIV of the Journal of Discourses in 1884, as pressure on the church over plural marriage kept rising. Senior speakers preach doctrine and endurance in these shorthand-preserved talks. Their words reached Saints across the world who would never hear a sermon in Utah.

The volume's value lies in its plainness: teaching as it was given, week by week, to a people under strain. Themes from the earliest volumes return, now carried by a later generation of leaders. Volume XXIV keeps the running record intact near the end of the twenty-six-volume whole.
zamyatin-we-1924:
Citizens are numbers in the glass-walled One State, and engineer D-503 keeps the diary that becomes Yevgeny Zamyatin's We, in Gregory Zilboorg's 1924 English translation. His orderly world of timetables and transparent walls cracks when love and an unruly soul enter his life. The novel effectively invented the modern dystopia.

Banned in Zamyatin's Russia, We reached print abroad and shaped the century's darkest fiction. Orwell's 1984 and Huxley's Brave New World both descend from its design, as their century admitted. Zamyatin writes in feverish, mathematical images that match his hero's cracking mind. The book remains startlingly prophetic about surveillance, conformity, and managed happiness. Few novels of the 1900s cast a longer shadow forward.
